search.t: 1 Chapter 1 What is innovation? In this chapter we examine the concept of innovation as defined by four elements drawn from the reference definitions: novelty, implementation, adoption and value. Our aim is to establish a shared language that distinguishes innovation from creativity, invention and improvement, and that delimits its types and degrees, since agreeing on the concept is a precondition for managing it.

Opening case: the annual planning meeting (composite case) At a meeting to prepare an organization’s annual plan, each department was asked to present its “innovative initiatives.” Human Resources presented an electronic leave-request form to replace the paper one; IT presented a project to pilot an AI assistant to answer enquiries; Services proposed an ideas competition for staff; and Quality showed how it had cut request processing time from ten days to six by reordering the steps of the procedure. The meeting ended with a list of initiatives, all labeled “innovation,” without anyone asking the essential question: which of these is innovation in the strict sense? Which is an operational improvement that simply needs to be done well? Which is an activity that prepares the ground for innovation without being innovation itself? And what does this distinction imply for how each should be managed? This scene has many counterparts in organizations, even if the details differ. Some of these initiatives may be of high value, but without a shared definition the organization ends up managing initiatives of very different kinds in the same way: a highly uncertain initiative is asked for a detailed implementation plan, an improvement whose solution is already known is treated as a bet that needs experimentation, and a motivational activity is counted as an innovation achievement before any of its outputs has become reality. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Define innovation in practical terms that bring together its four elements, and compare its main reference definitions. Determine the degree of novelty of an initiative: new to the organization, new to the sector, or new to the world. Distinguish innovation from creativity, invention, improvement, transformation and entrepreneurship. Classify an initiative by type and degree, and infer the management approach that suits it. Explain the eight principles of innovation management in the international ISO 56000 series of standards. Identify inaccurate notions of innovation in an organization’s discourse and practice.

search.s: 1.1 The need for a shared definition
search.t: Attention to definition may look like an academic concern, but in innovation management it is a practical decision with direct consequences: the definition an organization adopts, explicitly or implicitly, determines what it funds, what it measures and what it rewards. Organizations usually fall into one of two opposite errors. The first error: defining too broadly. When every change is called innovation, it becomes impossible to distinguish initiatives that require exploration, experimentation and learning from improvements that can be managed with quality and continuous-improvement tools. The result is reports full of “innovative” initiatives while what the organization delivers to the people it serves stays much the same. Blank called this phenomenon “innovation theater”: activities that imitate innovation in appearance, such as workshops, competitions and labs, without changing products, services or ways of working ( Blank, 2019 ) . The second error: defining too narrowly. When innovation is restricted to inventions, advanced technologies and patents, wide opportunities are neglected in services, procedures, the beneficiary experience, the operating model and the relationships between organizational units. Many of the highest-impact innovations in government and service organizations rested on rethinking how the service is delivered and needed no new technology at all. A good definition avoids both errors: broad enough to include every area where value is created, and precise enough to distinguish innovation from what it is not.

The modern economic use of the concept of innovation goes back to Joseph Schumpeter, who held that economic development comes from carrying out “new combinations” of resources and knowledge, and identified five forms: introducing a new good or a new quality of an existing good, introducing a new method of production, opening a new market, securing a new source of raw materials, and reorganizing an industry ( Schumpeter, 1934 ) . Two points in this early view deserve attention: innovation goes beyond the product to methods, markets and organization, and it is tied to implementation rather than completed by discovery alone. Later definitions built on this foundation. Here we look at three of them, as they are the most widely used in public policy, standards and measurement tools. The Oslo Manual The Oslo Manual, published by the OECD and Eurostat, is the international reference for measuring innovation in national surveys. Its fourth edition defines an innovation as a new or improved product or process (or combination thereof) that differs significantly from the unit’s previous products or processes and that has been made available to potential users (product) or brought into use by the unit (process) ( OECD/Eurostat, 2018 ) . The decisive condition in this definition is implementation : an idea that never left the document, a prototype that was never launched, or a system that was purchased but never switched on is not an innovation by the Oslo standard, however novel it is. The Manual adds a second condition, “significant difference,” so that a routine minor adjustment does not count as innovation. The international ISO 56000 series The International Organization for Standardization defines innovation as a new or changed entity that realizes or redistributes value ( ISO, 2025 ) . The notion of an entity here is deliberately broad: it may be a product, a service, a process, a model or a method. The definition places value at its center, since novelty is not enough unless it brings benefit, whether financial, social, environmental or otherwise. The phrase “redistributes” allows the inclusion of innovations that change who benefits from value without necessarily increasing its total, as when a service reaches a group that was previously excluded from it. Innovation as what is perceived as new In the literature on the diffusion of innovations, Rogers defined an innovation as an idea, practice or object that is perceived as new by an individual or other unit of adoption ( Rogers, 2003 ) . Damanpour’s definition of organizational innovation is close to this: the adoption of an idea or behavior that is new to the adopting organization ( Damanpour, 1991 ) . The value of this perspective is that it shifts the question from “is this new to the world?” to “is it new in this context, and does it require the people in it to change what they are used to?.” Table 1.1 Comparison of reference definitions of innovation Source Core of the definition Element it highlights Management implication Schumpeter (1934) Carrying out new combinations of resources and knowledge Breadth of types; implementation Innovation may occur in the market or the organization as well as the product Oslo Manual (2018) A new or significantly improved product or process, made available or brought into use Actual implementation An idea or prototype does not count as innovation until it reaches use ISO 56000 (2025) A new or changed entity that realizes or redistributes value Value The first question about any initiative: what value is expected, and for whom? Rogers (2003) An idea, practice or object perceived as new by those who adopt it Relative novelty; adoption A solution known elsewhere may be an innovation in this context, and adoption must be managed The working definition used in this book From these definitions we derive a working definition that we use in the chapters that follow: Definition used in this book Innovation is a new or significantly improved applicati

A recurring question in management discussions is whether applying a solution that already exists elsewhere counts as innovation. The answer on which the measurement literature agrees is that novelty is measured relative to a reference unit, and the Oslo Manual distinguishes three degrees ( OECD/Eurostat, 2018 ) : New to the organization New to the sector or market New to the world New to the organization: already applied in other organizations, but new to this one. This is the broadest and most common degree, and often the quickest to show results because the solution has been tested in another context. New to the sector or market: not previously applied in the sector, geographical area or market in which the organization operates. New to the world: not previously applied anywhere; the rarest and the riskiest. Figure 1.2 Degrees of novelty: every innovation new to the world is necessarily new to the market and to the organization, but not the reverse. Two practical consequences follow from this distinction: First, transferring a successful solution from one context to another can be a genuine innovation, provided it requires meaningful adaptation and change in the adopting organization. Second, the degree of novelty affects how the initiative should be managed. A solution new only to the organization can draw on others’ experience, and its uncertainty lies mainly in fit, adaptation and adoption. A solution new to the world is uncertain in almost every respect: whether it works, whether it is needed, and what it will cost. Example When a government agency adopts an appointment-booking system that other agencies introduced before it, it invents nothing new. But it may need to redistribute staff across time slots, change how walk-in visitors are received, and replace performance indicators that counted daily transactions. These changes are what make the application an innovation at the level of the organization, and they are also what determines its success.

In general usage the term innovation is used as a synonym for several related concepts. Distinguishing between them matters, because each has its own management logic, even if they overlap in practice. Creativity Is the idea original and appropriate? Generating new and useful ideas. A main source of innovation, but no guarantee of implementation. Invention Has new knowledge or technology been produced? May remain a scientific achievement without use, or may become an innovation. Innovation Has something new been implemented, adopted and created value? The focus of this book. It draws on the neighboring concepts and differs from them. Improvement Has the performance of what exists increased? May rise to innovation if the difference is substantial, or remain routine development. Transformation Has the whole model changed? Broader than a single initiative; requires a portfolio of innovations and changes. Figure 1.3 Innovation and its neighboring concepts, with the question that distinguishes each. Creativity and innovation Researchers in the psychology of creativity agree that a creative product combines originality and appropriateness: it is new and unusual, and useful or suited to a given purpose ( Amabile, 1996; Runco & Jaeger, 2012 ) . Creativity in this sense is a main source of innovation, but there is a wide gap between them: a creative idea may stay in its author’s head or in the minutes of a meeting, whereas innovation requires what creativity does not: resources, organization, experimentation, decisions and adoption. Rhodes proposed early on that creativity be viewed from four interrelated aspects: the creative person , with their abilities and motivation; the process by which ideas are generated and developed; the surrounding press or environment, with the pressures it imposes and the opportunities it offers; and the product in which creativity is embodied ( Rhodes, 1961 ) . The value of this view for innovation management becomes clear when it is set against the common practice of focusing on the product alone, such as the number of ideas, projects or patents, without attention to the people expected to innovate, the environment in which they work, and the processes that take up their ideas. Amabile showed that organizational innovation depends on the interaction between the creativity of individuals and teams and the work environment, including its resources, management practices and organizational motivation to innovate ( Amabile, 1988 ) . We devote Chapter 7 to this relationship. Invention and innovation Invention is the production of new knowledge, technology or combination, often documented by a patent. An invention becomes an innovation when it finds use and is incorporated into a product, service or process that creates value. A well-known example: in 1975 a Kodak engineer built an early prototype of the digital camera, yet the company was very slow to make digital photography central to its business, while the same technology became, in other companies’ hands, an innovation that transformed the industry. Invention and innovation are thus two overlapping circles: an invention may remain confined to the laboratory, and many innovations, especially in services and business models, involve no new technology at all. Improvement and innovation Improvement raises the performance of what already exists: shortening the time a procedure takes, removing an unnecessary step, or raising the quality of a service. Improvement and innovation lie on a continuum. An improvement rises to innovation when it differs substantially from previous practice, is brought into use and creates value. It remains operational development when it is a limited adjustment whose method is already known. The most useful criterion for telling them apart is the degree of uncertainty , which says more than the size of the change. If the solution is known, the cause understood and what is required is disciplined execution, continuous-improvement tools

Innovation can occur in any element that contributes to creating or delivering value. The literature offers several classifications of its types; we present two that complement each other. The Oslo Manual classification The Oslo Manual groups innovation into two main types: product innovation , whether a good or a service, and business process innovation , which it subdivides into six functions ( OECD/Eurostat, 2018 ) . Product innovation What the organization offers to the people it serves Goods New or improved tangible products. Services New or improved services in their features, ease of use or quality. Business process innovation How the organization works Production and delivery Methods of producing goods or delivering services. Distribution and logistics Logistics services and delivery. Marketing and sales Channels, pricing and promotion. Information and communication Data and technology systems. Administration and management Structures, roles and decision-making methods. Product and process development The way of innovating itself. Figure 1.4 Types of innovation according to the Oslo Manual (2018). Source: adapted from OECD/Eurostat (2018) . Note that in this classification “product and process development” is itself a type of innovation: an organization that improves the way it explores opportunities and tests solutions is innovating in its very capacity to innovate, which is the subject of Part Two of the book. The four Ps of Tidd and Bessant Tidd and Bessant suggest looking at “innovation space” through four dimensions: product , what the organization offers; process , the way it is produced and delivered; position , the context in which it is offered and to whom; and paradigm , the underlying mental model of what the organization does ( Tidd & Bessant, 2021 ) . The last two dimensions are useful because they draw attention to innovations that change neither the product nor the process, such as offering an existing service to a new group, or redefining what the organization provides: a product, an outcome, or an integrated solution. In Practice Map your organization’s list of initiatives onto these two classifications. If the initiatives cluster in a single cell, such as technology or product, your organization’s view of innovation is narrower than the opportunities open to it. The largest opportunities often lie in the neglected areas: structure, networks, channels and the way decisions are made. These types are complementary: an influential solution may combine a change in service, process, technology and operating model at the same time. Technology in particular is one enabler among others, and it enters into innovation when it substantially changes value, experience or performance; digitizing a flawed procedure may speed up the problem rather than solve it.

Innovations differ in the amount of change they bring. The literature uses several classifications of these degrees, each with a different point of view. Core, adjacent and transformational innovation Incremental innovation builds on a known product, service, capability or group of beneficiaries, so its uncertainty is relatively low. Adjacent innovation takes an existing capability to a new group or market, or adds a new capability to a familiar field. Radical or transformational innovation changes the underlying assumptions, or offers substantially different value and a different model ( Nagji & Tuff, 2012 ) . These degrees describe the extent of change and the uncertainty that comes with it, and each has its place and value: successive improvements may accumulate into a large effect, and a radical idea may prove unsuitable or impossible to adopt. What matters is that the organization identifies the degree of uncertainty, the risks and the capabilities each initiative entails, and manages it accordingly. We return to this distribution when we discuss strategy and portfolio management in Chapters 4 and 10. Components and architecture Henderson and Clark observed that the binary classification (incremental/radical) hides two important types of innovation, because every product or service consists of components and an architecture that links them. Crossing these two dimensions gives four types ( Henderson & Clark, 1990 ) : Core concepts reinforced Core concepts overturned Linkages unchanged Incremental Improving components within the same architecture, such as making one step of an existing procedure more efficient. Modular Replacing a component with a new technology or method without changing the architecture, such as an e-signature instead of a paper one. Linkages changed Architectural Linking known components in a new way, such as combining scattered services into a single journey. Radical New concepts and new linkages together, such as an unprecedented service model. Adapted from Henderson & Clark (1990) ; examples by the author. Figure 1.5 The innovation matrix by components and architecture. Architectural innovation is particularly important in service and government organizations, because many service problems stem from how the components are linked rather than from their weakness. Each department may do its work efficiently while the problem lies in how they connect: hand-offs between units, repeated requests for the same information, and fragmented ownership of the journey. Henderson and Clark showed that this type is especially challenging for established organizations, because it looks limited on the surface while requiring knowledge of the architecture of the whole system, knowledge that is usually embedded in structures and habitual communication channels. Sustaining and disruptive innovation Christensen distinguished between sustaining innovation , which improves product performance on the dimensions that existing customers value, and disruptive innovation , which often starts with lower performance on those dimensions but is simpler, cheaper or more accessible, attracts neglected or new groups, and then improves until it competes with the prevailing solutions ( Christensen, 1997 ) . The “dilemma” of successful organizations is that their very good practices, such as listening to their best customers and investing in the most profitable opportunities, lead them to ignore this type until it is too late.

search.s: 1.7 Innovation in the public and nonprofit sectors
search.t: The innovation literature grew up in the context of firms and markets and carried many of their assumptions, such as competition, profit and a customer free to choose. Yet innovation in government bodies and nonprofit organizations is just as important, and may be more so, because its effects reach large groups of beneficiaries who usually have no alternative to the service. Mulgan and Albury defined successful public-sector innovation as the creation and implementation of new processes, products, services and methods of delivery that result in significant improvements in outcomes, efficiency, effectiveness or quality ( Mulgan & Albury, 2003 ) . Value in this context is what Moore called “public value”: what society and its members value, which is broader than financial return ( Moore, 1995 ) . Table 1.3 How innovation differs between the two sectors Dimension Firms Public agencies and nonprofits Measure of value Return, market share and customer satisfaction Social outcomes, equity of access, trust and efficiency Driver of innovation Competition and growth National priorities, beneficiaries’ expectations, limited resources and crises Beneficiary A customer who chooses and pays A beneficiary who may have no alternative and may differ from the funder Risk-taking Acceptable within the expected return More sensitive, owing to public accountability and the effect of errors on trust Diffusion Innovation is a competitive advantage to be protected Innovation should preferably be shared across bodies and scaled One consequence of these differences is that corporate tools need adapting before they are carried over to the public sector; return on investment alone, for instance, cannot adequately assess an initiative that aims to bring a service to an underserved group. In this book we use the term “beneficiary” to cover the customer, the citizen and the internal user, and the term “value” to cover both economic and public value.

If innovation is the outcome, innovation management is the set of practices and capabilities that make that outcome possible and repeatable. It includes directing opportunities, ideas and initiatives, and managing their flow from the front end of innovation , where needs are explored and ideas generated, to implementation and the realization of value. The international ISO 56000 series rests on eight principles that distill accumulated experience in the field ( ISO, 2025; Fernandez & Swart, 2025 ) ; we present them here because they sketch a concise map of the book’s topics. Realization of value Realization of value The goal is value realized; the number of ideas and activities is an intermediate indicator. Chapters 16, 17 Future-focused leaders Future-focused leaders Leadership that combines managing the present with exploring the future. Chapter 3 Strategic direction Strategic direction Innovation directed by clear goals and stated priorities. Chapter 4 Culture Culture Values and behaviors that combine creativity with disciplined execution. Chapters 7, 8 Exploiting insights Exploiting insights Drawing on diverse sources of knowledge inside and outside the organization. Chapters 11, 18 Managing uncertainty Managing uncertainty Dealing with risk through learning and calculated experimentation. Chapter 14 Adaptability Adaptability Adjusting structures and processes in response to change. Chapters 6, 10 Systems approach Systems approach Viewing innovation as a system of interrelated elements. Chapter 5 Figure 1.6 The eight principles of innovation management in the ISO 56000 series, and the chapters of this book that address each. These principles stand above any particular tool, such as design thinking or hackathons. Tools change; the principles determine when a tool is useful and when it becomes a formality.

We close the conceptual part of the chapter with five inaccurate notions that recur in how organizations talk about innovation. Each leads to specific management decisions, so correcting them goes beyond precision of wording to correcting practice. Innovation starts with ideas The more accurate starting point is a need, problem, opportunity or change that calls for a response; the idea comes later as a hypothesis for a solution. An organization that starts by collecting ideas without direction receives a large number of scattered proposals that are hard to evaluate, and few of them ever reach implementation. Chapter 11 discusses this in detail. Innovation is technology Technology is an important enabler, but many of the highest-impact innovations lie in services, procedures, business models and structures. Large technology projects have failed to deliver value because they were built for a problem that was not sufficiently understood. Innovation is for creative people only An organization needs people who spot problems, analyze evidence, design experiments, implement, sponsor and bring operational expertise. The person not known for a wealth of ideas may be the one who makes an idea workable. Having a lab or platform proves innovative capacity Labs, platforms and awards are tools, and they may become part of innovation theater if they are not linked to priorities, resources, decisions and an operating owner, or if they remain isolated from the daily work of units and their people. The test of innovative capacity is an organized flow of opportunities, learning from experiments, evidence-based decisions and results achieved. Launch is the end of the road Launch proves that a new application exists; innovation is proven only after it has been adopted and its effect realized. An organization that is content to celebrate the launch and then move on usually loses the hardest and most important part of the journey.

search.s: Applied cases: is this initiative an innovation?
search.t: In this section we return to the initiatives in the opening case and apply the four elements to them. The cases are illustrative, and their details have been shaped to show the method of analysis. The electronic leave-request form Operational improvement ? Novelty ✓ Implementation ✓ Adoption ? Value The electronic form replaced the paper one, and staff used it because it was the only route available. But the approval path stayed the same, with five successive sign-offs, and the average completion time did not change. The novelty here is formal, and the value is limited to saving paper. When would it rise to innovation? If the path itself were redesigned, for example by approving short leave automatically under clear rules and requiring a single approval in other cases, and a substantial reduction in time and workload were then measured. The enquiries assistant A potential innovation, not yet complete ✓ Novelty ? Implementation ? Adoption ? Value Novelty is present at the level of the organization, but the initiative is still an idea: the reasons for the high volume of enquiries have not been studied, nor the quality of the information the assistant would rely on, nor who would be responsible for updating it. Calling it an innovation is therefore premature. When would it rise to innovation? If it began by understanding why the enquiries arise, was then piloted on a limited scale, the reduction in repeated enquiries and user satisfaction were measured, and an owner were named to keep the content up to date. The staff ideas competition An activity that prepares for innovation — Novelty — Implementation — Adoption — Value The competition is a mechanism for capturing opportunities; it sits upstream of innovation, and its value depends on what follows it: its link to priority challenges, the time and resources available to evaluate proposals and test the best of them, and whether participants receive a response to their proposals. When would it be worthwhile? If it were framed around a specific challenge, if what would follow from selecting ideas were announced in advance, and if a modest budget were set aside to test some of them. Reducing request processing time An innovation at the level of the organization ✓ Novelty ✓ Implementation ✓ Adoption ✓ Value Quality reordered the steps of the procedure after finding that requests waited for days between two units without being processed. The two review stages were merged and a shared view of request status was created. Processing time fell from ten days to six, and the reduction held six months later. This is an architectural innovation new to the organization, even though it used no new technology. What would strengthen the judgment? Comparing the time against a documented baseline, and checking that errors have not simply moved to a later stage. What the cases show The initiative whose name suggests innovation may be the furthest from it, and the initiative that looks modest may be the closest. Classifying an initiative determines how it is managed: improvement is managed through disciplined execution, a potential innovation through experimentation and staged decisions, and a preparatory activity through clarity about what will follow from it.

search.s: Chapter Tool: The Initiative Classification Card
search.t: Use this card to establish the nature of any initiative before deciding on it, at the proposal stage or when reviewing existing initiatives. Its purpose is to put the right questions to you; it is a diagnostic tool rather than a scoring scale. Initiative Classification Card Takes about twenty minutes to complete 1 What is the need or opportunity? Describe it without mentioning the solution. What evidence shows it matters? Strong evidence Initial evidence Impression 2 What is the degree of novelty? New to whom? To the organization To the sector To the world No meaningful novelty 3 What type of innovation? More than one type may apply. Product or service Process User experience Business model Organization and management Technology 4 What is the degree of uncertainty? Is the solution known? Is the cause understood? Is adoption assured? Low: improvement Medium: incremental or adjacent innovation High: radical innovation 5 What value is expected, and for whom? Which indicator will change if the initiative succeeds? Beneficiary Employee Organization Society 6 Who will adopt and operate the solution? A specific, named unit. Named and involved Named but not involved Not named 7 What management approach fits? The conclusion from the answers above. Execution and continuous improvement Innovation path with experiments and stages Initial exploration before deciding Limited novelty and low uncertainty The initiative is an improvement: carry it out well, without loading it with the language and tools of innovation. Real novelty and medium or high uncertainty The initiative needs an innovation path: stated assumptions, experiments, staged funding and decision gates. Unclear need The first step is a short exploration to understand the problem before committing to any solution.

Innovation is a new or significantly improved application that addresses a need, is adopted by users and creates observable value. The absence of any of the four elements is enough to keep an initiative short of innovation. The reference definitions (Schumpeter, the Oslo Manual, ISO 56000 and Rogers) agree that novelty alone is not enough, and differ in the aspect they emphasize. Novelty is relative: to the organization, the sector or the world. Transferring solutions between contexts is genuine innovation when it requires adaptation and change. Creativity produces ideas, invention produces knowledge or technology, improvement raises the performance of what exists, and transformation changes the whole model. The practical criterion for distinguishing improvement from innovation is the degree of uncertainty. A broader view of creativity takes in the person, the process and the environment alongside the product, aspects on which an organization’s capacity to innovate depends. Innovation occurs in products and services, in business processes, and in position and paradigm. Technology is one enabler, not a synonym for innovation. Innovations range from incremental to radical; architectural innovation matters particularly in service organizations; and each degree has a management approach that suits it. Public-sector innovation has a different logic of value, risk and diffusion, and requires adapted tools. Innovation management rests on eight principles, headed by the realization of value and completed by viewing innovation as a system. Key Terms Innovation Innovation A new or significantly improved application, adopted by users, that creates value. Innovation management Innovation management The practices and capabilities that direct the flow of opportunities, ideas and initiatives, and manage experimentation, decisions and resources through to the realization of value. Front end of innovation Front end of innovation The stage before a project is formally launched, including discovering needs, exploring opportunities and generating ideas. Degree of novelty Degree of novelty The novelty of a solution relative to a reference unit: the organization, the market or the world. Business process innovation Business process innovation A new or improved change in how the organization performs one of its functions. Incremental innovation Incremental innovation Innovation that builds on an existing offer or capability without changing its basic nature. Architectural innovation Architectural innovation Linking known components in a new way. Disruptive innovation Disruptive innovation Innovation that starts at the low end of a market or in a new market, then improves until it competes with prevailing solutions. Intrapreneurship Intrapreneurship Entrepreneurial behavior by individuals within an established organization to lead a new innovation. Public value Public value What society and its members value in the outcomes of public services and policies. Innovation theater Innovation theater Activities that imitate innovation in appearance without changing products, services or ways of working. 2 Chapter 2 Why innovation now? In this chapter we trace the shifts that have moved innovation from a seasonal activity to a permanent organizational need: accelerating change, artificial intelligence and what it means for the value of people, and the changing skills that work demands. We then read these shifts in the Saudi context and show that investment in the inputs of innovation pays off only to the extent that an organization is able to turn them into results.

Opening case: an innovation center (composite case) Three years ago, a public agency set up an innovation center. It gave the center a budget and a fully equipped space, launched a platform to collect employees’ ideas, and ran a series of hackathons. Its annual report carried striking figures: hundreds of ideas, dozens of participating teams, prizes for the winners. Then an internal review asked a simple question: how many of these ideas are in actual use today? The answer: very few. The agency had every input in place: funding, space, a platform and enthusiasm. The fault lay in the distance between inputs and results. This leads us to two linked questions in this chapter: why has innovation become a permanent organizational need under present conditions, and why does investment in its inputs fall short of achieving it on its own? Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain how operational discipline and innovation discipline complement each other, and when work calls for each. Distinguish between an organization’s external and internal realities, and use both to read the need for innovation. Identify the main forces reshaping work, including artificial intelligence and changing skills. Interpret Saudi Arabia’s position in international innovation indices, and explain the gap between innovation inputs and outputs. Weigh the risks of innovating against the risks of not innovating, and distinguish situations in which innovation is the appropriate response from those in which it is not.

search.s: 2.1 From the logic of stability to the capacity for renewal
search.t: Traditional management had good reason to care about discipline and standardization. In the early twentieth century, the principles of scientific management, with their division of labor, standardized procedures and performance measurement, delivered enormous gains in productivity and quality ( Taylor, 1911 ) . This logic remains essential for any work that must be done correctly every time, such as dispensing medicine, paying salaries or processing regulatory transactions. Yet this logic was designed for problems whose causes and solutions are known, where the challenge lies in skilled execution. Its limits show when it is applied to shifting opportunities and uncertain paths, where the need is not fully understood and the link between intervention and outcome is unclear. In such situations, insisting on a detailed plan drawn up in advance becomes a source of error, because the plan rests on assumptions that have not been tested. The shift required, therefore, is to hold two kinds of discipline that work together: operational discipline , which protects quality and reliability, and innovation discipline , which guides exploration, experimentation and learning. The management literature calls the combination of the two organizational ambidexterity, which we discuss in detail in Chapter 3. Operational discipline For what must work every time Nature of the problem Causes and solutions known Purpose Reliability and reduced variation Management tool Detailed plan, standards and control Meaning of deviation A fault to be corrected Success criterion Adherence to plan and quality Complementary, not conflicting Innovation discipline For what is not yet known Nature of the problem Not fully understood; solution unknown Purpose Learning and reducing uncertainty Management tool Hypotheses, experiments and staged decisions Meaning of deviation New information to be put to use Success criterion Quality of evidence and speed of learning, then value Figure 2.1 How operational discipline and innovation discipline complement each other. One of the most common management errors is to apply one discipline where the other belongs. An exploratory initiative is judged by the standards of an operational project and is stifled before it can learn, or sensitive operational work is handled with the logic of experimentation and the service is exposed to needless errors. The first management question in any situation is therefore: do we know the solution and need to implement it, or do we first need to discover it?

The value of any organization rests on a set of assumptions about the world around it: who its beneficiaries are, what they need, what alternatives are open to them, and what technology and regulation allow. The conditions surrounding the organization, and the ways they change, make up its external realities . These include shifts in markets, society, legislation and technology, and the points where they intersect, as when a social shift in young people’s expectations meets a technological shift in the ways services are accessed. The danger is that external realities usually change gradually and quietly, while the organization carries on working on assumptions that held true in the past. As the changes accumulate, the organization may find that the foundation on which its value was built is no longer there. The pace of this change is quickening. A study of corporate longevity among firms in the S&P 500 index of large US companies tracked the average tenure of a company in the index and found that it fell from about thirty-three years in 1964 to about twenty-four in 2016; the authors projected that it would approach twelve years by 2027, and linked the decline to shifts in technology and business models and to waves of mergers and acquisitions ( Anthony et al., 2018 ) . The phenomenon resembles what Christensen described as disruptive innovation, in which a new solution starts out simple at the margins of the market and then improves until it displaces leaders that served their existing customers well ( Christensen, 1997 ) . Government organizations are less exposed to being pushed out of the market, but they face the mirror image of this phenomenon: a widening gap between what they provide and what beneficiaries expect, having grown used to fast digital services in their daily lives. Set against these are the organization’s internal realities : its current state in terms of leadership, culture, structures, roles, internal relationships and the skills of its people. If external realities determine what the organization should innovate, internal realities determine its capacity to deliver it. The distinction is close to the familiar SWOT analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats: opportunities and threats belong to external realities, strengths and weaknesses to internal realities. The difference is that an innovation perspective treats strengths and weaknesses as things that can be built and developed. Teece described an organization’s capacity for renewal in a changing environment as dynamic capabilities , and identified three components: sensing , which means detecting opportunities and threats and listening to beneficiaries before changes force themselves on the organization; seizing , which means mobilizing resources and making decisions to capture the opportunity; and reconfiguring , which means continually adapting structures, assets and practices ( Teece, 2007 ) . Sensing without seizing produces reports that no one acts on; seizing without sensing produces activity in the wrong direction. Building these capabilities is a responsibility shared across every level of the organization. Sensing often happens at the organization’s edges, with the employee closest to the beneficiary; seizing requires leadership decisions and resources; and reconfiguring calls for the participation of all levels. The organization therefore needs a vision that makes renewal part of its purpose, and an environment that encourages initiative at every level, so that responding to change becomes an organizational habit. As change accelerates, building this capability becomes a condition for survival and excellence, and a priority that takes precedence over many operational ones. In Practice Ask yourself: when did your organization last learn of a change in its beneficiaries’ needs, and how? Innovation management has gained importance because the sources of value and competition, and the very nature of work, are changing. The most influential forces can be summed up in five: 1 Accelerating technology Artificial intelligence above all, with the possibilities and new business models it opens up and the risks it carries. 2 Rising beneficiary expectations An easy experience in one sector raises the bar of expectations in others. 3 Blurring sector boundaries Competition comes from a platform, a partner or a distribution model, as well as from similar organizations. 4 Changing skills The relative value of routine tasks declines, while judgment, creativity and learning matter more. 5 Interconnected problems No single unit can understand the whole journey or address it alone. Figure 2.2 Five forces reshaping work. The fourth force is evident in the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025, in which employers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030. Notably, the list of skills expected to grow in importance goes beyond technical skills such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to include creative thinking, resilience and flexibility, curiosity and lifelong learning, and leadership and social influence ( World Economic Forum, 2025 ) . This finding bears directly on innovation management: the capacity to innovate depends on people who are ready to question, experiment and learn, and on a work environment that nurtures these abilities, as much as it depends on technology and structures.

search.s: 2.4 Artificial intelligence and the value of people
search.t: Generative artificial intelligence is changing how much a single person can accomplish. In a field experiment with 791 employees at Procter & Gamble working on real product-development challenges, an individual working with AI performed on a par with a team working without it. Those using AI also produced solutions that were better balanced between technical and commercial considerations, whatever their specialty, as though the tool had softened the effect of functional silos ( Dell'Acqua et al., 2026 ) . What once required a team and a long stretch of time may now be accomplished by one person, faster and at comparable quality. The picture has another side, however. In a study of short-story writing, AI-generated ideas raised the creativity of each individual writer, with the largest gains among the less creative, but the stories became more similar to one another, so the diversity of ideas across the group declined ( Doshi & Hauser, 2024 ) . When everyone uses the same tools in the same way, their ideas converge. How the tool is used is what makes the difference. In a study of 123 university students working on entrepreneurial projects, the students followed a structured five-stage collaboration protocol that asked the tool to question their assumptions and suggest alternatives, while leaving evaluation, revision and reflection to them. Of these students, 91.9% reported a marked development in their project ideas, and many showed improvement, to varying degrees, in aspects of their strategic analysis ( Alsamani, 2026 ) . These are self-perceptions from an exploratory study, but they suggest that the tool can act as a thinking partner when collaboration with it is deliberately designed. In this sense, we argue in this book, artificial intelligence raises the value of people in the innovation system. When generating alternatives and building prototypes becomes easy and available to everyone, the sources of distinction shift to what the tool cannot produce on its own: choosing the problem worth solving, understanding the context and the beneficiaries, exercising judgment when weighing alternatives, diversity of perspectives, and the motivation to keep trying. This shift requires innovation management to revisit entrenched assumptions: team size, the division of roles, the cost of experimentation, which has fallen sharply, and the way individuals and their contributions are evaluated. The management question A more productive question than “How do we use artificial intelligence?” is “What has it made possible, and what remains for people to add?”

Innovation holds a central place in Saudi Vision 2030 as a means of diversifying the economy, raising public-sector efficiency and improving quality of life (Saudi Vision 2030, 2016 [Arabic]) . On June 30, 2022, the national aspirations and priorities for the research, development and innovation sector over the next two decades were announced. They set out four priorities: health and wellness, sustainable environment and supply of essential needs, energy and industrial leadership, and economies of the future. They also set targets for annual spending on the sector to reach 2.5% of gross domestic product by 2040 and for the sector to contribute some SAR 60 billion to GDP, with the Research, Development and Innovation Authority (RDIA) serving as the sector’s enabler and regulator (Saudi Press Agency, 2022 [Arabic]) . These efforts are reflected in the Global Innovation Index published by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO): Saudi Arabia rose from 66th place in 2020 and 2021 to 42nd out of 139 economies in 2026 ( World Intellectual Property Organization [WIPO], 2026 ) . 40 50 60 70 66 66 51 48 47 46 42 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Innovation input rank, 2026 30 Institutions, human capital and research, infrastructure, and market and business sophistication. Innovation output rank, 2026 62 Knowledge and technology outputs, and creative outputs. Figure 2.3 Saudi Arabia’s rank in the Global Innovation Index (vertical axis: rank; higher on the chart is better), and the gap between input and output ranks in 2026. Bar length reflects the strength of the rank. Source: WIPO (2025, 2026) . A careful reading of the index, however, goes beyond the overall rank. In 2026 Saudi Arabia ranked 30th on innovation inputs and 62nd on innovation outputs, and the report notes that the country produces less innovation output than its level of investment would warrant. The picture was similar in 2025, when it ranked 31st on inputs and 61st on outputs ( WIPO, 2025, 2026 ) . Among the notable strengths the report identifies are Saudi Arabia’s first place worldwide in the use of information and communication technology and its strong position in startup financing and e-government services; among the weaknesses is its lower ranking in knowledge and technology outputs and in creative outputs. This gap matters for the subject of this book. Inputs such as funding, infrastructure, centers and programs are a necessary condition for innovation, but they do not turn into outputs automatically. The conversion happens inside organizations: in the way priorities are set, opportunities captured, ideas tested and decisions made, in how people are involved and motivated, and in how solutions are moved into operation. This is the domain of innovation management. Setting up an innovation center in a university or government agency without linking it to the daily work of departments and units, and to the way their performance is assessed, raises the inputs while the outputs remain contingent on what happens inside those units. A caution on reading indices International innovation indices are tools for comparison at the national level, and they are affected by changes in methodology and data sources from year to year. Their general trends and major gaps are what should be read, and they should be used alongside other sources when judging the performance of a particular organization.

search.s: 2.6 Relevance and risk: when is innovation the answer?
search.t: The aim of renewal is for the organization to maintain its relevance to its beneficiaries’ needs, now and in the future, which is what reconfiguring means in the dynamic capabilities framework. The difference between an organization that responds and one that reacts is that the first reads change before it is forced upon it, and so is prepared, while the second reads it after the effect has been felt, and so acts under pressure. Innovation has its risks, because it pursues what has not yet been tried. Risk management in this context is an ally of innovation: it sets the boundaries within which experimentation can proceed without unacceptable harm, and it uses methods such as limited experiments and staged funding to reduce risk. Yet not innovating is not as safe an option as it seems; an organization that stops renewing itself gradually loses its relevance. The right comparison, then, is between risks that can be managed and risks that accumulate unseen. The need for efficiency persists through all these shifts; skilled operations are what fund renewal. Some problems, moreover, need only adherence to a known standard or the application of a proven practice, and using innovation tools on them slows the solution and undermines the credibility of innovation itself. Table 2.1 Indicators that help in choosing the appropriate approach Situation Indicators Appropriate approach Execution failure The cause is known, the solution proven, and the gap lies in compliance or resources Operational management and follow-up Opportunity for improvement Performance is below standard, the causes can be analyzed, and solutions are mostly known Continuous improvement and quality tools Technically complex problem Requires specialized expertise, but can be broken down and planned Expert analysis and design Unresolved need or opportunity The solution is unknown, and there are essential assumptions about the user, the implementation or the value Innovation approach: experimentation and staged decisions A distinction drawn by Bennett and Lemoine helps with this diagnosis. They observed that describing the environment as “volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous” becomes an excuse for not planning when it is used as a blanket label for every difficulty, and that its value lies in identifying the type of challenge: volatility is met by building reserves and flexibility, uncertainty by gathering information, and complexity by restructuring and building expertise, while ambiguity , where causal relationships are unclear and there are no precedents to go by, calls for experimentation ( Bennett & Lemoine, 2014 ) . Experimentation is the core of the innovation approach, which is why innovation is the most fitting response precisely when ambiguity defines the situation, and why other approaches take precedence for the remaining difficulties. Organizational maturity shows in diagnosing the situation and choosing the approach that creates value with no more complexity than necessary.

The contemporary organization needs two complementary disciplines: operational discipline for what must work every time, and innovation discipline for what is not yet known. The common error is to apply one where the other belongs. External realities determine what an organization should innovate; internal realities determine its capacity to deliver it. The organization needs all three dynamic capabilities: sensing, seizing and reconfiguring. Five forces are reshaping work: accelerating technology, rising expectations, blurring sector boundaries, changing skills and interconnected problems. Among the skills growing in importance are creative thinking, flexibility and curiosity. Artificial intelligence multiplies what an individual can accomplish, yet it may reduce the diversity of ideas. The value of what people add therefore rises: choosing the problem, understanding the context, judgment, diversity of perspectives and motivation. Saudi Arabia rose in the Global Innovation Index from 66th to 42nd between 2020 and 2026, with a clear gap between its input rank (30) and output rank (62). Converting inputs into outputs is the work of innovation management inside organizations. Innovation carries risks that can be managed; not innovating carries risks that accumulate unseen. Maturity shows in diagnosing the situation and choosing the approach that suits it; experimentation is a response specific to situations of ambiguity. Key Terms External realities External realities The conditions surrounding an organization and the ways they change, in markets, society, legislation and technology. Internal realities Internal realities The organization’s current state in terms of leadership, culture, structures, roles and skills. VUCA VUCA A description of the environment in four dimensions: volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity. Dynamic capabilities Dynamic capabilities An organization’s capacity to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure its resources and practices in a changing environment. Relevance Relevance The continued fit between what an organization offers and the needs of its beneficiaries, now and in the future. Innovation inputs / outputs Innovation inputs / outputs Inputs are the resources and conditions that enable innovation; outputs are its knowledge, technological and creative results. 3 Chapter 3 Leading innovation In this chapter we examine the role of leadership in innovation management: how leading the unknown differs from leading the known, which functions fall to the leader alone, how the leader balances running the present with exploring the future, and why employees take the meaning of innovation from their leader’s everyday behavior more than from what the leader says.

Opening case: a new director (composite case) At his first meeting with staff, a new director called for “bold ideas” and promised to back them. A few weeks later, an employee presented an idea for simplifying a procedure carried out every day, which she had tried on a small scale with two colleagues. The first question put to her in the meeting was: “Who authorized you to do that?” The idea was not rejected, its results were not discussed, and the meeting moved on to the next item. No one in the room tried anything similar again. From a single incident they had learned a lesson that the opening speech could not erase: taking initiative is a personal risk. This is the heart of what we address in this chapter: in innovation, leadership is measured by what people learn from everyday reactions more than by what is announced. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Distinguish between leading known work and leading work surrounded by uncertainty. Explain the effect of people-centered leadership on motivation and innovation in light of its theoretical foundations. Identify the core leadership functions in innovation management. Explain the concept of organizational ambidexterity and the ways of balancing exploitation and exploration. Recognize the leadership behaviors that encourage innovation and those that unintentionally stifle it. Match the leadership decision and the type of evidence required to the stage of the initiative.

Traditional management is built on achieving known goals with defined resources, schedules and procedures, and the leader is held accountable for adherence to the plan. Innovation, by contrast, deals with situations in which aspects of the problem, the solution, adoption or feasibility are still unknown. The leader therefore asks of an innovation team what suits the nature of its work: clear assumptions, sound experiments, fast learning and disciplined decisions, in place of the precision expected of an operational project whose requirements are fully defined. The leadership question shifts accordingly, from “Can we guarantee the initiative will succeed?” to “What do we need to know before we increase our commitment?” The leader’s role here is to keep ignorance from being turned into false confidence, to spread investment across stages, and to tie each stage to the evidence appropriate to it.

Innovation remains a leadership responsibility even when a specialized department takes it on. An organizational innovation initiative begins with an explicit mandate from top leadership that gives it legitimacy, and with a sustained commitment to support those who run it and to protect them when their initiatives collide with the status quo. This is why the international standard for innovation management systems places it first among the requirements of leadership ( International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2024 ) . The role of leadership can be summed up in seven interrelated functions: Setting direction Linking innovation to the organization’s goals, and defining areas of focus and the value expected. Granting legitimacy Declaring that exploration and experimentation are an integral part of everyday work. Providing protection Shielding disciplined experiments from premature rejection and from the standards of stable operations. Allocating resources Time, funding, expertise, and access to beneficiaries and data, scaled up as evidence accumulates. Designing decisions Clear criteria and review points for continuing, adjusting or stopping. Building learning Welcoming uncomfortable news, revisiting assumptions and sharing lessons. Enabling implementation Removing obstacles, and ensuring there is an operating unit ready to take ownership of the solution when it succeeds. Figure 3.1 The seven leadership functions in innovation management. In these functions the leader acts more as an architect of context than as the person with the best idea. The leader’s task is to design a context in which people with diverse knowledge can discover problems and build solutions, and to make sure that effort turns into decisions and value. This role faces in two directions: outward , by following external realities and securing the organization’s long-term relevance; and inward , by shaping the values, culture and structures that make innovation possible and sustainable.

An organization needs efficiency and reliability to deliver its current work, and at the same time it needs flexibility and experimentation to explore the future. March described these two activities as exploitation , refining and deepening what the organization already knows, and exploration , searching for what it does not yet know. He showed that organizations tend to favor exploitation because its returns are nearer and clearer, so that their capacity for renewal weakens over time ( March, 1991 ) . The capacity to combine the two is called organizational ambidexterity ( O'Reilly & Tushman, 2013 ) . Exploitation Exploitation Refining and deepening what exists Rewards adherence to plan and reduced variation Near and clear returns Measured by efficiency and quality Exploration Exploration Searching for new value Requires adjusting the plan and accepting unexpected results Distant and uncertain returns Measured by quality of learning, then by value When exploration is subjected to the standards of exploitation alone, the organization always chooses what is closest to the familiar Figure 3.2 Exploitation and exploration: two different logics that the organization needs together. The tension arises because the operating system rewards adherence to the plan, while exploration requires changing it. When the usual profitability or productivity criteria are applied to emerging initiatives, the organization will mostly choose ideas close to the familiar. When exploration is left without controls, it turns into scattered activity. Organizations handle this tension in one of two ways, or by combining them: structural separation , which creates separate units or budgets for exploration that report to top leadership; and contextual ambidexterity , which enables individuals and teams to divide their time between the two logics within the same job ( O'Reilly & Tushman, 2013 ) . In both cases the aim is to provide a temporary space for learning, and then to build an orderly bridge to operations.

search.s: 3.4 The leader as shaper of the environment
search.t: At the highest levels of leadership, people work for the leader more than they work because of the leader’s authority to assign tasks: because the leader values their effort, is mindful of their circumstances and trusts their ability. This kind of leadership has foundations in research that go beyond personal temperament and disposition, and they explain why it leads to deep work and loyalty, and why innovation needs it in particular. The first foundation: social exchange and the sense of support Social exchange theory holds that working relationships rest, alongside the formal contract, on an unwritten exchange of trust and care ( Blau, 1964 ) . When employees perceive that their organization and their leader value their contribution and care about their well-being, they develop a sense of obligation to reciprocate, which shows in stronger attachment to the organization, greater effort and a readiness to go beyond what is required. A broad review of research on perceived organizational support has confirmed this relationship ( Rhoades & Eisenberger, 2002 ) . Innovation is, at its core, work that goes beyond what is required: no one is obliged to expose a problem, propose an alternative or take the risk of an experiment. The second foundation: basic psychological needs Self-determination theory shows that intrinsic motivation grows when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy , the sense that one chooses what one does; competence , the sense of capability and progress; and relatedness , the sense of being valued and connected to others ( Gagné & Deci, 2005 ) . An empathetic leader meets these needs by trusting the team and giving it room, acknowledging its progress, and treating its members as partners in the work. The theory connects with what has come earlier in this book: intrinsic motivation is the foundation on which creativity stands ( Amabile, 1996 ) . The autonomy meant here is cognitive autonomy in how people think and solve problems, and it remains tied to the organization’s purposes. The leader sets out clearly the what and the why : the problem to be solved, the needs of the system the solution serves, and the constraints that must not be crossed; then leaves the how to the team. Amabile put it this way: people are more creative when they are given freedom to choose how to climb the mountain, without necessarily choosing the mountain itself ( Amabile, 1998 ) . Autonomy in this sense is consistent with the book’s starting point that innovation begins from a priority problem. The third foundation: people-centered leadership styles Transformational leadership includes a dimension called “individualized consideration,” attending to each person’s needs and supporting their growth, and a meta-analysis of study findings has shown a positive relationship between this style and employee creativity ( Koh et al., 2019 ) . Servant leadership goes further, making service to followers and attention to each one’s needs and growth an end in itself rather than merely a means of raising performance ( Eva et al., 2019 ) . A meta-analysis of 130 studies found that this style has explanatory power beyond that of transformational leadership, and that its effect operates through trust in the leader, a sense of fairness, and the quality of the leader–employee relationship ( Lee et al., 2020 ) . 1 Leader behavior Appreciation, consideration and recognition of effort, with independent room over the “how” within clear limits on the “what and why.” 2 What the employee feels Perceived support, and basic psychological needs met: autonomy, competence and relatedness. 3 What develops Intrinsic motivation, trust and a sense of obligation to reciprocate. 4 What the employee does Deep work, initiative beyond what is required, loyalty and a readiness to experiment. Few leaders declare their opposition to innovation, yet an organization can suppress it through practices that each seem reasonable on their own. Among the most common: Making innovation extra work, to be done after the full operational workload is finished. Demanding a detailed feasibility study for an idea that still rests on untested assumptions. Putting a small experiment through the same chain of approvals required to roll out a solution across the whole organization. Leaving ideas unanswered, crediting them to the wrong people, or implementing them without involving those who proposed them. Rewarding error-free operations alone, without recognizing the discovery of problems or the quality of experiments. The greatest danger lies in the message others learn from the rejection of a single idea. When employees realize that exposing problems adds to their workload, and that ideas vanish without a response, they learn to stay silent. The literature on employee voice shows that when individuals withhold their suggestions and concerns, the organization is deprived of information that may be critical ( Morrison, 2014 ) .

An executive sponsor has a real role that goes beyond having their name listed on the initiative document. The sponsor’s job is to link the initiative to strategy, to secure legitimacy and access for it, to intervene when departmental interests clash, and to ensure that there is a unit ready to adopt it. The sponsor’s tasks also include taking under their wing ideas that belong to no particular department in the existing structure, even though they may be the basis of future value. Studies have shown that innovations usually need someone to take them up and defend them against resistance, and that this role extends beyond formal authority to persuasion and coalition building ( Howell & Higgins, 1990 ) . The sponsorship rule Good sponsorship protects the team so that it can learn; it does not protect the idea from testing. If the evidence shows that the need is weak or adoption difficult, it is the sponsor’s responsibility to support adjusting or stopping the initiative.

The nature of the decision differs with the stage of the initiative, so the information a leader asks for should increase step by step as the stages progress. A detailed feasibility study at the outset of a highly novel idea may produce figures that look precise but rest on weak assumptions. It is better for the precision of decisions to develop as the evidence develops. Table 3.1 The leader’s question and the type of evidence at each stage Stage Leader’s question Sufficient evidence Opportunity Is it consistent with our priorities, and does it merit exploration? A clear description of the need, and early indications of its importance Development Have we understood the problem, and what have we learned? Stated assumptions, and results of small experiments Pilot Are the ethical, operational and regulatory risks acceptable? A pilot plan with clear limits and stopping conditions Scaling Will the solution last and retain its value at a larger scale? Evidence of adoption, actual cost, and an operating unit ready to take it on One of the most damaging forms of leadership decision for innovation is making no decision at all. An idea that is neither accepted nor rejected, and hangs between meetings, dies without anyone learning from it, and its originator learns not to try again. Not deciding is in fact a decision, but one that relieves the decision-maker of responsibility and squanders the chance to learn. In Chapter 10 we present governance mechanisms that keep initiatives from remaining in this zone.

Leading innovation is, at its core, leading the unknown: it calls for clear assumptions, sound experiments, fast learning and disciplined decisions. Leadership has seven functions in innovation management, beginning with setting direction and granting legitimacy and ending with enabling implementation. An organization needs both exploitation and exploration, and combines them through structural separation, contextual ambidexterity, or both. Employees learn the meaning of innovation from their leader’s everyday behavior, and small negative actions weigh more heavily than positive ones. Leadership that people work for rests on foundations in research: social exchange, basic psychological needs, and transformational and servant leadership. It produces the deep work and initiative that innovation needs. Management can unintentionally extinguish the spark of innovation through practices that each seem reasonable on their own; the most dangerous are those that teach people silence. Good sponsorship protects the team so that it can learn, while keeping the idea subject to testing. The precision of decisions develops as the evidence develops, and leaving an initiative undecided is the worst decision of all.
