4 Chapter 4 Innovation strategy and foresight In this chapter we examine innovation strategy as a system of choices that determines where the organization looks for value, with what degree of ambition, and by what means. We show how strategy sets out the “what and why” and entrusts the “how” to people, and how foresight supplies it with a systematic reading of the future.

Opening case: a strategic plan (composite case) One organization’s strategic plan included a goal that read: “To be an innovative and pioneering organization.” A year later, its ideas platform had received more than three hundred proposals heading in dozens of directions, from improving the parking lots to building new apps. The evaluation committee could not choose among them, because no one knew which mattered most to the organization, so it picked the ones that were most appealingly presented. Only a handful were ever implemented. There was no shortage of ideas, and those who proposed them were enthusiastic; the flaw lay in the absence of choice. “To be innovative” is a wish that never rose to the level of a strategy. It says nothing about where people should look, what the organization will decline to invest in, or the criteria by which ideas will be judged. These are the questions from which we set out toward the strategy that answers them. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Define innovation strategy as a set of interconnected choices. Derive search fields and challenge questions from the organization’s goals. Identify the components of an innovation strategy and formulate it on a single page. Balance the time horizons of innovation according to the nature of the organization. Use foresight in building and reviewing strategy.

An innovation strategy is a set of interconnected choices that determines why the organization needs innovation, where it will look for value, at what level of ambition, by what means, and how it will allocate its resources. Pisano observed that many organizations invest in innovation without a clear strategy, and so accumulate scattered initiatives that are hard to judge or weigh against one another; a strategy, he argued, is defined by the choices it commits to, and equally by those it rules out ( Pisano, 2015 ) . It follows that a strategy is not a wish list, a general statement, or a table of every proposed initiative. Its essence can be distilled into two questions used throughout the strategy literature: where to play, and how to win ( Lafley & Martin, 2013 ) . In innovation, the first refers to the arenas in which the organization looks for new value, and the second to the means by which it will get there: building internally, partnering, or acquiring a ready-made capability ( Capron & Mitchell, 2012 ) .

search.s: 4.2 From organizational strategy to search fields
search.t: Innovation strategy grows out of the organization’s own context. It starts from the organization’s overarching goals, the challenges that hold it back, and the shifts that may affect its ability to fulfill its mission. Copying fashionable innovation themes detached from these goals is a mistake. Broad goals are translated into search fields , specific opportunity areas that direct exploration, and then into challenge questions to which employees and partners can contribute. Instead of inviting everyone to propose any idea at all, exploration is steered toward questions such as: How can we make access to the service simpler for a group that current channels do not reach? How can we cut the time lost between two units? Such questions define the what and the why , and leave the solution open. Organizational goal Improving quality of life for beneficiaries From the organization’s strategic plan ↓ Search field Access to services for older adults A priority opportunity area ↓ Challenge question How can we enable older adults to complete their service without having to appear in person or rely on constant assistance? Defines the problem without imposing the solution ↓ What the strategy defines The problem, the target group, the boundaries of experimentation, and the criteria for value What is left to people How to solve it: a procedure, a channel, a partnership, or a technology Figure 4.1 From organizational goal to challenge question: strategy defines the “what and why” and leaves the “how” open. (Illustrative example) In this way, strategy aligns with what Chapter 3 presented on cognitive autonomy within boundaries. Search fields and challenge questions are the clear boundaries that give people freedom to think within them, and they make people’s contributions comparable and open to evaluation.

A good innovation strategy has six components, each answering a specific question: Table 4.1 The components of innovation strategy Component The question it answers Example wording Rationale Why do we need innovation now? Rising demand with flat resources Target outcomes What value do we want to achieve? Halve the time it takes to obtain the service Search fields Where will we look, and where will we not look for now? Three priority fields, with everything else explicitly excluded Level of ambition How do we divide our effort between the near and the distant? Most effort on improvement, with a defined share for future bets Means of delivery How will we get there? Internal development, plus partnerships with universities and startups Principles and boundaries What risks are acceptable, and what must never be sacrificed? No experiment that compromises the security of personal data Each component needs capabilities to support it, including data, expertise, funding and governance; these are the subject of the following chapters in this part.

search.s: 4.4 Level of ambition and the balance of horizons
search.t: Dividing initiatives into three time horizons offers a useful language for balancing the present against the future ( Baghai et al., 1999 ) . Horizon 1 Improving the existing Purpose Maximizing value from current services and capabilities Uncertainty Low Success criterion Efficiency, quality and satisfaction Horizon 2 Adjacent expansion Purpose Extending existing capabilities to new groups or domains Uncertainty Medium Success criterion Adoption in the new group and growth in value Horizon 3 Building the future Purpose Creating new foundations of value that may redefine the organization’s work Uncertainty High Success criterion Quality of learning first, then value Figure 4.2 The three horizons of innovation. Source: adapted from Baghai et al. (1999) . The horizons are best understood as a flexible framework for thinking, and the common allocation ratios, such as 70/20/10, as indicative estimates; the right allocation depends on the sector, the pace of change, the organization’s maturity and its acceptable level of risk. The model’s core value is that it makes investment in the future visible and deliberate, and keeps Horizon 1 from dominating simply because it is the easiest to forecast and measure. For public sector organizations, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) proposes viewing the portfolio through four facets: enhancement-oriented innovation , which improves the performance of what already exists; mission-oriented innovation , which mobilizes effort toward a specific, ambitious outcome; adaptive innovation , which responds to emerging changes; and anticipatory innovation , which explores future issues that have not yet taken shape ( OECD, 2022 ) . The national research, development and innovation priorities presented in Chapter 2 serve as an example of mission-oriented innovation.

Top-down innovation , directed by leadership, identifies priority challenges and mobilizes resources around them. Its strength is clarity and alignment with strategy; its risk is that leaders assume a complete understanding of reality and close off room for discovery. Bottom-up innovation , emerging from employees, draws on knowledge close to the work and to beneficiaries; its risk is that it produces a great many local ideas unconnected to priorities, as in the opening case. A balanced approach combines the two: strategy sets search fields and boundaries from the top, and employees, beneficiaries and partners fill those fields with opportunities and solutions from below. This combination is the organizational application of the principle “the what and why from leadership, the how from people.” Bottom-up innovation stays disciplined by priorities, while leadership direction stays open to solutions that were not drawn in advance. Clear fields also give participants a sense of meaning in their contribution, since they know which goal their effort serves.

Strategy rests on assumptions about the future, and these assumptions are often implicit: that beneficiaries will keep behaving the same way, that regulations will not change, that available technology will stay as it is. Foresight is the organized effort to make these assumptions explicit and to test them against plausible alternatives. Ansoff noted early on that strategic surprises are usually preceded by weak signals , that is, early and ambiguous information about a coming change, and that an organization which learns to detect them gains time to prepare before the picture becomes clear to everyone ( Ansoff, 1975 ) . Among the most widely used foresight tools is scenario planning , which sketches several plausible and divergent futures rather than predicting a single one, so that the organization’s decisions can be tested against all of them ( Schoemaker, 1995 ) . Signals Regular scanning for early information about possible change in beneficiaries, technology or regulations. Trends Grouping related signals into trends and estimating their speed and impact. Scenarios Sketching several plausible futures based on the most important uncertainties. Options What do we do now regardless, what do we explore, and what do we monitor? Figure 4.3 From signal to option: how foresight feeds innovation strategy. The value of foresight is measured by what it changes in decisions. What it should yield is new challenge questions, adjustments to search fields, or exploratory initiatives in Horizon 3. Here foresight connects with the external realities scanning matrix introduced in Chapter 2: the matrix is its tool for regular scanning, and scenario planning its periodic tool.

Assumptions, markets, technologies and legislation all change, so an innovation strategy is reviewed periodically, and also whenever a strong signal emerges that alters the organization’s understanding of its situation. The purpose of the review is to verify that the search fields are still the most important, that resources are not all concentrated in Horizon 1, and that experiments have not exposed an error in a strategic assumption. A strategy does its job when it reaches beyond those who wrote it to those who carry it out. It should be translated into clear challenge questions, published evaluation criteria, funding priorities, and messages explaining why these fields were chosen, and every sector or unit should know its role in it: discovering opportunities, contributing expertise, running experiments, or adopting solutions. In Practice Write down the names of five innovation initiatives your organization is working on now, and ask of each: Which search field in the strategy does it serve? Which challenge question does it answer? If you find initiatives that serve no field, then either the strategy is overlooking a genuine priority that needs to be added, or the initiative is consuming resources outside the chosen direction.

Innovation strategy is a system of interconnected choices, defined as much by what it rules out as by what it commits to. Strategy rests on two inseparable questions: where we innovate, and how we reach our goal. The organization’s goals are translated into search fields, and then into challenge questions that define the “what and why” and leave the “how” to people. Strategy has six components: rationale, outcomes, search fields, level of ambition, means of delivery, and principles and boundaries. Balancing the three horizons makes investment in the future deliberate, with the allocation set according to each organization’s circumstances. A balanced approach combines top-down and bottom-up innovation, giving people freedom within clear fields and a sense of meaning in their contribution. Foresight feeds strategy by turning weak signals into trends, scenarios and options on which decisions can be made. 5 Chapter 5 The innovation management system In this chapter we present the framework that moves innovation from scattered efforts, hostage to personal connections and chance, to a regular practice that can be understood and improved: the difference between a process and a system, the system’s six stages and where decisions sit within them, and the requirements of the international standard for innovation management systems, ISO 56001 .

Opening case: an innovation procedure (composite case) One organization adopted a six-stage “innovation procedure,” published it in an elegant handbook, and hung its flowchart in the building’s corridors. A year later, a review revealed that dozens of proposals were still sitting in the “evaluation” stage with no decision, that two successful pilots had stalled at their conclusion because no one had been assigned to run the solution, and that most employees did not even know how their idea could reach the first stage. This organization had a written process , but it did not have a system . The flowchart describes the road; traveling it requires someone to decide at every turn, someone to fund, someone to take over the solution at the end, and a channel that connects the road to people where they work. These elements, which make the road passable, are the focus of this chapter. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Distinguish between the innovation process and the innovation management system. Describe the six stages of the innovation management system, the output of each, and its common failure. Design decision points that keep initiatives from remaining unresolved. Bring the system closer to people so that it captures opportunities from everyday work. Explain the structure of the ISO 56001 standard and the limits of its usefulness.

Organizations usually have more ideas than capacity to test and implement them. The problem, more often than not, is the absence of a pathway that singles out the important opportunities, gives resources to the promising ones, stops those that are not progressing, and ties success to adoption. This is where we need to distinguish between two concepts that are frequently confused. Innovation process How does a single initiative move forward? Successive stages from opportunity to implemented solution Activities and tools at each stage Drawn up in a flowchart or handbook The innovation management system What keeps initiatives moving continuously? A strategy that steers what enters the process Governance and decision rights at each stage Roles, resources and staged funding Measurement, learning and improvement A culture and channels that connect people to the process Figure 5.1 The process is part of the system: the former describes the road, and the latter ensures it is traveled. The international series of standards defines an innovation management system as a set of interrelated and interacting elements of an organization aimed at realizing value ( International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2025 ) . This covers managing the daily flow of opportunities and involving people in it, as well as the governance that determines who decides and how resources are allocated. It now becomes clear what happened in the opening case: the process was there, but the system was missing.

Models of the innovation process essentially agree on a path that begins with searching for opportunities, moves on to selecting what merits investment, then to implementation, and finally to capturing value ( Tidd & Bessant, 2021 ) . In this book we break that path down into six stages that operate in a continuous cycle: strategy, opportunity capture, evaluation and selection, initiative setup, pilot, and scaling. The first stage is foundational; the next three form the engine of the system, turning inputs into projects; and the last two carry the solution into practice. 1 Strategy 2 Opportunity capture 3 Evaluation and selection 4 Initiative setup 5 Pilot 6 Scaling and operation Foundation The system’s engine: from opportunity to project From project to value ↺ What is learned at each stage feeds back into the strategy and the earlier stages Figure 5.2 The six stages of the innovation management system. Source: prepared by the author based on Tidd & Bessant (2021) and ISO (2024) . Table 5.1 The purpose, output and common failure of each stage Stage Purpose Output Common failure Strategy Steering what enters the system Search fields, challenge questions and criteria An open call for any idea, with no priorities Opportunity capture Discovering needs and opportunities worth considering Opportunities described and grouped, kept separate from solutions Storing ideas instead of understanding needs Evaluation and selection Determining what merits the cost of the next round of learning A declared decision: explore, merge, defer or decline Long waits with no decision or response Initiative setup Turning the opportunity into a learning project A leader, a small team, a sponsor, initial funding and hypotheses No unit identified to take over the solution later Pilot Testing the solution in a real-world setting Evidence on value, adoption and cost A pilot without success criteria defined in advance Scaling and operation Turning the solution into a sustainable operational capability An owner, a budget, training and indicators A successful pilot that stalls because no one took it over These stages are not a rigid production line. An initiative may return to an earlier stage, change direction, or stop. The value of the system lies in its shared language and clear decisions and responsibilities, combined with enough flexibility to accommodate the different paths initiatives take. In Part III of the book we examine in detail what happens within these stages: understanding problems, developing solutions, experimentation, and adoption and scaling.

Every transition between stages ends in a decision, and that decision takes one of five forms: continue, continue with modifications, merge with another initiative, suspend temporarily, or stop. It should rest on what has changed in the evidence, the risks and the expected value, independent of the effort already spent or the standing of the person behind the idea. Yet the absence of a decision is more damaging to the system than a wrong one. An initiative that is neither accepted nor rejected remains in what we call decision limbo : it consumes its owners’ attention, nothing is learned from it, and it teaches those around it that taking the initiative is not worth the trouble. This is what happened to dozens of proposals in the opening case. A good system prevents this limbo through three simple means: A published response time at each stage, for which the person responsible for the decision alone is held accountable. A written, reasoned response to every proposal, even when it declines to take the proposal further. A periodic review of initiatives that have overrun their time, so that they are either resolved or the reason for their suspension is made public. These means may look procedural, but their effect is above all human: a reasoned response preserves the idea owner’s sense of being valued and teaches them something, and a published time frame respects their time. We return to decision rights and gates in Chapter 10.

The system’s value begins at the opportunity capture stage, the stage that connects the system to people. Organizations often limit this stage to a single channel removed from everyday work, such as an online platform, an annual competition or a standalone center, and wait for people to bring their ideas to it. As a result, only an enthusiastic few reach it, while most people, and with them their close-up knowledge of problems, remain outside the system. The system best able to capture opportunities is the one that goes to people where they work: in unit meetings, in performance reviews, in everyday work tools, and in dealings with beneficiaries. At a university, for example, capture channels widen when some course assignments and projects become an entry point into the innovation ecosystem, rather than the innovation center remaining an entity cut off from the classrooms and unknown to many students. In Practice Trace the last ten opportunities that entered your organization’s innovation system: where did they come from? If they all came from one channel or from the same people, the system sees only a small part of the organization.

The first edition of ISO 56001 was published in September 2024. It specifies requirements for an innovation management system that an organization can use to develop and demonstrate its innovation capability ( International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2024 ) . It differs from the guidance standard ISO 56002 in setting out requirements that can be audited and certified by accredited independent bodies ( Fernandez & Swart, 2025 ) . The standard follows the harmonized structure of the International Organization for Standardization’s management system standards and comprises seven main clauses: 4 Context Understanding the organization, interested parties and the scope of the system 5 Leadership Policy, strategy, culture and roles 6 Planning Objectives, risks, portfolios, structures and collaboration 7 Support Resources, competence, communication and intellectual property 8 Operation Initiatives and innovation processes 9 Performance evaluation Measurement, internal audit and management review 10 Improvement Continual improvement and corrective action Direction Preparation and enablement Execution Learning Figure 5.3 The main clauses of ISO 56001:2024 . Source: adapted from ISO (2024) . Clause 8 specifies five innovation processes: identifying opportunities, creating concepts, validating concepts, developing solutions, and deploying solutions ( ISO, 2024 ) . These processes correspond to the stages of the system in this book as follows: Table 5.2 Correspondence between ISO 56001 processes and the stages of the system ISO 56001 process Corresponding stages of the system Where it is covered in the book Identifying opportunities Strategy; opportunity capture Chapters 4 and 11 Creating concepts Evaluation and selection; initiative setup Chapters 12 and 13 Validating concepts Initiative setup; pilot Chapter 14 Developing solutions Pilot Chapters 12 and 14 Deploying solutions Scaling and operation Chapter 15 The limits of the standard’s usefulness The standard is a useful organizational tool for diagnosis and comparison, but it does not produce innovation by itself. Certification can become a new form of innovation theater if effort shifts toward completing documentation rather than improving the actual flow of opportunities, decisions and value. The more productive question when applying it is: has the road from idea to value become shorter and clearer for those who travel it?

Examine your organization’s innovation system stage by stage. Each stage has a sign that it is working and a sign that it has broken down. Start with the stage where the sign of breakdown is most evident, for it is the bottleneck that determines the performance of the whole system. Chapter tool Signs of health and breakdown at each stage Stage A sign that it is working A sign that it has broken down Strategy Employees know the current search fields and challenge questions Proposals scattered in every direction Opportunity capture Opportunities come from a variety of units and levels A few recurring sources, or a single channel Evaluation and selection Every proposal receives a reasoned response within a published time frame Proposals stuck without a decision for months Initiative setup Every initiative has a leader, a sponsor, hypotheses and a likely operating unit Initiatives that belong “to everyone” and are owned by no one Pilot Success criteria are defined before the pilot Every pilot is declared a success Scaling and operation Successful solutions are handed over to an owner and a budget Successful pilots that stall once they end

The process describes the initiative’s road; the system ensures that the road is actually traveled, resting on strategy, governance, roles, resources, measurement, and channels that connect people to the road. The innovation management system has six stages that operate in a continuous cycle, each with a specific output and a common failure. Every transition ends in a decision that takes one of five forms, and the most damaging thing that can befall the system is the absence of a decision. Decision limbo is prevented through a published response time, a reasoned response, and periodic review. The system best able to capture opportunities goes to people where they work and makes reaching it part of their day. ISO 56001 sets out certifiable requirements in seven clauses and specifies five innovation processes. Its real value shows in improving the actual flow of initiatives. Key Terms Innovation management system Innovation management system The formal framework through which an organization manages the flow of opportunities and initiatives through to value realization, including strategy, governance, roles, resources and measurement. search.s: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.t: 6 Chapter 6 The organizational architecture of innovation In this chapter we explore how an organization arranges itself to house innovation: where innovation sits in the structure, the enablers it requires, how units can work together rather than each in isolation, and who leads this effort. We take the university as an applied case whose thread runs through later chapters.

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.t: Opening case: a Saudi university (composite case) One university has what many organizations aspire to: a business accelerator, a Fab Lab for digital fabrication, an innovation oasis, research centers, a program for gifted students, and a Deanship of Student Affairs that organizes competitions. Each of these units has its own plan, indicators and annual reports. Yet a student survey showed that many students did not know these units existed, and those who did saw no connection between them and their courses. Assignments in most courses measure the ability to answer exam questions; a student with an idea does not know where to take it; and each unit waits for students to come to it. This university has all the inputs. What it lacks is the architecture that would bring these units together into a single ecosystem reaching students where they learn. That architecture is our concern in this chapter: how an organization arranges itself so that its side-by-side entities become an organizational capability for innovation. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Distinguish between the success of a standalone initiative and building an organizational capability for innovation. Compare centralized, distributed and hybrid models for organizing innovation. Identify the enablers that innovation needs, with time foremost among them. Analyze the opportunities hidden in the gaps between units and design integration among them. Design an orchestrating unit that links the components of the ecosystem without becoming a new isolated entity. Define the role and competencies of the chief innovation officer and the ways they influence units and leadership.

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.s: 6.1 From standalone initiatives to organizational capability
search.t: An innovation initiative may succeed thanks to an enthusiastic leader or an exceptional team, but that does not mean the organization has become capable of innovation. Organizational capability shows itself when the flow of opportunities, experiments and implementation is supported by a structure of roles, resources and relationships that endures when the organization’s standout members move on, and through which innovation is spread across the whole organization. This is why the international standard defines the innovation management system as the organization’s means of developing and demonstrating its innovation capability ( ISO, 2024 ) . When innovation stalls, organizations tend to blame a shortage of ideas or a lack of employee enthusiasm. It is more useful to ask about the architecture: Does innovation have a clear place in the structure? Are its enablers in place? Do units work together? Does the system reach people where they work?

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.s: 6.2 Where does innovation sit in the structure?
search.t: Organizations follow one of three models in organizing innovation, each with its strengths and limits. From their study of large firms pursuing radical innovation, O’Connor and DeMartino concluded that building the capability for it requires turning scattered efforts into a clear organizational function ( O'Connor & DeMartino, 2006 ) . Centralized Form An independent unit that leads innovation for the whole organization Suited to Building standards, and long-term bets Risk Isolation from the units’ problems and difficulty transferring solutions to them Distributed Form Each unit innovates within its own scope Suited to Proximity to problems and speed of adoption Risk Duplication and fragmentation, and missed cross-unit opportunities Hybrid Form A small central team that runs the system and the portfolio, with focal points and teams in the units Suited to Most organizations of medium maturity and size Risk Ambiguous roles between the center and the units if they are not defined Figure 6.1 Three models for the place of innovation in the organizational structure. A particular form of the centralized model, the innovation lab , has spread widely in the public sector. A study of 35 government labs found that the motives for setting them up included tackling complex problems and technical challenges, but also imitating other agencies and seeking legitimacy ( Tõnurist et al., 2017 ) . A lab created because others have created one, or to make the organization look innovative, risks remaining an input with no output.

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.t: Wherever it sits in the structure, innovation needs enablers that are a precondition for its work. An organization’s declared support for innovation remains incomplete as long as people are innovating with the same resources they use for their routine work. Table 6.1 The core enablers of innovation Enabler What it means Sign of its absence Time Protected time for exploration within official working hours “Innovate once you’ve finished your tasks” Skills Understanding beneficiaries, formulating hypotheses and designing experiments, alongside generating ideas Repeated brainstorming workshops with no progress Data and tools Access to data and to prototyping and testing tools Teams waiting months to obtain data Spaces Places for collaborative work and experimentation, close to people An elegant space in a remote building that no one visits Networks Connections to experts and partners inside and outside the organization Every team starts from scratch Funding Funding that increases in step with the evidence Either no funding at all, or large early funding with no stages Time deserves particular attention, because it is the scarcest and most overlooked of the enablers. Amabile and her colleagues analyzed the diaries of 177 employees and found that time pressure undermines creative thinking when people feel they are on a treadmill or working on autopilot, whereas creativity remains possible under pressure when people feel they are on a meaningful mission, know its purpose, and are protected from distraction ( Amabile et al., 2002 ) . The issue, then, goes beyond the amount of time to its meaning: do individuals feel that their time is directed toward a clear purpose, or spread across scattered tasks that never end?

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.t: Many innovation opportunities lie in the gaps between organizational units. One unit may carry a burden created by a decision in another; an employee may re-enter data because systems are not integrated; a beneficiary may wait between two service points because ownership of their journey is fragmented. Each unit may look efficient on its local indicator, while the overall journey remains slow. Unit A Its indicator: excellent Unit B Its indicator: excellent Unit C Its indicator: excellent Unit D Its indicator: excellent The beneficiary’s journey across the four units: waiting between each unit and the next, being asked for the same information again and again, and no one owning the journey as a whole Figure 6.2 When every unit excels on its own indicator yet the overall journey stays slow: the territory of architectural innovation. This does not mean that the answer is more meetings and joint committees. Hansen showed that collaboration between units has a cost, that it pays off only when its expected value exceeds that cost, and called for disciplined collaboration : collaboration measured by the specific result toward which it is directed ( Hansen, 2009 ) . Productive integration between units requires: A shared purpose and an outcome that goes beyond each unit’s indicator. A single picture of the journey: the flow of data and decisions, and the waiting points. Clear decision rights: who recommends, who decides, and who implements. Time, data and resources allocated to actual experimentation. An owner who takes responsibility for sustaining the solution once it has been tested.

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.t: The opening case returns with a practical question: how can the university’s side-by-side units become a single ecosystem? The common response is to set up a new unit in charge of “innovation.” The risk is that this unit becomes a seventh isolated entity alongside the other six. A better alternative is an orchestrating unit that reports to senior leadership and works in the background. Its function is limited to connecting the existing units with one another and connecting all of them to the student, without owning initiatives or competing with those units. A unit that becomes a new, isolated entity Launches its own programs and competes with existing units Measures its success by the number of its activities Waits for students to come to it Reports to a mid-level official An orchestrating unit Connects existing units and supports their work Measures its success by the flow of students and ideas between units and the results achieved Goes to students in their classrooms and courses Reports to senior leadership so that it has the authority to coordinate Figure 6.3 The difference between a unit that adds a new isolated entity and one that builds bridges between existing entities. At a university, integration can take several possible forms, depending on what the diagnosis reveals. Three pathways stand out: Linking to formal learning: redesigning the assignments and projects in a limited number of common courses so that they become graded creative and innovative tasks, connecting them to the accelerator, the lab and university competitions, and then scaling up what works. The student’s extended pathway: from attracting gifted students at the secondary school stage, to nurturing and empowering them during their studies in ways that fit their majors, to alumni services that keep them connected to the ecosystem. Linking to the external ecosystem: partnerships with government and industry bodies in the region that open up real problems and opportunities for application to students. We return to these pathways in the chapters on the innovator and their environment, adoption and scaling, and innovation ecosystems, and then bring them together in Chapter 20 on the university innovation ecosystem. Principle An ecosystem is built by designing the flow between its entities more than by adding new ones. The question that reveals the quality of the architecture is: how many steps does an idea’s owner need to take to reach someone who can help?

search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.s: 6.6 The chief innovation officer: role and competencies
search.t: The orchestrating unit needs someone to lead it. Many organizations assign this to an innovation officer who goes by various titles: director of the innovation unit, head of innovation, or chief innovation officer. The role carries a paradox: its holder is responsible for results that are mostly achieved within units they do not head, by people who do not report to them. Their success is therefore measured more by their ability to make others succeed than by what they carry out themselves. What the role takes on and what it avoids The chief innovation officer’s role is consistent with the logic of the orchestrating unit: they build capability and leave ownership of ideas with those who originated them. Table 6.2 sets out the main domains of the role, what the officer takes on in each, and what they would do well to avoid. Table 6.2 Domains of the chief innovation officer’s role. Prepared by the author. Domain What they take on What they avoid Strategy Works with leadership to formulate search fields and the level of ambition, and translates them into understandable priorities Writing the strategy alone, or copying it from another organization Portfolio Manages gates and staged funding, and ensures a reasoned response to every idea Owning initiatives in place of their originators, or deciding on them unilaterally Enablers Provides tools, skills and protected time, and removes procedural obstacles Becoming the organization’s only source of ideas Connection Connects units with one another, and connects the organization with partners and beneficiaries Competing with existing units through parallel programs Measurement Measures flow and impact, and learns from failure Measuring their success by the number of events and competitions Communication Tells the story of what is achieved and credits it to those responsible Attributing success to their own unit Competencies The OECD identified six core skills for public sector innovation that public servants need to varying degrees, and that those who lead innovation need to a greater degree: iteration , that is, developing solutions through rapid rounds of prototyping and testing; data literacy ; user centricity ; curiosity , that is, seeking out new ideas and different perspectives; storytelling , that is, explaining change through a narrative that builds support for it and links the past to the present and a possible future; and insurgency , that is, challenging the status quo, working with unusual partners, and treating setbacks as opportunities to learn ( OECD, 2017 ) . The chief innovation officer’s position between units adds a critically important competency: influence without authority . Cohen and Bradford argue that such influence rests on exchange: the person making a request understands what the other party cares about and what they can offer in return, whether resources, information, support or recognition, so that the relationship shifts from a request to a partnership ( Cohen & Bradford, 2005 ) . Those who lead innovation by instruction alone usually obtain formal compliance; exchange is more likely to generate commitment. Winning leadership attention The chief innovation officer also needs to place on leadership’s agenda issues that were not there before. Dutton and Ashford described this phenomenon and named it issue selling : the efforts employees make to direct senior management’s attention to issues they consider important and to shape how management understands them ( Dutton & Ashford, 1993 ) . A later study identified three sets of moves that distinguish successful attempts: packaging moves, such as linking the issue to the organization’s goals and presenting it in the language of results and cost; involvement moves, such as building a coalition of supporters before the pitch; and process moves, such as careful preparation, choosing the right timing, and combining formal and informal channels ( Dutton et al., 2001 ) . search.c: Chapter 6: The organizational architecture of innovation
search.t: Organizational capability for innovation rests on a structure of roles, resources and relationships that holds firm when individuals move on, and so goes beyond reliance on a few of them. There are three models for placing innovation in the structure: centralized, distributed and hybrid. The hybrid model suits most organizations, provided roles are clearly defined between the center and the units. Labs and centers set up out of imitation or in pursuit of legitimacy risk remaining inputs without outputs. Innovation needs enablers: time, skills, data, spaces, networks and staged funding. Time is the scarcest of these, and what matters is its meaning more than its quantity. Many opportunities lie in the gaps between units, and productive integration is disciplined collaboration directed toward a specific result. An orchestrating unit connects existing units with one another and with people, removing the need to add a new isolated entity. The chief innovation officer leads results achieved in units they do not head. They build capability and leave ideas to their originators, rely on influence without authority and on issue selling to leadership, and begin by understanding before building. Influence without authority Influence without authority A person’s ability to mobilize people who do not report to them, through exchange and partnership building. search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.s: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: 7 Chapter 7 The innovator and their environment: people in the innovation system Having covered strategy, the system and the architecture in the preceding chapters, we now return to the one for whom all of these are built: the person who carries the idea. We look at the characteristics and motivation of innovators, trace the path an idea travels with them, and consider what they need from their environment at each stage along the way.

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: Opening case: a university student (composite case) During her field training, a third-year student noticed that people visiting one agency waited for hours to complete a procedure that could easily be shortened, and she pictured a simple fix. She took the idea to the professor of one of her courses, who praised it and then reminded her that the final exam covered chapters one through ten. She went to the university's business accelerator, where she was asked for a full business plan she did not know how to write. She then logged the idea on the ideas platform and received an automated acknowledgment; nothing came after it. Two semesters later, she had forgotten the idea. No one rejected it, and no one accepted it. The student noticed the problem, imagined the solution and knocked on three doors. Where, then, did her idea stall? And what did she need in order to take a single step forward? That is the question this chapter takes up, and we approach it from the innovator's own vantage point: who the innovator is, what they need, and how the environment and systems around them are designed. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain why well-funded innovation systems remain empty when they overlook people. Describe the characteristics of innovators without reducing them to innate talent. Trace the innovator's path from thinking to practice, and identify what the innovator needs at each stage. Distinguish between barriers to and enablers of a creative environment, and diagnose them in one's own organization. Review existing innovation systems from the perspective of the innovator's experience.

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.s: 7.1 Why does innovation begin with people?
search.t: Many organizations have innovation centers, platforms and budgets, yet they do not produce innovation on a recurring basis. In our view, one of the most important reasons is that these systems were designed around procedure and overlooked people: they specify stages, templates and criteria, and then assume that ideas will flow into them. An idea, however, is born in the mind of someone who notices, questions and connects, and who then decides to make an extra effort that no one asked of them. It is this final decision that the environment either wins or loses. Amabile offered the most influential model for explaining this relationship, the componential model of creativity ( Amabile, 1988, 1996 ) . It holds that individual creativity is shaped by three components within the person, all of which are surrounded and influenced by the work environment, as Figure 7.1 shows. Domain-relevant skills Knowledge, experience and technical skill in the field in which the person works. This is the material from which they build their ideas. Creativity-relevant processes Ways of thinking and working: viewing a problem from different angles, connecting what seems unrelated, and persevering. Intrinsic task motivation Interest in the work itself and enjoyment of its challenge. This is what turns knowledge and skill into actual effort. Work environment Encourages or weakens all three components, and affects motivation more than the others. Figure 7.1 The components of individual creativity and the surrounding work environment, adapted from Amabile (1996) . For innovation management, the significance of this model lies in the third component. Skills and processes grow slowly through education and experience, whereas motivation responds quickly to what happens to a person on a given day: how their idea was received, whether they found time for it, and whether they saw any result from their effort. This is why a poor environment can extinguish in weeks what years of education have built. Amabile and Pratt later developed the model to link individual creativity with organizational innovation, adding two elements: the progress a person perceives in work they consider meaningful . Together these feed motivation and keep it renewing itself ( Amabile & Pratt, 2016 ) . Putting people first does not mean neglecting the system. The preceding chapters built the strategy that identifies which problems are worth working on, the system that turns ideas into value, and the architecture that connects the various units. This chapter places people at the center of all this, for the system is what connects people to problems; if either side is missing, there is nothing left for it to connect. Innovators themselves see it this way. In a phenomenological study with ten innovative Saudi entrepreneurs, each with fifteen to twenty-five years of experience building innovative ventures, participants described a supportive community as one that begins by recognizing the innovator's distinctiveness and understanding their personal and cognitive style, and then invests in them and connects them with suitable economic environments. The study concluded that effective support invests in the innovator as a strategic human resource and goes beyond tracking their outputs (Alsamani, 2026 [Arabic]) .

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: A popular image casts the innovator as a rare genius born with a gift. The research does not support this image in any absolute sense. In a meta-analysis of personality studies, Feist found that creative people in the sciences and the arts tend to share certain traits, most notably openness to new experiences, autonomy, self-confidence and high motivation ( Feist, 1998 ) . These traits, however, are distributed among people along a continuum. Every organization has some people who possess them to a high degree, and a larger number who possess them to a degree sufficient to innovate if they find the right environment. The characteristics of innovators can be grouped into three clusters, as classified in the “innovator's path” model presented in the next section: Knowledge and skill: broad knowledge and high skill in the field of interest, higher-order thinking skills, and the ability to research and gather information. Self-regulation: the ability to evaluate one's own work, focus on a long-term goal, self-confidence, self-awareness and autonomy. Openness and learning: curiosity, flexibility, openness to new experiences, and the capacity for self-directed learning. One characteristic that deserves managers' particular attention is creative self-efficacy : a person's belief in their ability to produce new and useful ideas. Tierney and Farmer found that it predicts employees' creative performance and is influenced by supervisor behavior and job experience ( Tierney & Farmer, 2002 ) . This means that part of an innovator's “talent” is built or broken in their work environment: an employee whose first ideas were met with ridicule learns that they are “not creative,” while a colleague who found someone to take their ideas seriously learns the opposite. The same pattern appears in the experiences of successful innovators. In a phenomenological study conducted in 2023 with eleven prominent Saudi innovators, each with fifteen or more years of innovative work and products and ventures of wide impact, certain factors recurred in their narratives of their journeys. Nine of them regarded self-confidence as a necessity without which the path cannot be completed, and some mentioned talented friends who did not finish their projects because they lost confidence in their abilities. All participants agreed that continuous self-directed learning, driven by love of the field, was one of the reasons for their success ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . Oldham and Cummings's research with employees at two manufacturing facilities sheds light on this question. They measured creativity through employees' suggestions, their patents and their supervisors' ratings, and found that the highest creativity emerged when three conditions came together: a creative personality, complex and challenging work, and supportive, noncontrolling supervision ( Oldham & Cummings, 1996 ) . A creative personality, then, is a disposition that the environment either reveals or conceals. Common misconception “The organization needs to hire innovators.” Hiring matters, but an innovator who enters an environment that rewards compliance and punishes mistakes adapts to it within months. The more useful step is for the organization to ask first: what happens today to the ideas of the people it already has?

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: A qualitative study with teachers of gifted students concluded that creativity and innovation are related yet distinct concepts: creativity is a complex, multifaceted process of generating ideas , which may be individual or collective and requires knowledge of the domain; innovation is the production of original, useful and tangible outcomes that society values ( Alsamani, 2019 ) . The difference between the two goes beyond definition to need: what a person needs while thinking differs from what they need while turning their idea into reality. Building on this distinction, we propose the innovator's path model, illustrated in Figure 7.2. The model reads an idea's journey from the perspective of the person who holds it. Environmental enablers: sufficient freedom · support for sharing ideas · autonomy of judgment · non-authoritarian attitudes The base: the person Intrinsic task motivation Knowledge and skill Self-regulation Openness and learning Stage one: thinking Defining the problem Imagining and connecting Generating ideas Evaluating and refining Stage two: practice The idea needs opportunities , resources and support Real-world testing Ongoing evaluation Outcomes Decision: the idea succeeds Decision: the idea is ineffective No decision: processing continues No decision: the process has stalled Learning loop: an idea that did not succeed returns to the start of the path with new knowledge, if its owner finds reason to try again Environmental barriers: excessive evaluation · no encouragement of risk-taking · criticism of new ideas · excessive time pressure · authoritarian monitoring Figure 7.2 The innovator's path from thinking to practice, and the environment surrounding it. Developed by the author (first developed in 2017–2018). The model rests on four ideas: The first is that the person stands on motivation. Cognitive and personal characteristics do not set themselves in motion; intrinsic motivation is what turns them into actual effort. This is why it is placed as the foundation on which the entire path rests. The second is that the path consists of two different stages. In the thinking stage, a person needs freedom to explore, time to reflect, and as little premature judgment as possible. In the practice stage, the need changes: the idea now requires an opportunity to be tried in a real setting, enough resources to test it, and support from people who hold the authority or the expertise. Many organizations do one of the two stages well and neglect the other: competitions and hackathons celebrate thinking and then leave the winners with no route to practice. This is consistent with Baer's finding that creative ideas get implemented when their originators have both the motivation to implement them and a network of relationships to help them do so ( Baer, 2012 ) . The finding also matches what the Saudi innovators in the study cited above described: they all agreed on the importance of interacting with peers, and eight of them saw their network of relationships as a route to opportunities. Eight of them likewise held that turning the innovation into a source of income early on is a condition for persisting, and one recounted how a talented friend, forced into a job far from his passion, lost interest in his project ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . In the practice stage, then, resources do more than allow the idea to be tried; they determine whether the innovator will stay on the path. The third is that the path has four possible outcomes. Besides the idea succeeding or proving ineffective, the path may remain without a decision. This outcome comes in two forms: continued processing, in which the person needs time to reflect, which is healthy; and a stalled process that no one has resolved, which Chapter 5 called decision limbo . The latter is the most damaging to motivation, because a reasoned rejection teaches its recipient something, whereas silence teaches them not to try again. search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: If motivation is the foundation of the path, the practical question is what nourishes it. Self-determination theory answers that intrinsic motivation grows when three psychological needs are satisfied: autonomy, competence and relatedness ( Gagné & Deci, 2005 ) . We translate these general needs into specific needs that innovators experience within the organization, summarized in Table 7.1. Table 7.1 What innovators need and what the organization does to meet those needs Need What it looks like when met What the organization does Discussed in Recognition of the idea The idea's owner feels it was read and understood, and receives credit for it A reasoned response within an announced time frame, and keeping the owner's name attached to the idea at every stage Ch. 5, Ch. 8, Ch. 10 Opportunity Finds a route to a real problem, and to someone who can try out the solution Opening problems up to people, and reducing the steps between the idea's owner and those who can help Ch. 6, Ch. 11 Deferred criticism The idea is explored before it is judged Separating idea-generation sessions from evaluation sessions, and judging each stage by its own criteria Ch. 12 Autonomy within boundaries Knows the problem and the goal, and owns the way to solve it Defining the “what” and the “why” clearly, and leaving the “how” to people Ch. 3, Ch. 4 Resources and support Finds enough to test the idea, and a sponsor who champions it Staged funding, protected time, prototyping tools and executive sponsorship Ch. 6, Ch. 10, Ch. 14 Understanding and fit Finds a system that suits their way of thinking and makes room for differences among people Flexible entry routes: a conversation, a prototype or a written proposal Ch. 5, Ch. 8 Meaningful progress Sees their idea moving, and sees its effect on a problem they care about Making the idea's status visible, and celebrating interim steps alongside final results Ch. 8, Ch. 15, Ch. 16 Two of these needs deserve a closer look. The first is deferred criticism . As early as the middle of the last century, Osborn called for separating the generation of ideas from judging them ( Osborn, 1953 ) . Amabile's research explains why this separation matters: expecting evaluation while working weakens intrinsic motivation and pushes people toward safe, familiar solutions ( Amabile, 1996 ) . Deferring criticism means putting it in its proper place along the path: an idea needs rigorous evaluation, but only after it has been given a chance to take shape. The second is autonomy within boundaries , the concept that ties the chapters of this book together. Innovators do not need absolute freedom; indeed, boundless freedom can scatter their efforts. What they need is a clear problem and an understood goal, and then to be left to choose the route ( Amabile, 1998 ) . Leadership that specifies the “how” in detail deprives them of autonomy, and leadership that fails to specify the “what” deprives them of direction. In Practice Take the last five ideas put forward by people on your team and ask yourself about each one: Does its owner know what happened to it? Were they told the reasons for the decision? Is their name still attached to it? Your answers reveal what your team has learned about whether thinking is worth the effort.

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: If motivation is the component of creativity most quickly affected by the environment, the next question is what in the environment raises or lowers it. Amabile and her colleagues developed an instrument for assessing the work environment for creativity and used it to compare projects rated as high and low in creativity within the same organizations. They found that the high-creativity projects were distinguished by encouragement at the level of the organization, the supervisor and the work group, by freedom in how the work was done, by challenge, and by sufficient resources. The low-creativity projects were marked by organizational impediments, such as internal conflict, conservatism and rigid formal structures, and by excessive workload pressure ( Amabile et al., 1996 ) . These findings intersect with the environmental arc in the innovator's path model, as Figure 7.3 shows. Barriers Excessive evaluation and monitoring Attention shifts from the work to the judgment expected of it Criticizing new ideas at the outset People learn to put forward only safe ideas No encouragement of calculated risk-taking Making a mistake becomes costlier than not trying Excessive time pressure No room is left for deep thinking Authoritarian interference in how the work is done Autonomy is taken away and motivation weakens Enablers Sufficient freedom in how the work is done Autonomy within the boundaries of the problem Support for sharing ideas Nearby channels, and a reception that respects the idea's owner Autonomy of judgment The person is treated as an expert in their own work Non-authoritarian attitudes The leader facilitates the work and backs those doing it Meaningful challenge and sufficient resources A task worth the effort, and enough to accomplish it Figure 7.3 Barriers to and enablers of a creative environment. Developed by the author, drawing on Amabile et al. (1996) . Three things stand out in the figure. First, most barriers are small everyday practices: a sarcastic remark in a meeting, a weekly progress report that no one reads, or an unnecessary deadline. Second, many of them arise from good intentions: monitoring is meant to ensure quality, and early criticism is meant to save effort. Third, the enablers cost little money, but they require awareness on the part of leaders and a change in their habits. This is why many organizations spend on visible inputs, such as centers and platforms, while keeping the everyday barriers that cancel out their effect. Chapter 8 treats culture as the wider frame for these practices: unwritten values and norms, psychological safety, and the handling of failure.

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: The opening case returns with one final question: if the university redesigned its system around the student rather than around its procedures, what would change? Each step in her journey can be read as an unmet need: In the course: she needed an opportunity . An assignment that measures memorization of information has no room for an idea. An assignment that asks students to identify a problem in their field of study and propose a solution to it, by contrast, turns the course itself into a channel for innovation and gives the professor the role of first supporter. At the accelerator: she needed fit . A full business plan suits someone who has reached the practice stage; someone still in the thinking stage needs a conversation, guidance and a small next step. On the platform: she needed recognition . A reasoned response within an announced time frame, even a polite decline, would have kept her on the path, and might have brought her back to it with a better idea. The first step on this list matters most, because it touches every student, whereas only a few of them ever knock on the accelerator's door. In a study of 373 undergraduates from several Saudi universities, faculty support in everyday teaching was associated with students' creative self-efficacy and their innovative behavior, and self-efficacy explained part of this relationship ( Alsamani & Alqahtani, 2026 ) . It follows that specialized structures, such as incubators and accelerators, and the daily work of faculty members with their students are two parts of a single system. Faculty members themselves believe that students with creative traits need, alongside thinking and problem-solving skills, to become aware of promising creative and innovative opportunities aligned with Saudi Vision 2030 (Alsamani, 2023 [Arabic]) . This reading extends beyond the university. In any organization, each stage of the innovation system can be reviewed with a single question: what does the idea's owner need here, and what do they actually find? A system that asks this question regularly evolves around people; one that does not evolves around itself. This question grows more important with artificial intelligence. AI tools now do much of what used to set the expert apart, including drafting the kind of business plan that stopped the student in her tracks. What remains for people is what the tool cannot do for them: noticing a problem no one asked them to notice, and caring about it enough to follow it through. These two things are precisely what the environment wins or loses. Principle A system built around procedure waits for ideas; a system built around people calls them forth. The difference between the two shows in what happens to one person's idea in its first week.

search.c: Chapter 7: The innovator and their environment
search.t: Innovation systems remain empty when they are designed around procedure and assume that ideas will flow into them of their own accord; an idea is born in a person who chooses to make an effort no one asked of them. Individual creativity is shaped by domain-relevant skills, creativity-relevant processes and intrinsic motivation. Of these, motivation is the most quickly affected by the environment. The characteristics of innovators are distributed among people in varying degrees, and some of them, such as creative self-efficacy, are built or broken by the work environment. The innovator passes through two different stages: thinking, which calls for freedom and time; and practice, which calls for opportunities, resources and support. The path has four possible outcomes, and the most damaging to motivation is “no decision” with the process stalled, because silence teaches the idea's owner not to try. Most barriers to a creative environment take the form of small everyday practices, whereas the enablers call for awareness and well-established habits more than for money. A professor's support in everyday teaching is associated with students' creative self-efficacy and innovative behavior, and it works together with incubators and accelerators as part of a single system. An innovation system is reviewed from the perspective of the idea's owner with one question at each stage: what do they need here, and what do they actually find? Creative self-efficacy Creative self-efficacy A person's belief in their ability to produce new and useful ideas. The innovator's path The innovator's path A model that reads an idea's journey from the perspective of its owner, from thinking to practice, along with its possible outcomes and the surrounding environment. Work environment for creativity Work environment for creativity The enablers and barriers within an organization that affect employees' creativity, particularly their motivation.
