search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.s: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: 8 Chapter 8 Innovation culture and the enabling environment In this chapter we approach culture as the unwritten rules that determine what people do when no one is watching: whether they put forward their ideas, whether they admit their mistakes, and whether they experiment. We examine how these rules take shape and the ways in which they change.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: Opening case: a government agency (composite case) A government agency launched an internal campaign titled “Try, Learn, Advance,” hung its posters in the corridors, and the CEO devoted his annual address to accepting failure as a path to learning. A few months later, a pilot launched by one team to simplify an online service ran into trouble, and the agency received complaints from some service users. An investigation committee was formed, and the team leader was transferred to another department. No circular was issued afterward, and none was needed; employees had understood the real rule. In the next round of the ideas competition, the number of submissions fell by half. The posters were sincere; they expressed a genuine wish on the part of the leadership. But employees learn culture from what they witness more than from what they are told, and in a single week they learned what an entire campaign could not teach them. It is this gap between what is declared and what is practiced that we examine in this chapter, in order to see how to build a culture in which innovators find what they need. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Distinguish between the three levels of culture, and explain the gap between espoused values and actual behavior. Describe the tensions whose two sides an innovative culture needs to hold together. Distinguish psychological safety from comfort, and link it to high standards. Classify types of failure, and identify the appropriate response to each. Identify forms of recognition and motivation that nourish intrinsic motivation, and design flexible entry routes for different thinking styles. Identify the mechanisms through which culture is formed and changed, and apply them to one's own organization.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: Organizational culture has many definitions, the most widely used being Schein's, which describes it as a pattern of shared basic assumptions that a group has learned as it solved its problems, and that has worked well enough to be taught to new members as the correct way to perceive, think and feel ( Schein, 2010 ) . Schein distinguishes three levels of culture, illustrated in Figure 8.1. ↑ Visible and easy to observe Artifacts Spaces, posters, job titles, events and written procedures Espoused values What the organization says it believes: vision, values, slogans and leadership speeches Basic assumptions What people actually believe without saying it: what is safe, what is risky, and what gets rewarded ↓ Hidden and taken for granted, and determines actual behavior Figure 8.1 The levels of organizational culture, adapted from Schein (2010) . The value of this distinction is that the deepest level is the one that governs behavior. In the opening case, the artifacts and the espoused values changed, while the basic assumption remained as it was: mistakes are punished. When what is declared conflicts with what is assumed, people follow the assumption. This is why many “innovation culture” programs that begin with colorful spaces and slogans fail: they work on the two upper levels and leave the third untouched. Alongside culture, the concept of climate is used to describe the patterns of behavior and feeling that people observe in their daily work, such as the degree of trust, openness to ideas and room for experimentation ( Ekvall, 1996 ) . Climate lies closer to the surface and is easier to measure, which makes it a useful indicator of culture; we return to it in the chapter on measurement.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.s: 8.2 The necessary tensions in an innovative culture
search.t: Innovative culture is usually described in attractive terms: tolerance of failure, freedom, collaboration and openness. Pisano argues that this description is incomplete, and that stopping at it explains why such a culture is so hard to build. Each of these qualities needs a counterweight to balance it, or it turns into its opposite: tolerance of failure without standards becomes laxity, and freedom without discipline becomes chaos ( Pisano, 2019 ) . Table 8.1 summarizes these tensions. Table 8.1 The necessary tensions in an innovative culture, adapted from Pisano (2019) Desired quality Its counterweight What happens when the balance is missing Tolerance of failure No tolerance for incompetence Avoidable mistakes are excused in the name of experimentation Willingness to experiment Rigorous discipline in experimentation Many experiments that test no clear hypothesis and are not stopped when they fail Psychological safety Candor in critiquing work Politeness that protects relationships and weakens ideas Collaboration Individual accountability Consensus decisions whose consequences no one owns Flat structure Strong leadership Endless debate, with no one to settle the direction This analysis is consistent with the concept that ties this book together: autonomy within boundaries . An innovative culture is clearer than others about its boundaries, and freer within them. That is what makes it difficult: it asks leaders to be supportive and demanding at the same time.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: Edmondson defined psychological safety as a belief shared by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking: asking a question, admitting a mistake, disagreeing or offering an unfinished idea without fear of embarrassment or punishment. In her study of fifty-one work teams in a manufacturing company, she found that psychological safety was associated with team learning behavior, such as seeking feedback and discussing errors, and that learning behavior was in turn associated with team performance ( Edmondson, 1999 ) . Psychological safety is sometimes understood as comfort, niceness or lowered expectations. Edmondson stresses that it is the opposite: it is what makes candid discussion possible. To illustrate, she places it on one axis and the standards expected of the team on another, as in Figure 8.2 ( Edmondson, 2019 ) . Standards and performance expectations Anxiety zone High expectations and fear of mistakes: people work hard, but they hide problems and do not put forward ideas that are not guaranteed Learning and innovation zone High expectations and safety: people speak candidly, experiment and learn from mistakes Apathy zone Low expectations and fear: perfunctory presence and effort spent on self-protection Comfort zone Safety and low expectations: good relationships and work that challenges no one Psychological safety → Figure 8.2 Psychological safety and standards: four zones, adapted from Edmondson (2019) . The top row represents high expectations, and the right-hand column high safety. The figure explains the point made in Chapter 3 that the environments most capable of innovation combine genuine care for people with high expectations of them. A leader who raises expectations without building safety pushes the team into the anxiety zone, where performance looks good until the hidden problems come to light. A leader who builds safety without expectations creates a comfortable team that does not innovate. The learning zone requires both together. Psychological safety is also tied to employee voice: safety is the condition that leads people to speak up, and an open leader is the first thing they test before deciding to do so. In Practice In your next meeting, before offering your own view, ask: “What could make this plan fail?” Then wait. If an objection comes, thank the person who raised it before you respond. A team learns more from how you respond to the first objection than from any talk about openness.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: Many organizations say they accept failure, then treat every failure the same way. Edmondson proposes distinguishing among types of failure according to their causes, because each type calls for a different response ( Edmondson, 2011 ) . Figure 8.3 illustrates this distinction. Preventable failure Source Deviation from a known procedure, negligence, or a lack of skill Where it occurs Clear, routine work Response Training, improving the procedure, and accountability if it recurs Complexity-related failure Source An interaction of many factors that had not come together before Where it occurs Complex systems such as hospitals and supply chains Response Early detection of small signals, and analysis of causes without looking for someone to blame Intelligent failure Source A thoughtful experiment in unknown territory that did not confirm its hypothesis Where it occurs Innovation, research and experimentation Response Documenting what the team learned, and acknowledging the value of the experiment ← Usually blameworthy Usually praiseworthy → Figure 8.3 Types of failure and the appropriate response to each, adapted from Edmondson (2011) . Intelligent failure has conditions: the experiment must take place in genuinely unknown territory, serve a valuable opportunity, build on what is already known, and be small enough that its loss is bearable. An experiment that fails after meeting these conditions yields knowledge that was not available before. In the opening case, however, an experiment of the third type was treated as if it belonged to the first, and employees learned not to experiment. Economic research supports this distinction. Azoulay and colleagues compared life scientists funded by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, which provides long-term funding, tolerates early failure and leaves researchers free to change direction, with comparable researchers funded by a government program with short cycles and predefined goals. They found that the first group produced high-impact papers at a markedly higher rate, and also produced more papers that attracted little attention; in other words, they experimented more and succeeded more ( Azoulay et al., 2011 ) . This is what theory predicts: incentives that tolerate early failure and reward long-term success are the best suited to motivating innovation ( Manso, 2011 ) . This complements what Chapter 7 presented about the learning loop in the innovator's path: an idea that did not succeed returns to the start of the path with new knowledge if it is treated as an intelligent failure, and its owner's willingness to try again ends with it if it is treated as a shortcoming. Caution Accepting failure does not mean celebrating it. An organization that celebrates every failure confuses the three types just as an organization that punishes every failure does. The test comes down to two questions: Was the experiment well designed? And did we learn from it?

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: Organizations often turn to awards and financial rewards to encourage innovation. These rewards raise a long-standing question in creativity research: do external incentives undermine the intrinsic motivation on which creativity depends? The meta-analysis by Byron and Khazanchi offers a balanced answer: rewards are positively related to creative performance when they are tied to creativity itself rather than to mere task completion, when they carry information about the quality of performance, and when they give the person some degree of choice ( Byron & Khazanchi, 2012 ) . Three practical principles follow from this: Reward what you actually want: a prize for the number of ideas submitted produces many weak ideas. It is more useful to recognize the quality of an experiment and what the team learned from it, even if it did not succeed. Make recognition informative: explaining why a piece of work is being recognized tells its author what they did well, and tells others what the organization values. Give non-material recognition its due: crediting the idea to its owner, involving them in implementing it, and giving them the opportunity to present it to the leadership. These are among the innovator's needs set out in Table 7.1. Yet reward, whether material or symbolic, remains only one form of motivation. An environment that meets the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness nourishes intrinsic motivation, which is the kind most closely aligned with creativity ( Gagné & Deci, 2005 ) . Amabile and Pratt's model adds that the most powerful driver of people's working day is their sense of progress in meaningful work ( Amabile & Pratt, 2016 ) . These are things shaped by the details of daily management more than by budgets. Recognition holds a special place for gifted and innovative people. In the phenomenological study with innovative entrepreneurs presented in Chapter 7, participants repeatedly stressed that a supportive community begins with appreciating and acknowledging talent. One of them described creative people as highly sensitive to recognition of their worth, adding that ignoring this need may drive them to withdraw or turn inward. For them, recognition extended from a kind word to smoothing the way for tasks, removing obstacles, and protecting creative people from having their energy drained by routine operational work (Alsamani, 2026 [Arabic]) . This is consistent with a study of distinguished, successful innovators, which showed that working with a supportive team that handled operational matters was among the main things that freed them to focus on developing their innovations ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . Table 8.2 presents forms of motivation, most of which call for attention more than budget. Table 8.2 Low-cost forms of motivation Form Need it meets Example from the university Acknowledgment and attribution Recognition of worth Naming the idea's owner at the college council or in the university newsletter, and keeping their name on the idea when it is implemented Involvement in implementation Meaning and belonging Assigning the proposer to lead its pilot or to serve on the pilot team Partnership in the work Belonging and competence A faculty member joining a student project as a partner and mentor, in addition to their role as assessor Access to leadership Recognition and influence Presenting the idea directly to the dean or vice dean and hearing their view of it Protected time and freedom Autonomy Hours set aside for the project in the schedule, and freedom to choose how to solve the problem Meaningful challenge Competence and meaning Assigning a real problem facing the university instead of a hypothetical exercise Removing obstacles Progress Streamlining procedures, and relief from some routine duties during the project Documentation Lasting recognition Recording the participation in the student's skills transcript or in the employee's performance file

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.s: 8.6 A culture with room for different thinking styles
search.t: Innovation programs tend to reward a single type of innovator: the person with a bold idea who presents it well. Kirton, however, showed that people differ in their style of creativity just as they differ in its level: some are adaptors , inclined to improve existing systems from within and with precision, while others are innovators , inclined to move beyond the existing framework and propose alternatives that differ from it ( Kirton, 1976 ) . An organization needs both styles: the first produces most of the incremental innovation on which operational efficiency depends, while the second opens up new possibilities. A culture that celebrates only one of them forfeits half its capacity. The differences extend well beyond creative style. Some people think out loud and need dialogue, some need time alone before they share an idea, and some express an idea better through a prototype than through words. An enabling culture therefore needs flexible entry routes for ideas: A short conversation with someone who has the authority to steer the idea to its next step. A prototype or a practical demonstration instead of a written document. A written proposal for those who prefer to think on paper. The option of submitting the idea in the name of a team or of its owner alone, as the owner prefers. The value of these routes depends on all of them leading into the same system and being held to the same standards. Flexibility of entry means removing barriers unrelated to the quality of the idea, while the standards remain the same.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: If people learn culture from what happens, then changing it runs through changing what happens. Schein identifies a set of primary mechanisms by which leaders embed culture, whether they intend to or not ( Schein, 2010 ) . Table 8.3 presents them, along with what people learn from each and an example from the university case we follow throughout the book. Table 8.3 Culture-embedding mechanisms, adapted from Schein (2010) Mechanism What people learn from it Example from the university What leaders pay attention to, measure and monitor What really matters If periodic reports ask only about exam pass rates, that is what professors will care about Responses to incidents and crises What is safe and what is risky How the first experiment was treated when a professor changed the way a course was assessed and some students objected Allocation of resources What the priority is Are hours or a budget allocated for developing courses through innovative projects, or does this remain voluntary effort? Role modeling and teaching What behavior is expected Leaders who take part in judging student projects and ask about them Allocation of rewards and status What is valued Does supervising students' innovative projects count toward promotion and the annual evaluation? Recruitment, selection and promotion Who succeeds here Is the ability to teach creativity taken into account when selecting new professors and department heads? The table reveals why campaigns fail: they work with a single tool, rhetoric, while the six mechanisms pull in the opposite direction. The reverse route is slower and harder, but it is the only one that changes assumptions: leadership starts with one or two mechanisms that everyone can see, such as its response to the first intelligent failure, or counting the supervision of innovative projects toward promotion, and then keeps them consistent until people believe them. Principle Culture is what happens after the first failure, after the first objection, and after the first idea that comes from the most junior employee. These moments are more truthful than anything written about values.

search.c: Chapter 8: Innovation culture and the enabling environment
search.t: Culture has three levels: artifacts, espoused values and basic assumptions. The last of these governs behavior and resists slogans. An innovative culture rests on combining balanced qualities: tolerance of failure with intolerance of incompetence, experimentation with discipline, safety with candor, and collaboration with accountability. Psychological safety is a condition for candid discussion, and the learning and innovation zone is reached when safety and high standards come together. Failure comes in types: preventable, complexity-related and intelligent. Each type has its own response, and confusing them teaches people not to experiment. Rewards support creativity when they are tied to creativity itself and carry information about the quality of performance. The most effective forms of motivation cost little: acknowledgment, involvement, autonomy, and a sense of progress in meaningful work. Gifted people in particular are highly sensitive to recognition of their worth. An enabling culture makes room for different thinking styles, offering ideas flexible entry routes governed by a single set of standards. Culture changes when leaders change what they pay attention to, measure and reward, and through how they respond to revealing incidents. Key Terms Organizational culture Organizational culture The shared assumptions a group has learned and passes on to its new members as the correct way to think and act. Creative climate Creative climate The patterns of behavior and feeling observed in daily work that encourage or hinder creativity. Psychological safety Psychological safety A shared belief within a team that asking questions, objecting and admitting mistakes will not bring punishment or embarrassment. Intelligent failure Intelligent failure An unexpected result of a small, thoughtful experiment in unknown territory that yields new knowledge. Culture-embedding mechanisms Culture-embedding mechanisms The practices from which people learn the actual culture, such as measurement, reward and responses to crises. search.s: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: 9 Chapter 9 Innovation teams and organization-wide participation In this chapter we move from the individual to the group: how innovation teams are formed and organized, and what distinguishes a team that carries its idea through to implementation. We then widen the lens to broader organizational participation: how an organization can open the door to innovation for all its employees without drowning in ideas it cannot respond to.

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Opening case: A technical team (composite case) An organization tasked a team of five outstanding engineers in its IT department with developing a solution to reduce data-entry errors in a service run by the operations unit. The team worked enthusiastically for four months, built a sophisticated automated validation system, and presented it at a closing meeting where it won the admiration of everyone in the room. Two weeks later, however, the operations staff refused to use it: it added three screens to a procedure they performed dozens of times a day, and no one had asked them during development how they actually worked. The problem was not the engineers' competence. It was that the entire team had come from one place and had worked within its own boundaries. The case shows that a good team requires more than good individuals. An innovative team is designed: whom it includes, what roles its members play, how it connects with people outside it, and where it sits in the structure. These questions are the focus of this chapter. We take them up one by one before moving on to the wider participation that opens innovation to every employee. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain why innovation increasingly relies on teams, and identify what distinguishes innovative teams. Form an innovation team that is balanced in knowledge and roles. Describe a team's activities with external parties and link them to its success. Compare team structures and choose the one that fits the degree of innovation. Design broad organizational participation that the organization is able to respond to.

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Wuchty, Jones, and Uzzi analyzed some twenty million scientific papers and two million patents spanning several decades. They found that teams have come to dominate knowledge production in nearly every field, and that work produced by teams is more likely to be highly influential than work produced by individuals ( Wuchty et al., 2007 ) . The explanation is that the problems worth innovating on have become too complex for any single discipline to encompass, and the knowledge needed to solve them is distributed among different people. Yet a team is not the sum of its members. A team of average performers may achieve what a team of stars cannot, if it knows how to combine its members' knowledge and reach the people it needs. Innovators need an environment, and the team is the environment closest to them; it is there that they find, or fail to find, much of what they need. This is borne out in the experiences of innovators themselves. In a phenomenological study of the experiences of prominent Saudi innovators, nine of the eleven participants counted working with a supportive team among the reasons for their success, as when a partner took over operational tasks so that the innovator could concentrate on development ( Alsamani, 2023 ) .

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Hülsheger, Anderson, and Salgado brought together more than thirty years of research in a meta-analysis of team-level predictors of innovation. They found that factors related to processes within the team had a stronger effect than factors related to its composition ( Hülsheger et al., 2009 ) . Figure 9.1 summarizes the most prominent of these factors. Shared vision A clear goal that members understand, agree on, and see as valuable Process factor: strong effect Support for innovation Practical expectation and encouragement of attempts to introduce new ways of working Process factor: strong effect External communication The team's contact with those outside it: beneficiaries, experts, and decision makers Process factor: strong effect Task orientation Commitment to quality, constructive mutual critique, and continuous review Process factor: moderate effect Cohesion Bonds among members; its effect is smaller than expected Process factor: moderate effect Job-relevant diversity Different disciplines and experience relevant to the problem Composition factor: small positive effect Background diversity Such as age and gender, with no direct bearing on the task Composition factor: near-zero or negative effect Team size and longevity A weaker effect, contingent on the nature of the task Composition factor: limited effect Figure 9.1 Team-level innovation factors, ranked approximately by strength of effect, adapted from Hülsheger et al. (2009) . The bars are illustrative and do not represent numerical values. This finding has a direct practical implication. Organizations invest considerable effort in selecting team members, then leave the team to work without a shared vision, without contact with beneficiaries, or without real support for experimentation. The research suggests that what happens within and around the team matters more than the list of its members' names. Note, too, that diversity helps when it is diversity of knowledge relevant to the specific problem. Another review showed that diversity cuts both ways: it broadens the knowledge available to the team, but it can also open the door to division, and the outcome depends on the team's ability to exchange and integrate information ( van Knippenberg & Schippers, 2007 ) .

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Team configurations vary as widely as their tasks, but innovation teams generally need five roles to be covered; in small teams, one person may hold more than one of them: Team leader: keeps the problem and purpose clear, coordinates the work, and protects the team's time. Voice of the beneficiary: someone who lives the problem or knows those who do, and who brings the team back to it whenever it drifts away. This role's absence is what caused the team in the opening case to fail. Technical expertise: the specialized knowledge needed to build and test the solution. Voice of operations: someone who knows how the solution will be used day to day, and what will hinder its adoption once the project ends. Sponsor: a leader from outside the team with the authority to remove obstacles and secure resources, as Chapter 3 explained. Composition is also tied to stage. While exploring the problem, the team needs wider diversity and closer proximity to beneficiaries. While developing the solution, it needs technical depth. At scale-up, it needs people with operational experience. Team composition is therefore best treated as a decision to be revisited as the initiative moves from one stage to the next. Equally important is the way members join the team. A team whose members join by choice, out of interest in the problem, starts with a different kind of motivation from one whose members were assigned without being asked. Many organizations combine the two: leadership defines the problem and the roles required, then opens the door to anyone who wishes to volunteer. This is another application of autonomy within boundaries.

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.s: 9.4 The team and its boundaries: working beyond the team
search.t: External communication was among the strongest innovation factors in the meta-analysis above. Ancona and Caldwell studied this aspect in product development teams and found that the most successful teams were not necessarily those with the most external contact, but those that carried out specific kinds of external activity, above all communicating with leadership to secure support and resources, and coordinating with the other units on which the work depended. Teams that confined themselves to gathering general information, without these two activities, performed worse ( Ancona & Caldwell, 1992 ) . Figure 9.2 illustrates these activities. Ambassador Communicating with leaders and sponsors: reporting progress, securing resources, and shielding the team from pressure Task coordination Working with the units the team depends on: operations, IT, legal, and beneficiaries Scouting Gathering knowledge: what has been tried before, who has the expertise, and what has changed in the environment The team Needs all three activities, and most often lacks the first and second Figure 9.2 The team's activities with external parties, adapted from Ancona & Caldwell (1992) . This finding casts the opening case in a new light: the engineering team succeeded at technical scouting and presented its final result skillfully to leadership, but it never coordinated with the unit that would use the solution. It also confirms what Chapter 7 said about the importance of a network of relationships in moving an idea into implementation ( Baer, 2012 ) . An innovative team works at its boundaries as much as within them. In Practice Write down the names of the people whose cooperation your team needs for its solution to be genuinely used. Then put a mark next to those you have spoken with in the past four weeks. The unmarked names are your project's biggest risks.

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Where a team sits in the structure depends on the degree of innovation required. Clark and Wheelwright distinguished four structures for development teams, graded by how fully members are dedicated to the team and how much authority its leader holds ( Clark & Wheelwright, 1992 ) . Table 9.1 presents them. Table 9.1 Innovation team structures, adapted from Clark & Wheelwright (1992) Structure What it looks like Suited to Risk Functional Each member works in their own unit, and the work passes from one unit to the next in sequence Small improvements within a single unit Slowness, and no one who owns the whole outcome Lightweight A coordinator follows up the work, while members remain attached to their units Improvements that touch more than one unit to a limited extent A coordinator without authority, so unit priorities prevail Heavyweight A leader with strong authority and members dedicated part- or full-time, who remain linked to their units Significant innovation that requires integration across units Tension between the leader and unit managers if authority is not settled Autonomous A dedicated team outside the usual structure, with its own rules and resources Radical innovation, or innovation that conflicts with the existing model Difficulty bringing the solution back into the organization once it succeeds Organizations frequently assign lightweight teams to tasks that call for heavyweight ones: employees are asked to devise a solution that will change how three departments work, they work on it after finishing their regular duties, and they are led by a coordinator who cannot ask anything of anyone. The result is predictable. This connects with what Chapter 6 showed about time as the scarcest enabler of innovation.

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Alongside assigned teams, many organizations seek to involve all their employees in innovation through idea platforms, competitions, and internal challenges. This is the right direction: valuable ideas can come from anywhere, and the employee closest to a problem sees it before anyone else. Yet such participation often fails for a simple reason. The organization opens the door to more ideas than it can respond to, most of them end up in decision limbo, and participants learn that taking part is pointless. A study of an open idea platform launched by a major technology company reveals another side of the problem. Bayus found that repeat contributors were better than others at offering ideas the company judged valuable, but they seldom repeated their first success once their ideas had been implemented, tending instead to propose ideas resembling what had worked before ( Bayus, 2013 ) . A steady flow of good ideas therefore takes more than a platform; it takes a design that keeps renewing broad participation. Successful participation tends to share four features: The challenge before the platform: time-bound campaigns that start from challenge questions set by the strategy, as Chapter 4 explained, rather than an open box for everything. The response before the invitation: before any campaign is launched, it is settled who will read the ideas, when, and how their authors will receive a reply. From idea to team: the best ideas become small teams that include their originators and receive time and resources to test them, rather than being handed to another unit to implement. A network close to people: individuals in different units who serve as innovation ambassadors. They know the system, help colleagues frame their ideas, and carry challenges from the field to the responsible unit. At a university, this might take the form of an annual innovation day at which students present their projects alongside their faculty supervisors, with senior leaders attending and taking part in the judging. The value of such a day lies in meeting several needs at once at modest cost: an opportunity to present, public recognition, connections between students and the bodies that could support their projects, and a signal from leadership about what it cares about. This is close to what one participant in the innovator study cited above recounted about a business incubator he had visited: he found that one secret of its success was that it brought emerging innovators together with innovators who had succeeded within the past three years, because they were closer to the obstacles the newcomers would face ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . Principle Broad participation is a promise to people that their ideas will be heard. The organization's capacity to keep that promise is what should determine how much participation it asks for.

search.c: Chapter 9: Innovation teams and organization-wide participation
search.t: Teams have become the predominant source of knowledge production and innovation, because problems require knowledge distributed among different people. What happens within and around the team, such as a shared vision, support for innovation, and external communication, affects innovation more than the team's composition does. Useful diversity is diversity of knowledge relevant to the problem, and its payoff depends on the team's ability to integrate that knowledge. Innovation teams need five roles: the leader, the voice of the beneficiary, technical expertise, the voice of operations, and the sponsor. The most successful teams work at their boundaries: they communicate with leadership and coordinate with the units they depend on. A team's structure is chosen according to the degree of innovation; assigning a lightweight team to a task that needs a heavyweight one is among the most common causes of failure. Broad participation is a promise of response, and so it should be designed to match the organization's capacity to keep that promise. Innovation ambassador network Innovation ambassador network People in different units who help their colleagues frame their ideas and connect the field with the innovation system. 10 Chapter 10 Governance and portfolio management In this chapter we address how innovation decisions are made: to whom each category of decision belongs, how the gates between stages are designed, how idea owners are treated fairly when the outcome is not what they hoped for, and why initiatives that should have been stopped keep going. We then turn to how initiatives are managed together as a balanced portfolio.

Opening case: An innovation committee (composite case) The innovation committee of one organization meets once every two months and is made up of eight senior managers. Each meeting's agenda carries between fifteen and twenty initiatives, with ten minutes allotted to each. An initiative is presented, a few general questions are asked, and the team is asked for “further study.” Two years on, the portfolio held forty-two active initiatives; not one had been stopped, and not one had been scaled. Every team was working with a quarter of the resources it needed, waiting for the next meeting. The committee was neither lenient nor strict; it was absent from the decision while present at the meeting. It never defined what it would decide itself and what it would leave to the teams, it never asked for different evidence at each stage, and it never stopped what needed stopping so as to free up resources for others. Closing these gaps is what the governance we set out in this chapter is built to do. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain how innovation governance differs from the governance of stable operations. Allocate decision rights between governance levels and teams. Design gates whose criteria progress from assumptions to evidence. Apply the principles of procedural justice in dealing with idea owners. Explain escalation of commitment, and set kill criteria in advance. Manage initiatives as a balanced portfolio funded in stages.

Most governance tools in organizations were designed for stable work: an annual plan, a budget approved in advance, fixed performance indicators, and accountability for deviations from the plan. These tools work well when the path is known. In innovation, however, the path itself is unknown, and departing from the original plan may be evidence of learning. Innovation governance therefore fails in two directions: when the tools of stable work are applied to innovation, they stifle it; when innovation is exempted from governance altogether, it consumes resources without results. Governance suited to innovation rests on a simple idea: investing in an initiative buys learning that reduces uncertainty, and every subsequent decision builds on what the team has learned. An initiative is not asked at the outset for what it cannot yet have, nor is it allowed at the end to continue without what it must have. This is what the following sections build.

Much governance confusion stems from ambiguous decision rights. Who decides whether an initiative continues? Who decides how it is carried out? Who decides how resources are allocated across initiatives? When these questions go unanswered, all decisions drift upward, and senior committees become crowded with details they lack the knowledge to judge, as in the opening case. Figure 10.1 proposes a distribution of decision rights across three levels that applies the principle of autonomy within boundaries: leadership determines the “what” and the “why,” and teams own the “how.” Level Decides Does not decide Senior leadership Board or steering committee, two or three times a year Search fields and challenge questions, total investment, portfolio balance, and the big bets The details of individual initiatives and how they are carried out Portfolio committee Monthly or at gates Gate decisions: continue, modify, merge, suspend, or stop, and funding for the next stage How the team works within a stage The team and its sponsor Continuously Designing experiments, ways of working, and use of the approved stage resources Exceeding the stage's limits or resources without returning to the gate Figure 10.1 The distribution of decision rights in innovation governance. Prepared by the author. In this distribution, senior leadership's role remains the most far-reaching even though it makes fewer decisions: it determines where the organization searches, how much risk it takes, and how it balances the near term against the long term. These decisions are often neglected because they are harder than reviewing individual initiatives. The international standard for innovation management systems assigns top management responsibility for setting innovation policy and strategy, providing resources, and defining roles and authorities ( ISO, 2024 ) , which is consistent with this distribution. Decision rights are best written down and announced, so that the team knows what it can decide on its own without waiting, and when it must return to the gate. Putting them in writing protects both sides: it shields the team from interference in the details of its work, and it shields the organization from initiatives expanding without a decision.

Among the most widespread tools of innovation governance is the Stage-Gate system developed by Cooper. The system divides an initiative's journey into stages separated by gates, at which a decision is made to continue, stop, suspend, or recycle the work according to criteria set in advance ( Cooper, 1990 ) . The value of a gate is that it turns a decision from a general impression into a specific question: has the initiative generated enough knowledge to merit investment in the next stage? The most important principle in gate design is that the criteria change from one stage to the next . At the early gates, it is enough that the problem matters and the assumptions are stated. With each gate, stronger evidence is required, until the initiative reaches the scaling gate with evidence of adoption, cost, and sustainability. Table 3.1 set out the leader's question and the type of evidence at each stage, and Figure 10.2 illustrates the logic of this progression. Opportunity gate Does the problem matter, and is it consistent with the search fields? Are the assumptions written down? Idea gate Have the riskiest assumptions been tested with small experiments? What have we learned? Pilot gate Is there preliminary evidence of value? Are the risks acceptable and the pilot's limits clear? Scaling gate Are beneficiaries actually adopting the solution? What is its actual cost? Who will operate it? Stated assumptions, small investment → Strong evidence, large investment Figure 10.2 Gate criteria progressing from assumptions to evidence, with investment increasing alongside them. Prepared by the author, drawing on Cooper (1990) . The Stage-Gate system has been criticized for becoming slow and bureaucratic, and for fitting poorly with highly novel initiatives in which the understanding of the problem itself shifts as the work proceeds. Cooper responded to this criticism with hybrid models that combine gates with agile ways of working: shorter stages, lighter gates for small initiatives, and short build-and-test cycles within each stage ( Cooper, 2014 ) . The lesson is that a gate is first and foremost a tool for learning and decision making, and that its depth should match the size of the risk: a small, low-cost experiment does not need the same gate as rolling out a solution across the entire organization, as Chapter 3 cautioned. Caution A gate that always ends in approval is not a gate. If no initiative has been stopped at a gate over a full year, then either the organization chooses its ideas with rare brilliance, or the gates are not working.

Chapter 5 presented three ways to prevent decision limbo: an announced response time, a reasoned response, and periodic review. One question remains: why does a reasoned response matter so much to the idea owner, even when it is a rejection? Research on procedural justice provides the answer. Kim and Mauborgne showed that people accept decisions that do not go their way, and continue to cooperate, if they see the process by which those decisions were made as fair. This fairness rests on three principles: engagement , giving those concerned the opportunity to present their views and ideas; explanation , setting out the reasons for the decision; and expectation clarity , making known what will be required next and the criteria by which it will be judged ( Kim & Mauborgne, 1997 ) . In innovation governance, these principles translate into specific practices: Criteria announced before evaluation: idea owners know in advance on what basis they will be evaluated, so they are not surprised by a criterion that was never mentioned. An opportunity to present in person: at major gates, the team presents its initiative itself and answers questions, rather than having it discussed in its absence. A response with four elements: what was decided, why, what would have changed the decision, and what next step is open to the idea owner. Attributing the idea to its owner: the idea owner's name stays attached to the idea through every stage, and they are involved in implementing it if they wish, rather than having it handed to another unit that carries it out without them. In this way, governance itself becomes a means of meeting the innovator's needs set out in Chapter 7, particularly recognition and understanding. An organization that rejects an idea fairly keeps its owner; one that accepts an idea without crediting its owner may lose them.

Innovation portfolios suffer from a problem that is the reverse of decision limbo: initiatives that continue even though the evidence does not support them. Staw studied this phenomenon, which he called escalation of commitment . In his experiment, participants who were personally responsible for a failing investment decision allocated more additional funds to it than did those who were not responsible for it ( Staw, 1976 ) . People tend to persist with a decision they have made in order to justify their original choice, even when new evidence points the other way. In innovation governance, escalation takes familiar forms: an initiative sponsored by a senior leader, which no one dares propose stopping; an initiative on which a great deal has been spent, prompting the refrain “we can't stop now”; and an initiative run by an enthusiastic team that, it is feared, would be demoralized by a stop. Three practices curb this escalation: Kill criteria set in advance: at the start of each stage, the results that would stop the initiative, whether achieved or missed, are defined before anyone becomes attached to it. Separating the decision from its original owner: parties other than the sponsor who championed the initiative take part in the decision to continue. Honoring a good stop: a team that stopped its initiative at the right time and documented what it learned has done good work, and is treated accordingly. This is a direct application of the concept of intelligent failure from Chapter 8. This explains the opening case: a committee that stops nothing spreads innovation resources across more initiatives than it can fund, and so weakens them all.

If gates govern the individual initiative, portfolio management governs initiatives collectively. In their study of company practices, Cooper, Edgett, and Kleinschmidt found that portfolio management pursues three goals: maximizing total value, balancing types of initiatives, and aligning with strategy. They also found that one of the most common problems is having more initiatives than resources allow, so that all of them are delayed ( Cooper et al., 2001 ) . Figure 10.3 illustrates these goals. Value Does the portfolio as a whole deliver the greatest possible value with the resources available? The decisive question: If we were starting today, would we choose these initiatives? Balance Does it combine core improvement, adjacent expansion, and transformational bets; the near term and the long term; low and high risk? The decisive question: What will we have left in five years? Alignment Do the initiatives serve the search fields set by the strategy, and are resources allocated according to its priorities? The decisive question: Does the portfolio resemble our strategy? Figure 10.3 The goals of innovation portfolio management, adapted from Cooper et al. (2001) . Balance is tied to the degrees of innovation presented in Chapter 1: incremental, adjacent, and radical. Nagji and Tuff propose that resources be distributed among them in proportions suited to the nature of the organization ( Nagji & Tuff, 2012 ) . The right proportion varies from one organization to another, but a portfolio that lacks any one of the three types calls for an explicit question about why. One of the most important tools of portfolio management is staged funding . Rather than approving an initiative's full budget at the outset, it is funded stage by stage, with each stage's funding tied to passing its gate. Gompers showed that venture capital firms rely on this approach because it preserves their ability to review and stop, and that they shorten the interval between funding rounds as uncertainty increases ( Gompers, 1995 ) . The logic of real options explains why: a small investment at an early stage is like buying an option that allows the organization to invest more if the opportunity materializes, or to stop with a limited loss if it does not ( McGrath, 1999 ) . By this logic, early failure becomes a reasonable price for knowledge that cannot be gained without experimentation. The portfolio concept extends beyond the initiatives within a single unit. In organizations with multiple innovation units, such as the university described in Chapter 6 with its accelerator, its digital fabrication lab (Fab Lab), and its centers, each unit manages its own portfolio in isolation, so initiatives are duplicated and ideas get lost in the gaps between units. The alternative is a shared portfolio: a single entry point for ideas, shared gates, and the movement of an initiative from one unit to another according to its stage. We return to this design in Chapter 20. In Practice List all the active initiatives in your organization, then ask of each: If it were presented to us today for the first time, knowing what we know now, would we start it? The initiatives for which the answer is “no” are candidates for stopping, and their resources are candidates for initiatives that deserve them more.

For each gate in your system, write a short charter that answers the following questions, and share it with teams before the stage begins. If you cannot answer one of the questions, that is a governance gap that should be closed before the stage begins. Innovation governance differs from the governance of stable work: investment buys learning that reduces uncertainty, and every decision builds on what the team has learned. Decision rights are distributed across three levels: senior leadership for direction and balance, the portfolio committee for gates, and the team for ways of working. Gate criteria progress from assumptions to evidence, and their depth is proportionate to the size of the risk. People accept decisions that go against their interests when they are confident the process is fair: through engagement, explanation, and clear expectations. Escalation of commitment keeps alive initiatives that should have been stopped; it is curbed by setting kill criteria in advance, separating the decision from its original owner, and honoring a good stop. Portfolio management seeks value, balance, and alignment, and avoids piling up initiatives on limited resources. Staged funding preserves the ability to review, and makes early failure a limited price for knowledge. Key Terms Decision rights Decision rights A specification of who has the authority to make each type of innovation decision. Stage-Gate Stage-Gate A system that divides an initiative's journey into stages separated by decision points with criteria set in advance. Procedural justice Procedural justice The fairness of the way a decision is made, based on engagement, explanation, and expectation clarity. Escalation of commitment Escalation of commitment Continuing to invest in a failing course of action in order to justify the original decision. Staged funding Staged funding Funding an initiative stage by stage, with each tranche tied to passing a gate. Real options Real options A logic that views a small early investment as a right to expand later or to stop with a limited loss. 11 Chapter 11 Understanding problems and opportunities With this chapter we begin the initiative journey at its proper starting point: the problem, which comes before the idea. We trace the sources of opportunity, ways of understanding a problem from the perspective of those who live it, and methods for framing and reframing it, and then the criteria for selecting, from among many problems, those worth investing in.

Opening case: A government service (composite case) A government agency was receiving repeated complaints about how long one of its services took to complete. It formed a team to improve the service, and the team started from an assumption that seemed self-evident: the problem lay in the slowness of the online system. Eight months and considerable expense later, a much faster system was launched, and the complaints did not decline. When a new team member sat down with a number of service users and traced their journey step by step, he discovered that most of the delay had nothing to do with the system: a third of all applications were being returned because applicants did not know which documents were required, and they found out only days after applying. The solution that ended most of the complaints was a clear checklist of documents displayed before an application began. The team had not been negligent; it had efficiently solved the problem it had defined. But it had solved the wrong problem. The subject of this chapter is the step that should have preceded its work and was overlooked: understanding the problem before seeking a solution. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain why finding and formulating a problem is creative work that determines the quality of the solution. Identify internal and external sources of opportunity, and recognize lead users. Use observation, interviews, and journey mapping to understand a problem from the perspective of those who live it. Formulate and reframe a problem in ways that open up new solutions. Prioritize problems by their importance and by current satisfaction with existing solutions.

search.s: 11.1 Why does the journey begin with the problem?
search.t: Chapter 1 corrected a common belief that innovation begins with ideas, showing that the more accurate starting point is a need, problem, or opportunity, with the idea coming afterward as a hypothesis for a solution. The opening case shows the price of ignoring this: the team began with a solution idea, invested in it, and revisited the problem only after the solution had failed. This case has many parallels. In a survey of 106 senior executives in 91 public and private organizations across 17 countries, 85 percent said their organizations were poor at diagnosing problems, and 87 percent said this weakness carried significant costs ( Wedell-Wedellsborg, 2017 ) . Organizations tend to jump to solutions because a solution feels like productive work, whereas pausing over the problem feels like delay. Problem finding has a creative dimension that many overlook. In a classic study, Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi followed art students who were asked to produce a drawing from a set of available objects. Students who spent more time exploring and selecting the objects, and who changed their conception as they worked, produced drawings that judges rated as more original, and seven years later they were more successful in their artistic careers ( Getzels & Csikszentmihalyi, 1976 ) . How they engaged with the problem before solving it was part of the creativity itself. This is why the innovator's path model, presented in Chapter 7, begins its thinking phase by defining the problem before generating ideas.

Drucker held that systematic innovation rests on an organized search for changes that create opportunities. He identified seven sources of such opportunities, four within the organization or its industry and three in the wider environment ( Drucker, 1985 ) , as Figure 11.1 shows. Within the organization and its sector The unexpected: a success, failure, or event no one anticipated The incongruity: a gap between what is and what ought to be Process need: a weak or missing link in the way work is done Changes in industry or market structure In the wider environment Demographic changes: in age, education, and distribution Changes in perception: in the way people view things New knowledge: scientific, technical, and otherwise Figure 11.1 The seven sources of innovative opportunity, adapted from Drucker (1985) . Drucker observes that the first sources are closer at hand and less risky, while new knowledge, for all its appeal, has the longest road to application and the highest risk. This matters for organizations that equate innovation with new technology; many of the nearest opportunities lie in complaints, recurring errors, procedures that people bypass, and unexpected results whose causes no one has asked about. Chapter 4 linked the wider environment to foresight and the external realities scanning matrix; this chapter focuses on the nearer sources. One source deserves particular attention: lead users . Von Hippel defined them as people who face a need months or years before most others do, and who expect to benefit significantly from meeting it, so they often innovate solutions for themselves before any provider offers one ( von Hippel, 1986 ) . Every organization has lead users: an employee who has built a spreadsheet to shortcut a repetitive task, or a service user who habitually brings a document that was not requested because they know it will be asked for later. The people closest to problems are those who work with them every day. For example, the student in Chapter 7's opening case noticed a real problem during her field placement that people who had worked at the organization for years had not. Field placements, applied projects in courses, and work with external organizations are all sources of problems that a university can turn into a structured entry point to its innovation system.

search.s: 11.3 Understanding the person who has the problem
search.t: If a problem lives in a person's experience, understanding it requires getting close to that experience. This principle is the foundation of design thinking , which begins with a deep understanding of people's lives and needs before moving on to generate solutions ( Brown, 2008 ) . Liedtka points out that the value of this approach lies less in its tools than in its capacity to counter well-known biases in thinking, such as the belief that others see the world as we do, settling for the first plausible explanation, and becoming attached to the first solution ( Liedtka, 2018 ) . Understanding a problem relies on three main tools: Observation: watching what people actually do in their context, not what they say they do. People are often unable to describe what has become habitual for them, or do not see a problem in it because they have adapted to it. In-depth interviews: open questions about specific experiences, such as “Tell me about the last time…”, rather than general questions or requests for opinions on a proposed solution. Journey mapping: charting the steps of a person's experience from beginning to end, how they feel at each step, and where they stumble. This is what uncovered the real problem in the opening case. Among the most telling indicators of need are workarounds : the ways people devise to cope with a problem no one has solved for them. The employee who keeps a separate notebook because the system does not allow what they need, and the service user who calls a friend working at the agency to learn the status of an application, both point to a real need that people are expending effort to meet. A need that people make no effort to work around may not be as important as it appears. The jobs to be done framework offers a complementary angle. Christensen and colleagues suggest asking: What is the person trying to accomplish in a particular circumstance? People draw on a service or product to make progress in their lives ( Christensen et al., 2016 ) . What the service user in the opening case wants is to complete the transaction in a single visit without surprises, and the system's speed is only a partial means to that end. This difference in framing is what would have changed the team's entire course. In Practice Before your next meeting about a problem in your organization, spend one hour with someone who lives it: an employee who carries out the procedure, or a beneficiary who goes through it. Do not present a solution, and do not ask for their opinion of an idea. Ask them to show you how they work, and write down everything that surprises you.

The way a problem is formulated determines which solutions can be seen. Wedell-Wedellsborg offers a well-known example: the tenants of a building complain that the elevator is slow. If the problem is framed as “the elevator is slow,” solutions turn toward speeding it up or replacing it at great cost. If it is framed as “the wait is annoying,” it may be enough to put a mirror next to the elevator; people waiting become absorbed in looking at it and no longer notice how long they wait ( Wedell-Wedellsborg, 2017 ) . This does not mean the second framing is always right; the elevator may really be slow. The point is that a single problem admits multiple framings, and searching for them reveals solutions that were previously invisible. Figure 11.2 illustrates the reframing in the opening case. Initial framing “The online system is slow.” Possible solutions: upgrading the system, adding servers, or replacing it. Reframing “Applicants don't know what they need before they start, so their applications are returned.” Possible solutions: a clear document checklist, instant verification at submission, or dropping documents that are not needed. Figure 11.2 Reframing the problem in the opening case, and its effect on the possible solutions. Simple questions can aid reframing. Are we looking at the problem from the perspective of the person who lives it, or of the one who provides the service? What happens before and after the problem? Is it a symptom of a deeper problem? Is there anyone in the same circumstances who does not suffer from it, and why? Asking “Why?” repeatedly until a root cause is reached is a useful tool here, provided it does not turn into a hunt for someone to blame. In the public sector especially, many problems are of the kind Rittel and Webber called wicked problems : they cannot be given a definitive formulation, their understanding is shaped by the solutions proposed for them, there is no clear rule for knowing when they have been solved, and every attempt to solve them changes the problem itself ( Rittel & Webber, 1973 ) . With problems of this kind, framing becomes an ongoing process renewed as the work advances, and small-scale experimentation, the subject of Chapter 14, becomes a tool for understanding the problem as much as for testing the solution. This stage ends with a clear problem statement on which the team can build. A good statement covers: Who is struggling? In what circumstances? What are they trying to accomplish? What is getting in their way? What is the evidence? It is then turned into a challenge question that opens the way to solutions without prescribing them, usually beginning “How might we…?”, as Chapter 4 showed in moving from search fields to challenge questions.

An organization discovers more problems than it can work on, so it needs a way to choose those worth investing in. Ulwick proposes a simple criterion: measure each need on two dimensions, its importance to the person who lives it and their satisfaction with the current way it is met. The biggest opportunities are important needs whose current solutions leave people dissatisfied ( Ulwick, 2002 ) . Figure 11.3 illustrates this logic. Importance to those who live the problem Major opportunity An important need, and current solutions fall short. The top priority for investment. Served need An important need, and current solutions satisfy. Improvement is possible, but the return is lower. Secondary need An unimportant need that goes unserved. Monitor it, but do not put it ahead of others. Overserved An unimportant need with satisfying solutions. Possibly an opportunity to simplify and cut costs. Satisfaction with current solutions → Figure 11.3 Prioritizing problems by their importance and by satisfaction with current solutions, adapted from Ulwick (2002) . The top row indicates high importance, and the right-hand column high satisfaction. To these two dimensions we add three questions. Does the problem fall within one of the search fields set by the strategy in Chapter 4? How strong is the evidence for its existence and scale? Is there anyone in the organization with the motivation and ability to work on it? An important problem that no one is enthusiastic about, or that falls outside the organization's priorities, may end up in decision limbo however valuable it is. Principle The time spent understanding a problem is the cheapest and most consequential stage of innovation, even if it looks like a delay to the solution. Changing how a problem is framed at the outset costs nothing; changing a solution after it has been built costs a great deal.

The initiative journey starts from the problem rather than the idea; in a large survey, most executives acknowledged that their organizations were weak at diagnosing problems and that this weakness was costly. Finding and formulating a problem is an integral part of creativity itself, closely tied to the originality of solutions. Opportunities have near sources, such as the unexpected, incongruities, and process needs, and more distant ones, such as demographic change and new knowledge. Lead users are a particular source of emerging needs. The person with the problem is understood through observation, interviews, and journey mapping, and workarounds are among the most telling indicators of need. How a problem is formulated sets the horizon of possible solutions, and reframing reveals solutions that were hidden; wicked problems, for their part, call for continual reframing. Problems are prioritized by their importance and satisfaction with current solutions, their link to strategy, the strength of the evidence, and whether someone will champion them.
