12 Chapter 12 Developing innovative solutions In this chapter we travel the road from a well-understood problem to a solution worth testing. We show how solution requirements are defined, how alternatives are generated and weighed against one another, what obstacles keep thinking trapped in the first solution, and why organizations tend, without meaning to, to reject the new. We then turn to how an idea matures into a testable concept.

Opening case: A hackathon (composite case) An organization ran a forty-eight-hour hackathon around a single question: How might we reduce food waste at social events? Within the first hour, someone on almost every team proposed an app connecting event hosts with charities, and the teams set off building near-identical versions of it. One team offered a different idea: estimating how much food an event would need in advance, using data from past events, so that the surplus would never arise in the first place. But the team could not prove the accuracy of its estimates in two days, the judging panel considered the idea immature, and the prize went to a polished app resembling ones already on the market. A year later, the advance-estimation idea was in use at a number of event halls, introduced by another organization. Three phenomena that form the subject of this chapter converged in this case: teams fixating on the first solution that occurred to them, a phase of searching for alternatives that was cut short, and evaluators' tendency to prefer the familiar and finished over the new and unfinished. These phenomena stem less from individual shortcomings than from well-known patterns in human thinking, and an organization can design its work in ways that limit them. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Translate a challenge question into requirements against which any proposed solution can be measured. Design idea-generation sessions that separate expanding from narrowing and avoid the obstacles of group work. Recognize fixation on the first solution and use methods to break it. Explain the bias against new ideas in evaluation, and design evaluation that limits it. Formulate a testable concept with explicit assumptions.

search.s: 12.1 From challenge question to solution requirements
search.t: The previous chapter ended with a challenge question that opens the door to solutions without prescribing them. Before idea generation begins, the team needs an intermediate step that is often neglected: defining the solution requirements , that is, what any solution must achieve to count as successful, whatever form it takes. In product development methodologies, user needs are translated into measurable target specifications before concept design begins, so that they serve as a reference for comparing alternatives ( Ulrich et al., 2020 ) . Requirements usually fall into two kinds: essential requirements , without which no solution is acceptable, and desirable requirements , which are used to choose among solutions. In the government service example from the previous chapter, essential requirements might include that applicants know every required document before starting their application, and that the solution work for people who are not comfortable with technology. A desirable requirement might be reducing the number of documents itself. This step yields two benefits. It keeps the team from judging ideas by impression, because it sets an agreed standard before any ideas appear. And it widens the search, because a requirement describes what must be achieved without saying how , leaving room for solutions of different forms that serve the same end. Here again we see the logic of autonomy within boundaries: the requirements are clear boundaries, and the solution is an open space within them.

Guilford distinguished between two kinds of thinking: divergent thinking , which produces many varied answers to a single question, and convergent thinking , which arrives at the most fitting answer ( Guilford, 1967 ) . Developing solutions requires both, but mixing them at the same moment weakens each: judging every idea the instant it appears halts the flow of ideas, while generating without ever deciding prevents a decision from being reached. This is why Osborn called for deferring judgment during generation, as Chapter 7 discussed ( Osborn, 1953 ) . Figure 12.1 illustrates this sequence. Expand Narrow Expand Narrow Problem (Chapter 11) Challenge question and requirements Solutions (this chapter) Testable concept Broad exploration of the problem Many varied alternatives Figure 12.1 The alternation of expanding and narrowing: once to understand the problem, and once to develop the solution. Prepared by the author, drawing on the concepts of divergent and convergent thinking in Guilford (1967) . Research offers specific guidance for designing the expanding phase. Group brainstorming, for all its popularity, produces fewer ideas than is commonly assumed. Diehl and Stroebe found that individuals working alone, whose ideas were then pooled, generated more ideas than the same number of people working in an interactive group. The main cause was what they called production blocking : only one person in a group can speak at any moment, and the others forget or abandon their ideas while waiting their turn ( Diehl & Stroebe, 1987 ) . Group work still has its place. Girotra, Terwiesch, and Ulrich compared teams that worked together throughout with “hybrid” teams whose members first thought alone and then met to discuss and develop the ideas. They found that the hybrid teams produced more ideas, and that their best ideas were of higher quality ( Girotra et al., 2010 ) . The practical rule: think alone, then build with others. Generative artificial intelligence deserves a pause here. It is a powerful tool for rapidly expanding the set of alternatives, but Chapter 2 presented a study finding that its ideas raised the creativity of each individual writer while making the results more similar to one another ( Doshi & Hauser, 2024 ) . Expansion needs diversity more than it needs volume. It is therefore advisable for individuals to generate their own ideas first and then draw on AI to develop and challenge them, so that it does not become a shared starting point around which everyone's ideas converge.

search.s: 12.3 The pull of the first solution
search.t: Ideas were not in short supply in the opening case; the problem was that most teams adopted the first idea put forward and spent the rest of their time refining it. Researchers call this phenomenon design fixation . Jansson and Smith found that designers shown an example solution before they began produced designs carrying that example's features, flaws included, more often than those shown no example at all ( Jansson & Smith, 1991 ) . The first solution, or the familiar one, acts like a magnet: it draws thinking toward it and makes it hard to move away. Several methods help break this fixation: Reframing: Returning to the alternative problem formulations produced by the problem card in the previous chapter; each formulation opens up a different set of solutions. Distant analogy: Looking for a different field that has faced a structurally similar problem: How do hospitals handle waiting? How do restaurants estimate quantities? Research on analogical thinking has shown that people rarely transfer a solution from one domain to another on their own, but they often do so when prompted to look for similarities ( Gick & Holyoak, 1980 ) . Imposed constraints: Asking questions such as: How would we solve the problem if we had no technology? Or if the budget were a tenth of what we have? Or if we had to remove a step rather than add one? Deferring exposure to known solutions: Having the team generate its ideas before looking at existing solutions on the market, and comparing only afterward. In Practice When your team grows enthusiastic about an idea, ask it, before going further, to write down three radically different solutions to the same problem, going beyond improvements to the first idea. If the first idea remains the best after the comparison, it has been chosen deliberately.

search.s: 12.4 Evaluating ideas and the bias against the new
search.t: Organizations say they are looking for new ideas, then reject them when they see them. This can happen in good faith. Mueller and colleagues found that people hold an implicit bias against creativity when they feel uncertain, even while professing to value it, and that this bias weakens their ability to recognize a creative idea when one is put before them ( Mueller et al., 2012 ) . A new idea is by its nature unproven, and the uncertainty it carries makes it look weaker than it is. Evaluation is also shaped by who does the evaluating. Berg studied how well different groups could predict the success of new ideas in an artistic field and found that creators were more accurate than managers in judging their peers' ideas, and that managers tended to undervalue the most novel ideas. Creators, however, overestimated their own ideas ( Berg, 2016 ) . These findings suggest involving in evaluation people whose expertise is close to creative work, and spreading the evaluation of an idea across multiple parties rather than leaving it to its originator or to management alone. This research explains the outcome of the opening case: the judging panel compared an unfinished new idea with a polished familiar one, and the familiar won. One way to limit this bias is to evaluate each solution according to its stage, as Chapter 10 showed in the graduated criteria of the gates: the question at this stage is not “Has the idea been proven to work?” but “Is it worth testing?” Figure 12.2 brings together the lenses through which a solution is viewed at this stage. Desirability Desirability Does it solve an important problem for those who live with it? Will they want to use it? Feasibility Feasibility Can it be built and operated with the capabilities available or attainable? Viability Viability Can it be sustained financially and organizationally, with some party taking responsibility for it? Responsibility Responsibility Is it fair, safe, and acceptable to those it will affect, and consistent with regulations and values? Figure 12.2 Solution evaluation lenses. The first three lenses are common in the design thinking literature ( Brown, 2008 ) ; this version adds the responsibility lens, which Chapter 19 addresses. The first lens comes first by design. A solution that is technically feasible and financially viable loses its value if it does not address a problem anyone cares about. The function of the lenses at this stage is to identify what needs testing before any final elimination: a solution that looks desirable but whose feasibility is unknown needs an experiment on feasibility, and so on.

An idea is a sentence or an image in the mind; a concept , by contrast, is a description of the solution clear enough for others to understand and test. A good concept specifies whom the solution is for, what problem it solves, how it works in broad outline, and what value it offers compared with existing alternatives, and, most important of all, the assumptions on which it rests, that is, what must be true for it to succeed. The idea of estimating food quantities in advance, from the opening case, rests on assumptions such as these: that data from past events are available and accurate enough, that event hosts will accept smaller quantities than they are used to, and that event halls have an incentive to reduce quantities. Each of these assumptions can be tested with a small experiment. Stating the assumptions this clearly is what would have changed the judging panel's verdict: instead of seeing an “unproven” idea, it would have seen an idea with clear assumptions and a plan to test them. From here the road branches into two chapters. If the solution requires a different model for delivering or funding value, Chapter 13 addresses business model innovation. Chapter 14 then examines how assumptions are ranked by how critical they are, and how experiments are designed to test them at the lowest cost. Principle An idea is judged by what we know about its assumptions, however novel or familiar it may be. A good concept states clearly what must be true, and how we will know.

Before solutions are generated, essential and desirable solution requirements are defined; they become an agreed standard and widen the search, because they describe what must be achieved without specifying how. Developing solutions calls for divergent thinking followed by convergent thinking, and keeping the two apart is a condition for both to work. Individuals working alone produce more ideas than interactive groups, and the hybrid approach, individual thinking followed by collective building, produces better ideas. Fixation on the first or familiar solution is common, and its hold can be broken through reframing, distant analogy, and imposed constraints. People hold an implicit bias against new ideas when they feel uncertain, and managers tend to undervalue them. Stage-appropriate evaluation and a diverse set of evaluators help limit this. A solution is viewed through the lenses of desirability, feasibility, viability, and responsibility to identify what must be tested before any final judgment. A testable concept states its critical assumptions and specifies the smallest experiment that tests the most critical of them. search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.s: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.t: 13 Chapter 13 Business model and value innovation Once a solution has proven its worth, a question with farther-reaching consequences comes to the fore: How is its value to be delivered, and how is its continuity to be secured? The material of this chapter is organized around that question. We set out the components of the business model, trace its form in the public sector, where public value takes precedence over profit, then review patterns of business model innovation and reflect on what makes changing the model so difficult for established organizations.

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.t: Opening case: A municipality (composite case) A municipality piloted a service for reporting streetlight faults through photos that residents sent from their phones; the photos were analyzed automatically and routed to maintenance crews. Over the six months of the pilot, funded from the innovation budget, the time needed to repair faults fell by half, and residents expressed their satisfaction. Then the pilot budget ran out. The service found no department to adopt it: the maintenance department saw it as a technology project, the IT department saw it as a maintenance service, and neither had a budget line for operating costs or for the developer's contract. The service was discontinued two months later, even though every one of its indicators had shown success. The pilot succeeded in proving that the solution worked, yet no one asked during it how the solution would continue: who would own it, who would bear its cost, and how its value would flow back to whoever paid. These are business model questions, and they extend beyond the commercial concerns of companies to every innovation; whatever its sector, an innovation needs a model to carry it. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain why a solution's success is not enough for an innovation to endure. Describe the components of the business model and the relationships among them. Apply the concept of public value and Moore's triangle to public sector initiatives. Use business model innovation patterns to design alternatives. Identify the obstacles that prevent established organizations from changing their models.

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.s: 13.1 Why is a good solution not enough?
search.t: Teece defines the business model as the logic by which an organization delivers value to those it serves and captures enough to sustain itself ( Teece, 2010 ) . In his view, a new technology or idea does not carry its value within itself; its value is determined by the model that brings it to people. This is why the same idea can succeed in one organization and fail in another. One of the clearest examples is the case Chesbrough and Rosenbloom studied at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center. The center developed numerous technologies that found no place in the company's business model, which was built on selling copiers and related services. They left in independent start-ups, and some went on to great success with entirely different business models ( Chesbrough & Rosenbloom, 2002 ) . The obstacle lay in the existing model, which could not see the value of these technologies. For innovation management, this idea has two implications. First, the model question should be raised early, alongside the testable concept discussed in the previous chapter, whereas in the opening case it was put off until after the pilot had succeeded. Second, the innovation may lie in the model itself: an existing service delivered differently, funded differently, or with a new party sharing in its delivery. This is what Chapter 1 called innovation in the “mental model,” an area often overlooked in favor of products and technology.

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.t: There are many frameworks for describing a business model, the most widely used being Osterwalder and Pigneur's nine-component canvas ( Osterwalder & Pigneur, 2010 ) . Johnson, Christensen, and Kagermann offer a simpler framework of four interlocking elements, which suffices for the purposes of this chapter ( Johnson et al., 2008 ) ; Figure 13.1 illustrates it. Value proposition Value proposition The job the solution helps people get done, and why it is better than their current alternatives Sustainability formula Profit formula How costs are covered: who pays, how much, what the cost structure is, and what volume of use is needed for it to continue Key resources Key resources The people, technology, data, partners, and relationships needed to deliver the value Key processes Key processes The procedures, rules, and metrics that make delivering the value repeatable and scalable Fit among them Fit The model works only if every element serves the value proposition and the elements are consistent with one another Figure 13.1 Elements of the business model, adapted from Johnson et al. (2008) . The model always starts from the value proposition , a direct extension of what Chapter 11 presented on jobs to be done: the value proposition describes the progress the solution brings to those who use it, compared with what they do today. Johnson and colleagues stress that most organizations that succeed in innovating their models begin with a precise understanding of this job before thinking about revenue sources. Applied to the opening case: the value proposition was clear and strong, and the resources were available during the pilot. The sustainability formula, however, was never designed at all: no one determined who would bear the operating cost, or how the savings the service achieved in maintenance crews' time would be calculated to justify that cost. The same was true of the key processes: no one specified who would own the service after the pilot, or how it would be integrated into routine maintenance procedures.

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.s: 13.3 Public value and the public sector model
search.t: In the public sector, profit is not the goal, and the beneficiary is not always the one who pays. The business model therefore needs a different form. Moore offers a framework for this known as the strategic triangle : a public initiative succeeds when three things are aligned. It must create public value that society appreciates, enjoy legitimacy and support from the bodies that hold the mandate and the funding, and have the operational capacity to deliver ( Moore, 1995 ) . Figure 13.2 illustrates this triangle. Public value What does society value, and what deserves resources? An initiative succeeds when all three sides are aligned Legitimacy and support Who authorizes, funds, and protects? Operational capacity Who delivers, and with what resources? Figure 13.2 The strategic triangle of public value, adapted from Moore (1995) . Reading the opening case through this triangle reveals where things went wrong. Public value was achieved, and operational capacity was demonstrated in the pilot, but the third side, the body that would adopt the service, authorize its continuation, and fund it, was never built. Had that side been built during the pilot, by involving the maintenance department from the start as the future owner and counting the savings in its time as part of the sustainability formula, the outcome would have been different. Chapter 15 returns to the transfer of ownership as a condition for scaling. In the public sector and in universities, the sustainability formula takes many forms: a line in the budget of an owning body, savings in existing costs that are redirected, fees charged to some beneficiaries, a partnership with the private sector in which the partner bears part of the cost in return for value it receives, or some combination of these. A university's digital fabrication lab (fab lab), for instance, might be sustained by university funding to serve students, along with revenue from services it provides to companies in the region and sponsorship from organizations that see its students as a source of talent they need. The absence of such thinking is what leaves many of these entities dependent on a start-up budget that runs out, after which they remain in place but inactive. The individual innovator has a model too. In a qualitative study, most of the prominent Saudi innovators interviewed held that turning their innovation into a source of income early on was a condition for continuing with it ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . An organization that supports innovators goes beyond funding their ideas to helping them think through the model that will make their innovation sustainable.

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.t: Gassmann, Frankenberger, and Csik studied hundreds of innovative business models and found that most of them, around 90 percent, were recombinations of pre-existing patterns, transferred from one industry to another or combined in a new way. They identified fifty-five recurring patterns ( Gassmann et al., 2014 ) . This finding means that business model innovation calls less for invention from scratch than for broad knowledge of patterns and the ability to transfer them, which links it to the analogical thinking discussed in the previous chapter. Table 13.1 presents a number of these patterns and the forms they might take in the public sector. Table 13.1 Selected business model innovation patterns and their possible applications, adapted from Gassmann et al. (2014) Pattern Core idea A possible form in the public sector or a university Self-service The beneficiary does part of the work in return for greater speed or flexibility Online services that beneficiaries complete without an in-person visit Pay-per-use The beneficiary pays in proportion to use Making university labs available to companies by the hour Freemium A basic service for everyone, with additional features for a fee Free initial consultations for entrepreneurs, and advanced incubation programs through paid partnerships Platform Connecting parties who need one another instead of delivering the service directly A platform connecting organizations' problems with students and researchers able to solve them Outcome-based contracting Payment is for outcomes achieved rather than for activity Maintenance contracts paid according to actual repair times Co-delivery partnership Another party contributes its own resources to delivering the service Nonprofit associations or companies delivering part of a public service A pattern should be chosen for how well it serves the value proposition and fits the organization's resources and capabilities, regardless of how fashionable it is. Many attempts to transfer successful models from one context to another fail because the pattern was moved without the resources and processes that made it work in its original setting. We return to this idea in Chapter 20, in discussing borrowed models in universities.

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.s: 13.5 Why is the model hard to change?
search.t: If business model patterns are well known, why do organizations not change their models more easily? Chesbrough identifies two kinds of obstacle ( Chesbrough, 2010 ) . The first is a conflict with existing assets : a new model may threaten existing revenue streams, positions, or investments, and those who hold them resist it. The second is a cognitive barrier : a successful model becomes the “dominant logic” through which the organization views every new opportunity, so an idea is assessed by the yardsticks of the existing model and appears less attractive than it really is. This is what happened with Xerox's technologies. Chesbrough proposes treating a new model with the same logic used for a new product: through experimentation. The model's assumptions, such as an organization's willingness to pay or a partner's ability to deliver, are tested with small experiments before full commitment. Chapter 14 takes up this experimentation. This connects to organizational ambidexterity and autonomous teams: a new model that conflicts with the existing one may need a separate space in which to grow before it returns to the organization. Caution A pilot funded from the innovation budget tests the solution, but it can mask the model question: as long as the cost is covered, it remains unclear who will bear it later. Every pilot should therefore include an explicit question: Who will pay afterward, and why will they pay?

search.c: Chapter 13: Business model and value innovation
search.s: Chapter tool: The value model canvas
search.t: Fill in this canvas for every initiative before its pilot begins. If you cannot answer a question, turn it into an assumption and test it in the pilot itself. The canvas combines the elements of the business model with the public value triangle, so that it serves both sectors. search.t: A business model is a logic for delivering value and securing its continuity, and an idea's value depends on the model that carries it; the same idea may therefore succeed with one model and falter with another. The model question should be raised early, in parallel with the testable concept and before the pilot. The model has four interlocking elements: the value proposition, the sustainability formula, key resources, and key processes. It always starts from the value proposition. In the public sector, an initiative succeeds when public value, legitimacy and support, and operational capacity are aligned. Most business model innovations are recombinations of existing patterns, and a pattern is chosen for its fit with the value proposition and resources. The model is hard to change because of its conflict with existing assets and the hold of the dominant logic; experimentation and separate spaces help overcome this. 14 Chapter 14 Experimentation and risk reduction Between an idea and a major investment lies a stretch of assumptions, and experimentation is what turns them into knowledge before the organization commits to something that is hard to reverse. Within this horizon we move step by step from ranking assumptions by how critical they are, to the types of tests available, to designing an experiment that yields genuine learning, and we close with the common mistakes made in pilots.

Opening case: An appointment system (composite case) A service organization developed a new appointment booking system for its branches and chose its main branch in the capital to pilot it: the newest branch, the most heavily staffed, and the closest to the project team. Three extra staff members were assigned to the pilot to help visitors, and the development team came in daily to fix any problem on the spot. After three months, the pilot was declared a success: waiting times had fallen and visitor satisfaction had risen. The system was then rolled out to forty branches. In most of them, work was disrupted for weeks: the small branches had no one to help visitors, some had slower networks, and the development team could not be everywhere at once. The pilot did not fail; it was designed to succeed. The system was tested under the best possible conditions, so the pilot proved that it worked under those conditions and said nothing about the conditions in which it would actually operate. This difference between an experiment that proves and one that teaches is what this chapter is about. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain experimentation as a means of turning assumptions into knowledge and reducing uncertainty. Rank an initiative's assumptions by their importance and the strength of the evidence behind them. Choose the appropriate type of test for each assumption and stage. Design an experiment with a hypothesis, a measure, and a success criterion set in advance. Avoid the common mistakes made in pilots.

In conventional projects, the plan is built on knowledge, and success is measured by adherence to it. In innovation, by contrast, the initial plan rests more on assumptions than on knowledge. McGrath and MacMillan observed that many new ventures fail because their founders treat assumptions as if they were facts, only to discover their errors after everything has been invested. They proposed what they called discovery-driven planning : writing the assumptions down explicitly and sequencing the stages so that each stage tests the most important assumptions before moving on, so that assumptions are gradually converted into knowledge ( McGrath & MacMillan, 1995 ) . Experimental evidence supports this approach. Camuffo and colleagues conducted a randomized trial with 116 start-ups in Italy, half of which received training in making decisions by a scientific method: formulating hypotheses, testing them, and judging the results. The trained start-ups were more likely to change direction or stop when the evidence did not support their idea, and they achieved higher revenues ( Camuffo et al., 2020 ) . The experimental approach leaves the odds of the first idea succeeding unchanged; its benefit lies in knowing when the idea needs to change. This is the logic underlying the gates of Chapter 10 and staged funding: each stage buys knowledge that reduces uncertainty, and the next stage is funded according to what the team has learned. Experimentation is the tool with which the team buys this knowledge. It is consistent with the principle of “managing uncertainty” among the principles of innovation management: dealing with risks by confronting them and learning from them.

search.s: 14.2 Critical assumptions and how to rank them
search.t: Chapter 12 ended with a testable concept that states its critical assumptions, and Chapter 13 noted that the business model itself rests on assumptions. Experimentation begins by gathering all of these assumptions and then ranking them. They can be classified by the four evaluation lenses: assumptions about desirability (Do people want the solution?), feasibility (Can it be built and operated?), viability (Can it be sustained?), and responsibility (Is it fair and safe?). Testing all the assumptions at once is neither possible nor useful. Priority goes to assumptions that combine two qualities: they are important , meaning that if they are wrong the entire initiative collapses, and the evidence for them is weak . Bland and Osterwalder propose ranking them along these two dimensions ( Bland & Osterwalder, 2019 ) , as Figure 14.1 shows. Importance of the assumption to the initiative's success Test first Important, with weak evidence. This is where the real risk lies. Monitor Important, with strong evidence. Periodically checking that it still holds is enough. Test later Less important, with weak evidence. Do not invest in it before testing what matters more. Ignore for now Less important, with strong evidence. Strength of available evidence → Figure 14.1 Ranking assumptions by their importance and the strength of the evidence behind them, adapted from Bland & Osterwalder (2019) . The top row indicates high importance, and the right-hand column strong evidence. Teams tend to start with what is easy to test before what must be tested. A technical team tests feasibility because that is what it does well, and postpones the desirability assumption because testing it means going out to people. The result is a solution that works technically and that nobody uses. Ranking assumptions in this way puts risk ahead of convenience.

Tests vary in their cost and in the strength of the evidence they provide. The principle of choice is simple: start with the cheapest test that could disprove the assumption, and move up to a costlier test only if the assumption survives the cheaper one. Figure 14.2 shows a ladder of such tests. Lower cost, weaker evidence Higher cost, stronger evidence ↓ Conversations and interviews Is the problem real? What do people do today? (Chapter 11) Paper prototype or sketch Do people understand the idea? What is the first thing they object to? Manual delivery of the service The team delivers the service by hand to a small number of beneficiaries before automating it, to find out whether they actually use it Limited initial version The smallest version sufficient to test the core value with real users Comparative experiment Comparing the solution with an alternative or with the status quo, using a comparison group whenever possible Pilot Implementing the solution under real operating conditions, within clear limits of time and place Figure 14.2 The testing ladder, from cheapest to costliest. Prepared by the author. Every rung on the ladder requires a prototype of some kind. Houde and Hill pointed out that the most important question in designing a prototype is not “What are we building?” but “What do we want to find out?” They distinguished among prototypes that test the role of the solution in the user's life, prototypes that test its look and feel , and prototypes that test its technical implementation ( Houde & Hill, 1997 ) . Each question has its own prototype: one that answers the feasibility question falls short on desirability, and perfecting a prototype that answers the wrong question is waste. One of the most widespread concepts in this area is the minimum viable product , the smallest version of a product that allows the team to learn as much as possible about users with the least effort ( Ries, 2011 ) . The key word in the definition is “learn”: the initial version is a tool for testing an assumption, not a stripped-down version of the final product that is launched and then added to. In Practice Before your team asks for a budget to build an initial version, ask: Which assumption will this version test? And is there a cheaper test lower down the ladder that could disprove it? Many questions can be answered through conversations or manual delivery of the service before a single line of code is written.

The difference between an experiment that teaches and one that merely proves lies in the design, before the start. A good experiment needs five elements defined in advance: A clear hypothesis: “We believe that [a specific group] will do [a specific behavior] because [a reason].” A behavioral measure: one that captures what people actually do; actual use is more telling than stated opinion. A success criterion set in advance: the figure that, if reached, means the hypothesis is supported, and if not reached, means it is rejected. Setting it after seeing the results opens the door to interpreting any result as a success. A comparison: with the status quo or with an alternative, because improvement may occur for reasons that have nothing to do with the solution. Duration, limits, and stopping conditions: when the experiment ends, to whom it applies, and what would halt it early if harm emerges. Comparison is the hardest of these elements and the most often neglected in the public sector. The UK government's Behavioural Insights Team has advocated the use of randomized controlled trials in public policy, showing that in many cases they are less costly and complex than is commonly assumed, and that they allow organizations to learn what actually works before scaling it up ( Haynes et al., 2012 ) . Where random assignment is not feasible, comparison with similar branches or periods is still far better than no comparison at all. At a university, these elements can become part of applied projects in courses: instead of presenting a solution and defending it, students present a hypothesis and test it with real users, and they are assessed on the quality of the experiment and what they learned from it, even if their hypothesis is rejected. This links the course to the innovation system and teaches students the method before it teaches them the result.

The pilot is the highest and costliest rung on the ladder, and it is run once the core assumptions have survived the cheaper tests. Its function is to reveal how the solution works under real operating conditions; it is a tool for learning more than for proof. Certain mistakes recur in pilots: Ideal conditions: choosing the best site, the most enthusiastic staff, and exceptional support from the project team, as in the opening case. The alternative is to run the pilot at a site that represents ordinary conditions, or at two different sites. The never-ending pilot: a pilot extended again and again without a decision, which either becomes a permanent service with no owner and no budget or dies quietly. This is one form of decision limbo. No future owner: a pilot run by the innovation team alone, which finds no one to adopt it once it ends, as in the opening case of Chapter 13. Measuring what is easy to measure: the number of users or their satisfaction in a survey, rather than the behavior that signals value: Did they come back? Did completion time change? Did errors decrease? Overlooking the true cost of operation: exceptional support during the pilot hides what routine operation will require. Every pilot has three possible outcomes, all of them useful if the pilot is well designed: the solution is scaled up, it is modified and tested again, or it is stopped. Chapter 15 addresses the move from pilot to scale. Caution An experiment that cannot fail teaches nothing. If the team cannot specify before the start the result that would lead it to stop or modify the initiative, then what it is running is a demonstration, even if it is called an experiment.

Organizations that experiment at scale uncover a seemingly discouraging truth: most ideas fail. Kohavi and Thomke reported that only 10 to 20 percent of experiments at major search engines produce positive results, and that small changes whose effect no one anticipated sometimes yielded large returns, such as a tweak to the way ad headlines were displayed that raised one search engine's revenue by about 12 percent ( Kohavi & Thomke, 2017 ) . The implication is that experience and intuition, however valuable, still need testing, and that an organization implementing its ideas without testing them implements many unhelpful ideas along with them. A culture of experimentation is broader than its tools. It requires what Chapter 8 discussed: psychological safety that allows a team to announce that its hypothesis was rejected, a distinction between intelligent failure and avoidable failure, and leadership that asks “What did we learn?” before it asks “Why did we fail?” It also requires respect for the people on whom experiments are conducted: the beneficiary of a public service is not a test subject, and has a right to be informed and protected from harm. Chapter 19 addresses the ethics of experimenting on people.

In innovation, the plan rests on assumptions, and experimentation turns them into knowledge before major investment; the most valuable thing about the experimental approach is that it reveals when an idea needs to change. Assumptions are ranked by their importance and the strength of the evidence behind them, with priority given to important assumptions with weak evidence. Start with the cheapest test that could disprove the assumption, and move up the ladder if it holds. A prototype is designed to answer a specific question. A learning experiment needs a hypothesis, a behavioral measure, a success criterion set in advance, a comparison, and limits and stopping conditions. Common mistakes in pilots include ideal conditions, the never-ending pilot, the absence of an owner, and measuring what is easy to measure. Most ideas fail when tested, which is why testing remains necessary however strong the intuition. A culture of experimentation requires psychological safety and respect for those on whom experiments are conducted. 15 Chapter 15 Adoption and scaling With this chapter, the initiative journey reaches its most demanding stage: moving a solution that succeeded in a pilot into broad, real-world use. We examine the gap between adopting an innovation and implementing it, the factors that make some innovations spread faster than others, and the concerns of those who are asked to change, before turning to scaling readiness and the transfer of ownership.

Opening case: a Saudi university (composite case) The center for teaching excellence at a university developed a model for innovation project assignments: students identify a real problem in their field and test a solution to it with actual beneficiaries. The model was piloted in three courses taught by enthusiastic faculty members, and the results were striking: serious projects, high engagement, and students who took their projects on to the business accelerator. Once the results were presented to the university council, a circular was issued requiring the model to be applied in sixty courses the following semester. A year later, the model was “implemented” in every course on paper: most faculty members had simply renamed their old assignments to match it, and what students actually did had not changed. The model succeeded when it was adopted by those who chose it, and it faltered when it was imposed on people who had never been consulted and were given neither the time nor the support to understand it. This story recurs across organizations in many forms, and it is our entry point into understanding why the move from limited success to wide use is the hardest stage of the journey. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Distinguish between adopting an innovation and actually implementing it, and explain the implementation gap. Assess the characteristics of an innovation that affect how quickly it is adopted. Recognize adopters’ stages of concern and provide the support suited to each. Assess a solution’s readiness for scaling, and distinguish between its core, which must be implemented faithfully, and its periphery, which can be adapted. Plan the transfer of a solution’s ownership and its scaling pathway.

The implementation literature distinguishes between the adoption of an innovation, that is, the organization’s decision to use it, and its implementation , that is, its actual and consistent use by the intended people. Klein and Sorra showed that many innovations are adopted and then never implemented, or are implemented only superficially. In their view, implementation effectiveness depends on two things: the implementation climate , meaning the extent to which people perceive that using the innovation is expected, supported and rewarded; and the innovation’s fit with their values , meaning the extent to which they see it as consistent with what they believe in their work ( Klein & Sorra, 1996 ) . When implementation is expected and required but fit is weak, people comply on the surface without being convinced, which is exactly what happened in the opening case. Klein and Knight observe that many innovations fail not because they are ineffective, but because they were never implemented with enough quality and consistency for their effectiveness to show ( Klein & Knight, 2005 ) . An organization may therefore pronounce a good innovation a failure when, in truth, it never implemented it at all. This is why scaling demands management as careful as that devoted to development.

search.s: 15.2 Why do some innovations spread faster?
search.t: Chapter 1 presented Rogers’s definition of innovation. Among his most important contributions is the identification of five characteristics of an innovation, as perceived by adopters, that explain much of the variation in how quickly innovations are adopted ( Rogers, 2003 ) . Table 15.1 sets them out, together with the question each one poses for the scaling team. Table 15.1 Characteristics of an innovation that affect the speed of its adoption, adapted from Rogers (2003) Characteristic Meaning Design question Relative advantage The degree to which people perceive the innovation as better than what they currently use What does the user personally gain, beyond what the organization gains? Compatibility Its consistency with their values, experience, needs and ways of working What must the user give up in order to adopt it? Complexity How difficult it is to understand and use What is the simplest form in which it can start? Trialability Whether it can be tried on a limited scale before commitment Can users try it without risking much? Observability How visible its results are to others How will others see its results among their colleagues? These characteristics underline that adoption turns on adopters’ perceptions of an innovation’s attributes. From the center’s perspective, the model in the opening case was undoubtedly better; to many faculty members, however, it looked like a complicated additional burden that did not fit courses designed around transmission and testing, and they were given no chance to try it before committing to it. Greenhalgh and colleagues’ review extended these characteristics to the context of service organizations, adding factors such as organizational readiness for change and adopters’ ability to adapt the innovation to their own context ( Greenhalgh et al., 2004 ) .

Where Chapter 7 dealt with the needs of the innovator, this section turns to the needs of those asked to adopt someone else’s innovation. Adoption is a change in a person’s work, and it raises legitimate questions and concerns. Working in the context of implementing educational innovations, Hall and Hord developed a model of the stages of concern that people pass through when asked to adopt an innovation. They showed that these concerns tend to shift from one level to another, that they may overlap within the same person, and that effective support responds to the stage the person is in ( Hall & Hord, 2015 ) . Figure 15.1 presents these stages in grouped form. Stage The person’s question Appropriate support Self Awareness, information and personal impact What is this? What will change for me? Can I do it? Clear information, dialogue about the effect on work and time, and honest reassurance Task Management and execution How do I organize my time? How do I deal with this practical problem? Hands-on training, ready-made tools, and close support during implementation Impact Consequences, collaboration and refocusing Does this benefit the beneficiaries? How can I improve it? Data on results, exchange of experience with colleagues, and room for development Figure 15.1 Adopters’ stages of concern grouped into three clusters, with the support appropriate to each, adapted from Hall & Hord (2015) . A common mistake is to address people with impact questions while they are still preoccupied with self questions: presenting the innovation’s results and its benefits to the organization while they are asking how it will affect their time, their work and how others see them. In the opening case, faculty members were shown the results of the three courses, but no one asked them about the extra time that supervising real student projects would require, or about the support they would need. Their superficial compliance was therefore less a rejection of the innovation than a response to concerns that no one had answered. This is consistent with what Chapter 8 said about culture: an administrative circular operates at the level of espoused values, while the faculty member’s basic assumption remains that the annual evaluation and promotion do not count this effort. Changing that assumption is beyond the reach of a circular; it requires culture-embedding mechanisms. In Practice Before rolling out an innovation to your colleagues, sit down with five of them who did not take part in the pilot and ask: What worries you most about it? Their answers will tell you which stage of concern they are in, and what support they need before any presentation of results.

Chapter 14 cautioned that a pilot run under ideal conditions says nothing about ordinary conditions. List calls this phenomenon the voltage effect : many programs that achieve strong results in their early trials lose much of their impact when they scale. The causes are largely predictable. Among them: the initial result was a false positive; those who took part in the pilot do not represent those who will later use the solution; pilot conditions differ from operating conditions; and costs rise with scale instead of falling ( List, 2022 ) . Most of these causes converged in the opening case: the faculty members teaching the three courses were enthusiasts who had chosen the pilot, whereas those teaching the sixty courses had not; and the three courses enjoyed the center’s direct support, which the sixty did not. This is why readiness questions should be asked before scaling: Has the solution been tested under conditions that represent reality? Does it work with people who did not choose it? What does it actually cost without exceptional support? Who will own and operate it? One of the most important things to settle before scaling is the distinction between a solution’s core and its periphery . Greenhalgh and colleagues’ review noted that innovations with a fixed, well-defined core and a flexible, adaptable periphery spread more easily than innovations that are either entirely rigid or entirely flexible ( Greenhalgh et al., 2004 ) . The core is what must remain unchanged for the value to survive; the periphery is what each unit can adapt to its own context. Figure 15.2 illustrates this distinction. Flexible periphery: adapted by each unit Fixed core A real problem from the field, testing with an actual beneficiary, and assessment of learning quality Type of problem, project size, weight in the grade, individual or group work, and duration Figure 15.2 The fixed core and flexible periphery of the innovation project assignment model. Developed by the author, drawing on Greenhalgh et al. (2004) . Had the core been defined this clearly in the opening case, each faculty member could have adapted the model to their course without losing its value, and genuine implementation could have been told apart from superficial implementation with a single question: Has the core survived?

It is common in organizations for an innovation team to develop a solution and then “hand it over” to the unit that will operate it, only for that unit not to adopt it. The opening case of Chapter 13 offered one version of this. The reason is that ownership is built during the journey; it is not handed over at the end. Building it requires: Involving the future owner from the start: a representative of the operating unit should be a member of the team from the pilot stage onward, taking part in decisions and coming to see the solution as an integral part of their own work. Embedding the solution in existing systems: the budget, procedures, job descriptions and performance indicators. A solution that remains outside these systems remains a temporary project, however long it lasts. Transferring knowledge alongside documentation: the tacit knowledge the development team has acquired does not travel through written manuals; it requires a period of working together. Defining the innovation team’s role after the transfer: Does it withdraw completely, or does it remain in a supporting role for a set period? And how will later improvements be passed on? This is why the “operations voice” is one of the five roles on an innovation team, and why “Who will operate it?” is among the questions at the scaling gate.

Scaling takes more forms than a single leap from one unit to the entire organization. Three pathways can be distinguished, differing in speed and risk: Phased scaling: moving from one unit to a small number of units with different conditions, then to more, learning along the way with each wave. It is the slowest pathway and the least risky. Pull-based scaling: making the solution available to those who wish to adopt it, with clear support, and making its results visible so that it draws others in. It respects autonomy and builds on observability. Comprehensive scaling: implementation across the whole organization at once. It suits simple, proven solutions, or those whose nature requires uniform implementation. At the university, we propose that embedding innovation in courses begin with a limited number of interdisciplinary courses and then scale through pull and phasing together: the model is offered to interested faculty members with support from the center for teaching excellence, their students’ projects are showcased at the annual innovation day, and supervising those projects counts toward the annual evaluation. When other faculty members see the results among their colleagues and find support and recognition, they adopt the model out of conviction. We return to this design in Chapter 20. Principle Administrative mandates produce compliance; conviction produces adoption. The quickest route to superficial compliance is to impose an innovation on people who were never consulted and never given what they needed to understand it.

Answer the following questions before any decision to scale, and give each dimension a rating: ready, partly ready, or not ready. A dimension that is not ready identifies what must be done before or during scaling, without necessarily requiring that scaling be halted. Chapter tool Scaling readiness check Dimension Check question Rating Evidence Has the solution been tested under conditions that represent reality, and with people who did not choose it? Core and periphery Has it been defined what must remain fixed and what can be adapted? Perceived characteristics Do adopters see its advantage, compatibility and simplicity? And can they try it out? Adopters’ concerns Do we know their current concerns? And is support designed around them? Implementation climate Is use of the solution expected, supported and recognized in the formal systems? Cost What is the actual operating cost without exceptional support? And who bears it? Ownership Who owns the solution? Did they take part in developing it? Has it been embedded in their budget and procedures? Pathway Has the appropriate scaling pathway been chosen: phased, pull-based or comprehensive? Follow-up How will we know that implementation is genuine rather than superficial?

There is a distance between adopting an innovation and implementing it, and implementation effectiveness depends on a climate that supports use and on the innovation’s fit with users’ values. The failure of many innovations owes more to shortfalls in the quality and consistency of their implementation than to any weakness in their effectiveness. Adoption is shaped by five characteristics as perceived by adopters: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability. Adopters pass through stages of concern, beginning with self, then task, then impact, and effective support responds to the stage the person is in. Many programs lose their impact when they scale because pilot conditions were far removed from reality. Defining a fixed core and a flexible periphery helps a solution scale while preserving its value. Ownership is built throughout the journey, by involving the future owner and embedding the solution in existing systems. Scaling can follow several pathways: phased, pull-based and comprehensive. Administrative mandates produce compliance; conviction produces adoption. Key Terms Innovation implementation Innovation implementation The actual, consistent use of an innovation by its intended users after the decision to adopt it. Implementation climate Implementation climate People’s perception that using the innovation is expected, supported and rewarded. Stages of concern Stages of concern The progression of adopters’ questions and concerns from self, to task, to impact. Voltage effect Voltage effect The decline in a program’s impact as it scales from pilot to wide implementation. Hard core and soft periphery Hard core and soft periphery The distinction between what must remain fixed in an innovation and what can be adapted to each context. Review and Discussion Questions What is the difference between adopting an innovation and implementing it? And why might a good innovation be judged a failure? Understanding Assess an innovation you are working to roll out against the five characteristics in Table 15.1, and identify the weakest. Application Analyze the opening case using the concepts of stages of concern, the voltage effect and implementation climate. Analysis Identify the fixed core and the flexible periphery of an innovation in your organization. Application “A formal mandate from leadership is the fastest route to adopting an innovation.” Evaluate this statement. Evaluation

16 Chapter 16 Measuring innovation and maturity How can an organization be confident that its innovation is creating value, and that its capability to innovate is growing? This question organizes the chapter: the results chain, the three levels of measurement, measuring people and the environment, and the errors that allow indicators to devour the very goals they were meant to serve, before arriving at the concept of maturity.

Opening case: the ideas indicator (composite case) A government agency added a new indicator to its employees’ individual performance targets: submit at least two innovative ideas a year through the ideas platform. At year’s end, the agency announced in its annual report that the number of ideas submitted had quadrupled. The platform’s evaluation team, however, found that most of the ideas were duplicates or generic, that some had been copied from other agencies’ platforms, and that many had been submitted in the final week of the year. Unable to evaluate such a volume, the team let the ideas pile up unanswered, and the few serious ones among them were lost in the crowd. The following year, employees spoke of the platform as a formality to be completed for the sake of the indicator. The indicator hit its numerical target and damaged the purpose it was set up to serve: it measured activity and overlooked value, rewarded quantity at the expense of quality, and flooded the system beyond its capacity to respond. In this chapter, we set out how measurement can be designed to support innovation rather than distort it. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain the difficulties of measuring innovation and the effect of indicators on behavior. Build a results chain that links inputs to impact. Design indicators at the initiative, portfolio and system levels. Measure the human and environmental dimensions of innovation. Avoid common measurement errors, and use maturity assessment as a tool for learning.

search.s: 16.1 Why is innovation hard to measure?
search.t: Innovation is hard to measure for at least three reasons. Its results are delayed : years may pass between an idea and its impact. They are uncertain : most initiatives do not succeed, and the few successes are the fruit of an entire portfolio of initiatives. And they are difficult to attribute : when an organization’s performance improves, it is hard to say how much of the improvement stems from any particular innovation. For these reasons, organizations tend to measure what is easy to measure: the number of ideas, events, participants and amounts spent. Measurement, however, is not a neutral tool. Hauser and Katz observed that organizations become what they measure: indicators direct people’s attention and effort, and people act in ways that improve the indicator even when this harms the purpose ( Hauser & Katz, 1998 ) . Decades earlier, Kerr had drawn attention to what he called “the folly of rewarding A while hoping for B”: organizations often reward one behavior and then wonder why the behavior they wanted is missing ( Kerr, 1975 ) . The opening case is a direct example: submitting ideas was rewarded, while innovation was what had been hoped for.

The results chain , known in the evaluation literature as the logic model, helps link what an organization spends to what it achieves ( W. K. Kellogg Foundation, 2004 ) . Figure 16.1 shows its links as applied to innovation. Inputs Budget, time, spaces, people and platforms Activities Campaigns, hackathons, training and experiments Outputs Evaluated ideas, tested concepts and implemented solutions Outcomes Improvements in service, cost, time or satisfaction for beneficiaries Impact Sustained value for the organization and society, and greater innovation capability What is easy to measure and within the organization’s control What really matters → Figure 16.1 The innovation results chain, adapted from the logic model in W. K. Kellogg Foundation (2004) . Most innovation reports concentrate on the first two links, because they are the easiest to measure and the most within the organization’s control. Outcomes and impact are what matter, but they take more effort to measure. Chapter 2 presented one version of this gap at the national level: the gap between the Kingdom’s ranking on innovation inputs and its ranking on innovation outputs in the Global Innovation Index. An organization that measures only its inputs and activities may consider itself successful while producing nothing. Inputs and activities remain necessary for understanding efficiency, but every indicator in the early links needs to be read alongside an indicator in the later ones: the number of ideas on its own says nothing, whereas the share that was implemented and the results it achieved say a great deal.

Innovation management needs measurement at three levels, each with its own questions and indicators, as Table 16.1 shows. Table 16.1 Levels of innovation measurement and suggested indicators for each Level Question Suggested indicators Initiative Is the initiative learning enough to deserve to continue? Number of critical assumptions tested, and which were confirmed or refuted; the cost and duration of each experiment; initiative-specific outcome indicators after implementation Portfolio Are initiatives flowing, balanced and delivering value collectively? Distribution of initiatives across types and horizons; average time an initiative spends at each stage; share of decisions made on time; number of initiatives stopped by decision; share reaching implementation; value realized from what was implemented System and capability Is the organization’s capability for repeated innovation growing? Creative climate; participation of different units; response time to ideas; share of ideas whose authors received a reasoned response; share of implemented solutions still in use after a year Two indicators in this table deserve particular emphasis, because they measure what this book regards as among the most serious breakdowns in the system. The first is the share of decisions made on time , together with the average age of ideas still awaiting a decision; these directly measure the extent of the decision limbo described in Chapter 5. The second is the share of implemented solutions still in use after a year , which distinguishes genuine implementation from the superficial implementation discussed in Chapter 15. Note that indicators for an initiative in its early stages measure learning; outcome indicators belong to later stages. Asking an initiative in the exploration stage for a financial return is like applying the criteria of the scaling gate at the opportunity gate.

If people are the heart of the innovation system, as this book holds, then measuring them is an integral part of measuring the system. What this means is measuring what people experience in their environment: Do they find recognition, opportunity and support? Counting how many ideas each employee submits, as in the opening case, measures something else entirely. Well-established research instruments exist for this purpose. Ekvall developed a measure of creative climate covering dimensions such as challenge, freedom, idea support, trust and openness, idea time, risk taking, and conflict as a negative dimension ( Ekvall, 1996 ) . Amabile and colleagues developed an instrument for assessing the work environment for creativity, measuring both stimulants and obstacles ( Amabile et al., 1996 ) . Such instruments allow an organization to know where it stands and to track the effect of what it does to improve its environment. The innovator’s experience of the system can also be measured directly, using indicators drawn from the needs set out in Table 7.1: Recognition: the share of ideas whose authors received a reasoned response, the average response time, and the share of implemented ideas whose authors remained involved in implementing them. Opportunity: the number of steps between the person with the idea and someone able to help, and the share of units from which ideas have come. Time and resources: the share of initiatives whose members received protected time. Climate: results of a short periodic creative climate survey, compared across units and years. At the university, the findings of a study on faculty support can be measured by asking students how far their instructors encourage their creative ideas in courses, and how confident they are in their own creative abilities ( Alsamani & Alqahtani, 2026 ) . This measures a link in the ecosystem that does not appear in incubator and accelerator reports, even though it touches every student. In Practice Pick ten ideas submitted in your organization six months ago and trace what became of each: Was a decision made on it? When? Did its author learn the reason? This simple measure says more about the innovation system than the number of ideas submitted.

search.s: 16.5 When the indicator devours the goal
search.t: The psychologist Campbell formulated an observation that has come to be known as his law: the more a quantitative indicator is relied upon for social decision-making, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the processes it was meant to monitor ( Campbell, 1979 ) . In the measurement of innovation, this phenomenon appears in recurring forms: Vanity metrics: numbers that look good in reports but say nothing about value, such as the number of ideas, events, attendees and followers. Tying the indicator to individual incentives: it then turns from a learning tool into a target to be chased, as in the opening case. Premature measurement: demanding results from an initiative before it has had time to achieve them, so that promising initiatives are halted or their early results are overstated. The single indicator: relying on one number that reduces innovation to a single figure, which is then improved at the expense of everything else. Measuring entities rather than flow: each unit measures its own activity in isolation, so what is lost in the spaces between them stays invisible, such as ideas that never find their way from the course to the accelerator. These errors can be limited by using indicators as a balanced, multidimensional set; reading activity indicators alongside outcome indicators; separating learning indicators from individual incentives; and periodically reviewing the indicators themselves by asking: Does this indicator still serve the purpose, or has it become an end in itself? The balanced scorecard offers a closely related idea: performance should not be reduced to a single dimension, and the different dimensions should be read together ( Kaplan & Norton, 1992 ) . Caution An indicator tied to an individual incentive stops measuring reality and starts shaping it. If the aim is for people to put forward good ideas, measure what happens to their ideas after they are submitted.

Many organizations use maturity models to assess their innovation management; these models describe successive levels of capability. Figure 16.2 offers a simplified version of these levels, derived from the logic of this book. Level 1 Scattered Initiatives that depend on enthusiastic individuals, with no system or strategy Level 2 Partly organized Innovation units and programs that work separately and measure their own activities Level 3 Systematic A clear strategy, system, gates and decision rights, and a managed portfolio Level 4 Integrated Innovation is part of daily work, evaluation and the budget, and units operate as a single system Level 5 Learning and renewing The system measures its impact, reviews itself and adapts to change, with people at its center Figure 16.2 Levels of innovation management maturity in simplified form. Prepared by the author. Maturity models have both uses and limits. They are useful in giving an organization a shared language for describing its situation and identifying the next step. Their limit is that they can turn into a ladder climbed for appearances: the organization meets a level’s requirements on paper, much as a certificate of conformity can become a stage for innovation theater. The international guidance on innovation management assessment recommends that assessment serve as a means of understanding the current situation and drawing out what can be improved ( ISO, 2019 ) . The most important question in any maturity assessment is not “What level are we at?” but “What is preventing us from innovating repeatedly, and what is the next step to remove it?”

Build a measurement dashboard for your organization’s innovation system with two or three indicators per cell, and no more. Make sure every indicator in the activities column is matched by one in the outcomes column. Then ask of each indicator: How could it be met on paper only? If you find an easy way, rewrite it. Chapter tool Balanced measurement dashboard (example from the university case) Level Inputs and activities Outputs Outcomes and impact Initiative Cost and duration of experiments Assumptions tested and those confirmed Improvement in the problem indicator for beneficiaries Portfolio Distribution of initiatives across types and units Share of decisions on time; initiatives stopped by decision Share implemented; value realized from it System and capability Courses that include innovation projects Response time to ideas; student movement between units Creative climate; students’ confidence in their creative abilities; solutions still in use after a year

Innovation is hard to measure because its results are delayed, uncertain and difficult to attribute to their source, and organizations become what they measure. The results chain links inputs and activities to outputs, outcomes and impact, yet most reports stop at its first two links. Innovation is measured at three levels: the initiative through learning indicators, the portfolio through flow and balance indicators, and the system through capability indicators. The share of decisions made on time measures decision limbo, and the persistence of solutions after a year distinguishes genuine from superficial implementation. People and the environment are measured with creative climate instruments and with indicators derived from innovators’ needs and the fate of their ideas. The more an indicator is relied upon and tied to incentives, the more it is distorted; balanced measurement and periodic review of indicators limit this. Maturity models are a shared language and a learning tool, and they lose their value once they turn into a ladder climbed for appearances. Key Terms Results chain / logic model Results chain / logic model A sequence linking inputs and activities to outputs, outcomes and impact. Vanity metrics Vanity metrics Numbers that look good in reports but do not indicate the value actually achieved. Campbell's law Campbell's law The more a quantitative indicator is relied upon in decision-making, the greater the pressure to corrupt it and to distort what it measures. Creative climate Creative climate The observable patterns of behavior and feeling at work that encourage or hinder creativity, and that can be measured. Maturity model Maturity model A description of successive levels of capability, used to assess the current situation and identify the next step. Review and Discussion Questions Why do organizations tend to measure inputs and activities? And what is the danger of stopping there? Understanding Analyze the opening case using Kerr’s and Campbell’s ideas, and propose two alternative indicators. Analysis Design three indicators for your organization’s innovation portfolio, one of which measures decision limbo. Application Build a balanced measurement dashboard for your organization’s innovation system, and test each indicator by asking: How could it be met on paper only?
