17 Chapter 17 Innovation and spending efficiency The relationship between innovation and money has two inseparable sides: innovation is a route to greater spending efficiency, and spending on innovation must itself be efficient. The chapter is built on these two sides. We show how early knowledge reduces the cost of error, why the total cost of a solution over its lifetime should be the yardstick, why large projects overrun their budgets, how feasibility can be assessed along multiple dimensions, and which costs never appear in any budget.

Opening case: two projects (composite case) A government agency decided to rebuild one of its main services digitally in a single large three-year project, following a detailed feasibility study and a contract with a major firm. By the third year, the project had run roughly double its budget and its launch was a year late; when it finally went live, users discovered that the regulations governing many of the steps it had been built around had changed during the implementation period. Meanwhile, a small team in another department had spent six weeks testing a change to a single step in a similar service, at negligible cost, cutting its completion time in half, and then gradually rolled it out to the remaining branches. The difference between the two projects lies less in the technical competence of those who carried them out than in how they handled uncertainty: the first committed to everything before it knew, while the second learned before it committed. This paradox is our starting point for explaining why the second approach usually makes more efficient use of money, even though the first may look more disciplined. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Distinguish between innovation as a means of spending efficiency and efficiency in spending on innovation. Explain why the cost of change rises as a project advances, and the value of spending early on learning. Calculate the total cost of a solution over its lifetime. Explain why large projects overrun their budgets, and the methods for limiting such overruns. Assess an initiative’s feasibility along multiple dimensions, and recognize the hidden costs of weak innovation management.

Governments, including the Kingdom under Vision 2030, are seeking to raise the efficiency of public spending, that is, to achieve greater value with the resources available (Saudi Vision 2030, 2016 [Arabic]) . Innovation relates to this direction in two ways. On the one hand, innovation is a means of spending efficiency : many public-sector innovations reduce costs, save time, prevent waste, or achieve a better result for the same cost. The change made by the small team in the opening case is an example. On the other hand, spending on innovation itself needs to be efficient : centers, platforms, accelerators and large projects consume resources, and may not produce enough to justify their cost. We bring the two sides together in a single question: How can an organization spend on innovation so that every riyal buys the greatest possible amount of learning and value? Here we build on the staged funding and real options logic presented in Chapter 10, and on the discussion of experimentation in Chapter 14.

search.s: 17.2 The cost of learning and the cost of error
search.t: One of the oldest observations in software engineering is that the cost of correcting an error rises the later it is discovered. Boehm showed that correcting a requirements error after a system is in operation can cost many times more than correcting it during the requirements stage, and that in large projects the difference can reach a hundredfold ( Boehm, 1981 ) . The same logic holds for innovation in general, as Figure 17.1 illustrates. Problem Concept Experiment Full build Operation Initiative stages → Cost of changing a decision Zone of cheap learning Change is cheap here Change is very costly here Figure 17.1 The rising cost of changing a decision as an initiative advances. Developed by the author, drawing on Boehm (1981) . The curve is illustrative. A simple principle follows: early spending on learning is the cheapest spending in innovation. Thomke and Fujimoto studied what they called front-loading problem solving in automotive development, and found that companies that identify and solve problems in the early stages of development, through simulation and prototypes, shorten development time and reduce its cost compared with those that discover problems late ( Thomke & Fujimoto, 2000 ) . In the opening case, most of the money was spent after commitment, when every change had become expensive. The small team, by contrast, spent a little in the zone of cheap learning and then spent on scaling once it knew what worked. This is what it means to understand the problem before the solution and to test assumptions before building: it is the most efficient way to spend money.

Organizations often make the mistake of evaluating a solution by its launch cost alone: the cost of building, buying or setting it up. Yet this may be the smallest part of the true cost. The concept of total cost of ownership proposes that a solution be costed over its entire lifetime: purchase, operation, maintenance, training, support, upgrades and indirect internal costs, and then the cost of decommissioning or replacement ( Ellram, 1995 ) . This concept explains a recurring phenomenon in innovation ecosystems: entities established with large start-up budgets whose annual operating costs, and the staff time needed to bring them to life, were never calculated, so that they remain standing but inactive. A digital fabrication lab (fab lab) at a university costs, in addition to the price of its equipment, technicians to run it, consumables, maintenance, faculty hours to integrate it into courses, and sustained effort to draw students to it. An organization that funds the set-up and overlooks these elements buys equipment, while the ecosystem remains outside its reckoning. This connects to the sustainability equation in the business model discussed in Chapter 13. In Practice Choose an innovation entity or platform in your organization and calculate its total cost over the past year: its approved budget, plus the time of staff who work in it or with it, licenses, space and maintenance. Then divide the total by the number of solutions actually implemented thanks to it. This figure may change the way you talk about it.

search.s: 17.4 Why do large projects overrun their budgets?
search.t: Flyvbjerg and colleagues studied a database of more than sixteen thousand large projects across different sectors and countries. They found that only about 8.5 percent were delivered on budget and on time, and only about 0.5 percent were delivered on budget, on time and with the expected benefits ( Flyvbjerg & Gardner, 2023 ) . They attributed this to multiple factors, chief among them optimism bias , which leads planners to underestimate costs and risks and overestimate benefits, along with the pressure to make a project look attractive so that it gets approved ( Flyvbjerg, 2014 ) . Flyvbjerg and Gardner propose several principles for limiting overruns, most of which are consistent with the logic of this book: Think slow, act fast: invest time in planning and experimentation while change is cheap, then execute quickly once delay becomes costly. This is what Figure 17.1 illustrates. Reference class forecasting: estimate a project’s cost and duration by looking at what actually happened in similar projects, since focusing solely on the details of the project at hand invites optimism. Small, repeatable modules: projects built from small units that are repeated and improved with each iteration are less prone to overruns than huge one-off projects. This is consistent with the phased scaling discussed in Chapter 15. This does not mean that large projects are wrong in themselves; some solutions cannot be broken down. It does mean that every part that can be tested small before a large commitment should be tested.

Feasibility studies are sometimes reduced to a financial calculation: cost against return. Public investment decisions, however, call for a broader view. HM Treasury’s guidance on appraising public investment offers a framework of five cases that any investment proposal should address ( HM Treasury, 2022 ) . Table 17.1 sets them out alongside their counterparts in this book. Table 17.1 The five dimensions of feasibility assessment, adapted from HM Treasury (2022) Dimension Its question Counterpart in this book Strategic Is there a genuine need for intervention? And is it consistent with priorities? Understanding the problem (Ch. 11), and search fields (Ch. 4) Economic Does this option deliver the best value for society compared with the alternatives, including doing nothing? Comparing alternatives (Ch. 12), and public value (Ch. 13) Commercial Can the solution be procured or delivered on suitable terms and through workable partnerships? Resources and partners in the business model (Ch. 13) Financial Is the total cost affordable and covered over the solution’s lifetime? Total cost (this chapter), and the sustainability equation (Ch. 13) Management Are the capability and governance needed for delivery and operation in place? Governance (Ch. 10), and ownership and scaling (Ch. 15) Drawing on the logic of this book, we add to these dimensions a sixth that is often overlooked: the human dimension . Is there anyone with the motivation and ability to work on this initiative? And will those who are to use and operate it accept it? An economically sound initiative that no one adopts fails just as surely as an economically weak one, and Chapter 15 showed why. The depth of analysis in each dimension should match the initiative’s stage. As Chapter 10 showed, criteria progress from assumptions to evidence, and the feasibility study progresses with them: brief questions at the start of an initiative, and deeper study before committing to scale.

search.s: 17.6 Costs that do not appear in the budget
search.t: Organizations count what they spend, but rarely count what they lose. In innovation management there are substantial costs that do not appear in any budget, as Figure 17.2 shows. What appears in the budget Establishing centers, labs and platforms Contracts and licenses Events, competitions and awards Budget line What does not appear in it The cost of indecision: the time of teams left waiting, and ideas that grew stale before a decision was made on them The cost of duplication: units carrying out similar initiatives without knowing about one another The cost of continuing what should be stopped: resources consumed by initiatives the evidence does not support The cost of missed opportunity: problems left unsolved and improvements that never happened The cost of lost innovators: people who stopped trying, or left for places where their ideas are valued Figure 17.2 Visible and hidden costs in innovation management. Prepared by the author. The heaviest of these costs is the last, and it is also the hardest to calculate. Chapter 7 recounted what one successful innovator said about a gifted friend who was forced into a job far from his passion, whereupon his interest in his project faded ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . Every organization has people who have stopped putting forward their ideas because they have learned that no one listens. This is the thesis on which this book rests, expressed in financial terms: a system that spends on visible inputs and neglects people pays twice over, once for what it built and again for what it lost of people’s capacity and desire to innovate. Principle The most efficient spending on innovation is early spending on learning and sustained spending on people. The least efficient is setting up large entities before it is known who will use them, how they will work, and who will bear their cost.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.s: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: 18 Chapter 18 Open innovation and innovation ecosystems In this chapter we look beyond the boundaries of the organization. We trace how an organization can benefit from the knowledge and ideas that exist outside it, how far it should open up, what capacity it needs to absorb what flows in, and which forms of partnership are available to it; we then turn to how innovation ecosystems work, bringing together universities, government, the private sector and society.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: Opening case: a services company (composite case) For years, a logistics services company struggled to improve the scheduling of its fleets, and its technical team worked on the problem with little to show for it. It then launched an open challenge with a modest prize, and an effective solution arrived from a graduate student in applied mathematics who knew nothing about logistics but recognized in the problem a mathematical model familiar from her own field. Yet the company could not make use of the solution. No one on its team understood the model well enough to integrate it into the company’s systems, and some engineers felt that a solution from outside the field “doesn’t understand our reality.” The solution stayed in the challenge report. The company succeeded in opening up and failed at absorbing. Knowledge reached it from an unexpected quarter, but it lacked both the internal capacity to understand and use that knowledge and a culture willing to accept what came from outside. These two sides together form the subject of this chapter: how an organization opens up, and how it absorbs what it opens up to. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Define open innovation and distinguish among its three directions. Explain why too much openness can be as harmful as closedness. Explain absorptive capacity and recognize resistance to what comes from outside. Choose the appropriate form of partnership for each purpose. Describe innovation ecosystems, the organization’s place within them, and their role in supporting innovators.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: For most of the twentieth century, the research laboratories of large companies operated on a closed logic: the organization innovates by itself, with the best minds it can hire, protects what it produces, and develops it all the way to the market. Chesbrough observed that this logic had lost much of its validity, because knowledge had become widely distributed, talented people moved between organizations, and no single organization could any longer monopolize the knowledge it needed. He proposed an alternative he called open innovation : the organization uses external ideas alongside internal ones and makes its unused ideas available to others ( Chesbrough, 2003 ) . Later, with Bogers, he defined it as a distributed innovation process based on purposively managed knowledge flows across organizational boundaries ( Chesbrough & Bogers, 2014 ) . The word “purposively” matters in this definition. Open innovation does not mean throwing the doors open to everything; it means designing the flows of knowledge between the organization and its surroundings. Three directions of these flows can be distinguished, as Figure 18.1 shows. → ● Outside-in Bringing ideas, knowledge and technologies from outside the organization for use inside it Open challenges, research collaboration, learning from users ● → Inside-out Making the organization’s ideas, technologies or data available for others to benefit from Technology licensing, open data, spin-offs ⇄ Coupled Joint development with partners, in which each party contributes and benefits Alliances, joint ventures, co-development with beneficiaries Figure 18.1 The three directions of open innovation, adapted from Chesbrough & Bogers (2014) . Chapter 11 presented one form of the first direction in lead users, who innovate for themselves before any provider offers them a solution. Chapter 13 presented one form of the second direction in the Xerox technologies that found no place in the company’s business model and left to become spin-offs.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.s: 18.2 How open should an organization be?
search.t: If openness is beneficial, does its benefit keep growing the more open an organization becomes? Laursen and Salter studied data on some 2,700 British manufacturing firms and measured their openness along two dimensions: breadth , the number of external sources a firm draws on, and depth , the extent to which it relies on each source. They found that the relationship between openness and innovative performance takes the shape of an arc: performance improves as openness increases up to a point, then declines once openness exceeds the organization’s ability to follow its sources and benefit from them ( Laursen & Salter, 2006 ) . An organization that opens channels with every possible party may drown in relationships it cannot manage, just as an organization that opens a platform to every idea does. Among the strongest arguments for openness is that a solution may come from where it is least expected. Jeppesen and Lakhani studied more than 160 scientific problems that companies had posted on an open challenge platform after their own laboratories had failed to solve them, and found that the likelihood of a solution was higher when the solver’s field of expertise was distant from the field of the problem ( Jeppesen & Lakhani, 2010 ) . The distant specialist sees the problem through the tools of their own field, just as the student in the opening case saw the scheduling problem as a familiar mathematical model. This connects with the discussion in Chapter 12 of distant analogy as a way of breaking design fixation.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: Knowledge reaching the organization is only a first step; what follows is the ability to understand and use it. Cohen and Levinthal coined the concept of absorptive capacity to describe this: an organization’s ability to recognize the value of new external knowledge, assimilate it and apply it. They showed that this ability depends on the organization’s prior related knowledge; an organization can absorb only what lies close to what it already knows. For this reason, they argued, internal research and development has two faces: it generates new knowledge, and it builds the capacity to absorb the knowledge of others ( Cohen & Levinthal, 1990 ) . An important practical consequence follows from this concept: open innovation rests on an internal capability that supports it and receives what it brings in. An organization that hollows itself out of expertise by relying on partners and suppliers loses the ability to judge what they offer and to integrate it into its work. This is what happened in the opening case: no one in the company understood the mathematical model well enough to use it. Absorption faces another obstacle, this time rooted in attitudes: resistance to what comes from outside, known as the not-invented-here syndrome. Katz and Allen studied R&D teams and found that the longer members remained together, the less the team communicated with external sources, and the more its performance declined along with it ( Katz & Allen, 1982 ) . This tendency can be countered by the boundary-spanning activities discussed in Chapter 9 and by the culture open to different ways of thinking discussed in Chapter 8. Respect for knowledge arriving from outside is another face of respect for ideas arriving from the most junior employee inside. In Practice Before you launch an open challenge or enter a partnership, identify by name who in your organization will receive what it brings: who will read the solutions, who has the knowledge to evaluate them, and who will integrate them into the work. If you cannot find these people, start by building this capacity before opening up.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: Openness takes many forms, each suited to a particular purpose and each carrying its own risks. Table 18.1 sets out the most prominent of them. Table 18.1 Forms of partnership in open innovation Form Suited to What it requires of the organization Risk Open challenges A specific problem that can be clearly formulated and might be solved from a distant field Precise problem formulation, and the capacity to evaluate and integrate solutions Solutions that go unused, as in the opening case Research collaboration with universities Problems that require deep scientific knowledge and a longer time frame Patience with the pace of research, and someone who translates between the language of research and the language of practice Published research that never turns into application Working with startups Fast-evolving technical solutions, and trying out new approaches Flexible procurement and contracting procedures suited to the size of a startup Procedures that exhaust the startup before it begins Co-development with beneficiaries Services whose value depends on the experience of those who use them Respect for beneficiaries’ time, and a clear response to their contributions Token participation in which beneficiaries’ views have no influence Partnership with the private sector in service delivery Services for which the private sector has capabilities or resources the agency lacks Contracts that specify the public value required and accountability for it Transferring risk without transferring the capacity to manage it Making data and technologies available Data or technologies held by the organization on which others can build Standards for privacy, quality and intellectual property Releasing what should not be released, a matter taken up in Chapter 19 Two conditions recur across most of these forms. The first is that the problem be clear before the partnership begins, as Chapter 11 showed; a partnership built around a vague problem usually ends in conflicting expectations. The second is that the organization have a person or unit that acts as a bridge between the partner and the inside: one that understands the language of both sides, follows the relationship, and ensures that what comes from outside reaches those who need it.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: An organization innovates within a wider system of actors, regulations and relationships. The concept of the national innovation system emerged to describe the network of public and private institutions that interact to produce, diffuse and use knowledge in a given country, and to stress that national innovation performance depends on the quality of these interactions as much as on the capabilities of each actor ( Lundvall, 1992 ) . The triple helix model focuses on three main parties in this system and holds that innovation arises from their interaction, to the point that each party sometimes takes on some of the roles of the others ( Etzkowitz & Leydesdorff, 2000 ) , as Figure 18.2 shows. University Knowledge, research, talent, and educating the next generation of innovators Industry and the private sector Turning knowledge into products and services, investment, and market knowledge Government Policy, funding, regulation, and demand for innovative solutions Zone of interaction Applied research projects, spin-offs, incubators, national challenges, and the movement of people between the parties Figure 18.2 The triple helix of the innovation ecosystem, adapted from Etzkowitz & Leydesdorff (2000) . In the Kingdom, this system is taking shape around the national research, development and innovation priorities presented in Chapter 2, and around the role of the Research, Development and Innovation Authority (RDIA) as enabler and regulator of the sector (Saudi Press Agency, 2022 [Arabic]) . This means that an organization, whether a university, a government agency or a company, can link the search fields in its strategy to these priorities and so find partners, funding and demand for its solutions. Ecosystems carry risks of their own. Adner warned that the success of an innovation may depend on other parties in the ecosystem whom the organization does not control: on partners who must also innovate for the solution to work, and on links in the adoption chain that must accept the solution before it reaches the end beneficiary ( Adner, 2006 ) . A government solution that requires another agency to change its systems, or a university solution that depends on acceptance by a field-training provider, is exposed to risks invisible to anyone who looks only at their own organization.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.s: 18.6 The community that supports the innovator
search.t: Innovation ecosystems are usually studied from the perspective of institutions; in this book we also look at them from the perspective of the person: what does the innovator need from the community around them? In a phenomenological study conducted with ten Saudi innovative entrepreneurs, participants identified four features of a supportive community: recognizing the innovator’s distinctiveness and understanding their personal and cognitive style; investing in the innovator, promoting them and connecting them to suitable economic settings; financial and operational empowerment of their initiatives; and building their innovative and entrepreneurial identity through flexible environments that allow deep learning and genuine practice (Alsamani, 2026 [Arabic]) . These features converge with the findings of another study of the experiences of prominent innovators, most of whom saw their network of relationships as a pathway to opportunities, and all of whom agreed on the importance of interacting with peers ( Alsamani, 2023 ) . In the innovator’s eyes, the ecosystem is people who know them, opportunities they can reach, and peers they learn alongside. The university holds a unique position in this ecosystem, because it is the party through which most innovators pass during their formative years. When it connects its students with the problems of government agencies and companies in its region, offers them internships and joint projects, and introduces them to opportunities aligned with national priorities, it builds for them the network of relationships they need before they graduate. We return to this role in detail in Chapter 20. Principle Openness brings in knowledge, internal capacity absorbs it, and culture accepts it. An organization that has only the first collects solutions in reports; one that has all three turns them into value.

search.c: Chapter 18: Open innovation and innovation ecosystems
search.t: Open innovation is a process based on purposively managed knowledge flows across organizational boundaries, in three directions: outside-in, inside-out, and coupled. Openness has an optimal level, beyond which it exceeds the organization’s ability to benefit from its sources. A solution may come from a field distant from that of the problem, and this is among the strongest arguments for openness. Absorptive capacity is a precondition for benefiting from external knowledge and depends on related internal knowledge, so openness is no substitute for internal capability. Each form of partnership has its purpose and its risks, and all share two conditions: a clear problem, and an internal bridge to receive what comes from outside. An organization works within an ecosystem that brings together university, industry and government, and the success of its innovation may depend on parties it does not control. In the innovator’s eyes, the ecosystem is people, opportunities and peers, and the university holds a unique position in building a network of relationships for its students before they graduate. 19 Chapter 19 Responsible innovation In this chapter we turn to the most neglected side of innovation management: its effect on those who were never asked about it. We propose a framework that builds responsibility into the initiative journey, and from there move on to the ethics of experimenting on people, the governance of data and artificial intelligence, fairness in the ownership of ideas, and the environmental impact of innovation.

Opening case: a reporting app (composite case) A city launched an app that automatically detects road defects from residents’ phones while they drive and ranks maintenance work by the number of reports from each neighborhood. The app looked like a clear success: thousands of reports, faster response, and lower costs than field inspections. A year later, an engineer noticed that maintenance had become concentrated in newer, higher-income neighborhoods, while it had declined in older ones. The reason was that residents of the older neighborhoods, many of them elderly, used the app less. The app had redistributed the service without anyone deciding that it should. There was no intended injustice in this case. The app was designed in good faith and succeeded on every measure applied to it. Yet the measure itself, the number of reports, reflected who used the app, while those who needed maintenance remained outside the picture. This paradox is our starting point for the question that occupies this chapter: how can responsibility be built into innovation management as part of its quality? Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain why innovations produce unintended consequences, and why these are hard to control once the innovations have spread. Apply the four dimensions of responsible innovation to an initiative in their own organization. Apply the core ethical principles when designing experiments involving people. Recognize the risks of data and artificial intelligence in innovation initiatives, and the frameworks for governing them. Design a fair policy for the ownership and attribution of ideas. Evaluate the environmental impact of an innovation initiative and identify the level of sustainability-oriented innovation to which it belongs.

search.s: 19.1 Why is responsibility part of innovation management?
search.t: As early as the 1930s, the sociologist Merton pointed out that every purposive social action produces consequences its actor did not intend, owing to incomplete knowledge, errors of judgment, and a focus on immediate rather than distant results ( Merton, 1936 ) . Innovation, by its very nature, is action in unknown territory, so its unintended consequences are all the more likely. One of the clearest examples is what Obermeyer and colleagues uncovered in an algorithm widely used in the US health system to identify patients in need of additional care. The algorithm used past treatment costs as a proxy measure for health need, and because less was spent on treating Black patients, for reasons related to access to care, it underestimated their need. The researchers found that correcting the measure would have raised the share of Black patients receiving additional care from about 18 percent to about 46 percent ( Obermeyer et al., 2019 ) . This case is another illustration of the point made in Chapter 16 that an indicator can swallow the goal: a proxy measure carries assumptions that those who use it may not see. Anyone who wants to control these consequences faces a dilemma formulated by Collingridge. In the early stages, an innovation is easy to change, but its consequences are not yet known. In the later stages, its consequences are clear, but changing it becomes difficult and costly because it has spread and interests and systems have become tied to it ( Collingridge, 1980 ) . Figure 19.1 illustrates this dilemma. At the outset Change is easy and cheap, but the consequences are unknown, so no one knows what needs to change. After diffusion The consequences are clear, but change is difficult and costly, because the innovation has become bound up with systems, interests and habits. Output Raise questions of responsibility early, monitor consequences during experimentation and scaling, and build the capacity to adjust before the solution hardens. Figure 19.1 The dilemma of controlling innovation, adapted from Collingridge (1980) . This dilemma mirrors the cost-of-change curve presented in Chapter 17: responsibility, like learning, is cheaper at the start. That is why Chapter 12 added the responsibility lens to the lenses for evaluating a solution, so that its questions are raised from the very first concept.

Stilgoe, Owen and Macnaghten proposed a framework for responsible innovation built on four dimensions that are practiced during the innovation process itself ( Stilgoe et al., 2013 ) . Figure 19.2 presents them together with the question each one raises. Anticipation Anticipation Systematic thinking about possible impacts, intended and unintended, before they occur What if the solution succeeds at scale? Who might be harmed? Reflexivity Reflexivity The team’s review of its own assumptions, values and the limits of its knowledge What are we assuming without noticing? Whom are we not seeing? Inclusion Inclusion Involving those who will be affected by the innovation in shaping it from the outset, before it is complete Have we heard from the least represented groups? Responsiveness Responsiveness The capacity to modify or halt the innovation when concerns or new knowledge emerge What would make us change course? And who holds the decision? Figure 19.2 The four dimensions of responsible innovation, adapted from Stilgoe et al. (2013) . These dimensions are consistent with what the book has built in earlier chapters. Inclusion extends the understanding of those who live the problem in Chapter 11; responsiveness extends the stopping criteria in Chapters 10 and 14; and reflexivity, that is, critical review of oneself and one’s assumptions, extends the discussion in Chapter 8 of the psychological safety that allows a team to admit what it does not know. Responsible innovation is simply good innovation management, with a wider circle of people it cares about. In the opening case, the anticipation question alone would have been enough to reveal the problem: who does not use the app, and do they need maintenance any less than others? Inclusion would have added an alternative reporting channel, such as a phone line or a neighborhood monitor, along with regular field inspections of the neighborhoods where use was lowest.

search.s: 19.3 The ethics of experimenting on people
search.t: Chapter 14 called for experimentation before scaling and cautioned that the beneficiary of a public service is not a test subject. The balance between the two rests on well-established ethical principles for research involving human beings. The Belmont Report set out three basic principles ( National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research, 1979 ) : Respect for persons: people are treated as the decision-makers in matters that concern them, so they know what is being tested on them and consent to it whenever possible, and groups less able to protect themselves receive special protection. Beneficence and non-maleficence: risks are minimized and benefits maximized, and no one is exposed to harm that the value of what is learned cannot justify. Justice: the burdens and benefits of an experiment are distributed fairly, so that no particular group bears the risks of experimentation while others benefit from its results. In innovation experiments, these principles translate into practical questions. Do participants know they are in an experiment? Can they withdraw without losing the service? Are there stopping conditions if harm appears? Was the participating group chosen because it is best suited for learning, or because it is least able to object? In universities, research involving human beings passes through research ethics committees, and it is advisable to apply the same principles to student projects that test solutions with real beneficiaries. In Practice Before any experiment with beneficiaries, ask yourself: if I, or a member of my family, were in the group to be experimented on, what would I want to know in advance? And what would I want guaranteed? Write down the answer and make it part of the experiment card.

Many innovation initiatives today depend on personal data and on artificial intelligence, both of which are sources of great value and of great risk alike. The Kingdom has established a legal framework for protecting personal data with the issuance of the Personal Data Protection Law (Personal Data Protection Law, 2021 [Arabic]) , and the Saudi Data and AI Authority (SDAIA) has published AI ethics principles intended to guide the development and use of AI in ways that safeguard rights and strengthen trust (Saudi Data and AI Authority, 2023 [Arabic]) . Internationally, these frameworks intersect with the OECD AI Principles, which emphasize values such as respect for human rights and fairness, transparency and explainability, robustness and safety, and accountability ( OECD, 2019 ) . Compliance with these frameworks does not remove the need for questions the innovation team must ask itself, the most important of which are: What do the data actually represent? The report data in the opening case, and the cost data in Obermeyer’s algorithm, represented something other than what they were assumed to represent. Who is missing from the data? Groups that use technology less, or appear less in records, may be excluded without anyone noticing. Can the decision be explained? A decision that affects people, and that those who made it cannot explain, is hard to defend and hard to correct. Where does the human remain in the decision? Artificial intelligence supports human judgment, but accountability remains with a specific person. This section returns us to a thesis presented in Chapter 2: that artificial intelligence raises the value of the human rather than eliminating it. The larger the share of work that tools take on, the more important human judgment becomes in determining what they should do, for whom, and at what cost.

search.s: 19.5 Intellectual property and fairness to idea holders
search.t: Innovation management raises questions about the ownership of ideas and solutions. Who owns an employee’s idea that the organization has developed? Who owns a student project that originated in a course or a university laboratory? What share of the value of an innovation goes to the innovator? Uncertainty about the answers harms both sides: innovators who do not know their rights may withhold their ideas or take them where they will be protected, and an organization that has not defined its policy faces disputes once an idea succeeds. Fairness here requires a clear policy, announced in advance, that specifies what the organization owns, what remains with the innovator, how any returns are to be shared, and how credit is attributed. This connects directly with the discussion in Chapter 10 of procedural justice and attributing an idea to its originator, and with the discussion in Chapter 7 of recognition as one of the innovator’s foremost needs. In universities in particular, such a policy needs to be understandable to students and to encourage them to develop their ideas within the university’s own ecosystem. Intellectual property also bears on the open innovation discussed in Chapter 18: an organization that makes its data available or collaborates with partners needs clear rules on what is shared, what is protected, and how individuals’ privacy is preserved in the data it releases.

The question of responsibility extends to innovation’s impact on the environment, one of its longest-lasting effects and the hardest to reverse. Adams and colleagues defined sustainability-oriented innovation as making intentional changes to an organization’s philosophy and values, as well as to its products, processes and practices, in order to create environmental and social value alongside economic value. From a systematic review of 127 sources, they derived three contexts through which such innovation progresses ( Adams et al., 2016 ) : Operational optimization: the organization does what it already does with greater environmental efficiency, for example by reducing energy and material consumption and waste in its operations. Organizational transformation: the organization offers new products, services or business models that create environmental or social value, accompanied by a change in its values and way of thinking. Systems building: the organization works with partners beyond its boundaries to change an entire system, such as a city’s transport or waste management system. This progression is especially useful for public sector organizations and universities. Digitizing a service so that beneficiaries no longer need to travel or use paper is an operational optimization with a direct environmental effect. Redesigning a service around the principle of sharing resources rather than owning them is an organizational transformation. Tackling an environmental problem in the region in partnership with other bodies is systems building, the level that connects with open innovation. The Kingdom has made environmental sustainability and essential needs one of its four national research, development and innovation priorities (Saudi Press Agency, 2022 [Arabic]) , so environmental impact has become a question put to initiatives from the outset, where it was once left until after implementation. Principle Responsible innovation is good innovation management with a wider circle of concern: those who use the solution, those who do not, and those affected by it without ever being asked.

search.s: Chapter tool: the responsibility check across the initiative journey
search.t: Add these questions to the gates of your organization’s innovation system, so that the team answers them at each stage as far as available knowledge allows. Their value lies in the discussion they open, more than in completing a formal compliance checklist. Chapter tool The responsibility check across the initiative journey Stage Responsibility questions Understanding the problem Who lives the problem? Which groups are least represented in it? Have we heard from them directly? Developing the solution Who might be harmed if the solution succeeds? Which proxy measures are we relying on, and what do they actually represent? Experiment Do participants know they are in an experiment? Can they withdraw? What are the stopping conditions? Have the burdens been distributed fairly? Data and artificial intelligence Are we complying with the Personal Data Protection Law? Who is missing from the data? Can the decision be explained? Who is accountable for it? Environmental impact What is the solution’s effect on energy and material consumption and waste? Could it create environmental value alongside its core value? Scaling Did we monitor unintended consequences during the experiment? Do we still have the capacity to adjust after scaling? Ownership and fairness Does the idea holder know their rights? Have they been given credit? Are the rules public to all parties?

Every purposive action has consequences its actor did not intend, and innovation is especially prone to them because it takes place in unexplored territory. Proxy measures may carry assumptions that disadvantage groups absent from the data, without anyone intending it. Early on, an innovation is easy to change but its consequences are unknown; once it has spread, its consequences are known but it is hard to change. The way out is to raise questions of responsibility early and to monitor consequences continuously. Responsible innovation has four dimensions: anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion and responsiveness. In essence, they are an extension of good innovation management. Experimenting on people rests on respect for persons, beneficence and non-maleficence, and justice in the distribution of burdens and benefits. Data and AI initiatives require compliance with regulations, along with questions about what the data represent, who is missing from them, explainability, and keeping a human accountable. A clear, published policy on the ownership and attribution of ideas is part of being fair to their originators, and part of the organization’s ability to retain them. Sustainability-oriented innovation progresses from operational optimization, to organizational transformation, to systems building with partners, and environmental impact is a question to be raised from the start of an initiative. Key Terms Responsible innovation Responsible innovation Taking care of the future through collective stewardship of science and innovation in the present, based on anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion and responsiveness. Unintended consequences Unintended consequences Outcomes of a purposive action that its actor neither intended nor foresaw. Collingridge dilemma Collingridge dilemma The difficulty of controlling innovation: it is easy to change while its consequences are unknown, and hard to change once they become clear. Proxy measure Proxy measure A measure used in place of the intended quantity because the latter is hard to measure directly; it may carry hidden biases. Sustainability-oriented innovation Sustainability-oriented innovation Intentional changes to an organization’s values, products and processes that create environmental and social value alongside economic value. Explainability Explainability The ability of those who use an automated system to explain the reasons behind its decisions. 20 Chapter 20 The university innovation ecosystem: from scattered initiatives to an integrated system In this chapter we gather the book's threads in a single applied setting, the university, and we argue for a specific thesis: that a university innovation ecosystem is built from within, starting from the university's own strengths, needs and distinctive character. We then trace what this thesis demands: a strategy that is understood and shared, integration among the parallel systems within the university, the everyday environment of classroom and administration, motivation and recognition, the continuity of initiatives, the contribution of faculty researchers and staff, and the governance that brings all of this together.

Opening case: an ordinary teaching day (composite case) On the morning of an ordinary teaching day, the fab lab at a university stands quiet: state-of-the-art equipment that cost millions of riyals, a single technician sorting materials, and two engineering students working on a graduation project. Two hundred meters away, in a crowded lecture hall, one hundred and fifty students from various majors are reviewing for a midterm exam. Most of them have never set foot in the lab; no course has ever asked them to, and many do not know it exists. That same week, at a meeting of the university council, a proposal was presented to establish a new entrepreneurship center modeled on one at a leading international university, complete with performance indicators lifted from that university's report. This university has both the resources and the ambition. What it lacks is a connection between what it has built and what its students experience day to day, and a way of thinking that starts from its own needs. We believe this situation recurs in many universities, and that the path from it to a functioning ecosystem runs through a review of the logic by which the ecosystem is built, before any new entity is created. Learning Objectives After studying this chapter, the reader should be able to: Explain why borrowed models fail in university innovation ecosystems. Diagnose a university's strengths and needs, and formulate from them an innovation strategy that is understood and shared. Analyze why innovation units, gifted-student services and formal education become disconnected, and design connection points among them. Evaluate the everyday environment of classroom and administration in terms of how far it supports initiative. Design forms of motivation and recognition suited to students, faculty and staff. Plan for the continuity and institutionalization of initiatives, and extend the ecosystem to include faculty researchers and staff. Design governance responsible for integration, and chart a phased roadmap whose content is determined by diagnosis.

When a university sets out to build an innovation ecosystem, the easiest route seems to be to look at successful universities and copy what they have: an accelerator like theirs, a lab like theirs, indicators like theirs. DiMaggio and Powell explained this tendency through what they called mimetic isomorphism : when goals are ambiguous and the environment uncertain, organizations tend to imitate those they regard as successful or legitimate, and so over time they come to resemble one another in form, whether or not this improves their efficiency ( DiMaggio & Powell, 1983 ) . Government innovation labs offer one illustration: some were established in imitation of other agencies and in pursuit of legitimacy ( Tõnurist et al., 2017 ) . Andrews, Pritchett and Woolcock went further, describing a phenomenon they called isomorphic mimicry : an organization adopts the forms of successful organizations, their structures, programs and titles, without the capability that makes them work. From the outside, the organization appears to possess what successful organizations possess; on the inside, it remains unable to perform its function. Mimetic isomorphism, then, is a tendency to imitate under uncertainty, while isomorphic mimicry is what results when form is transferred without function. As an alternative, they proposed what they called problem-driven iterative adaptation , built on four principles: local solutions to local problems, a search for successful attempts within the system itself, continuous experimentation, learning and adaptation, and scaling through diffusion ( Andrews et al., 2013 ) . This literature explains what happens in many universities. An accelerator transplanted from another university presupposes students who arrive with ready-made projects, an entrepreneurial culture in the colleges, and a network of investors around it. Where these conditions are absent, the accelerator remains form without function. The same holds for transplanted indicators: a number of startups appropriate for a university in a mature entrepreneurial ecosystem may push another university to inflate figures that do not reflect its reality. The problem is not learning from others, which is essential, but allowing imitation to take the place of diagnosis.

search.s: 20.2 A strategy from within, understood and shared
search.t: In this book we propose the opposite logic: that a university's innovation strategy begin with a diagnosis of its strengths, needs and distinctive character ; that the strategy then be designed; and that the system of ideas and initiatives that puts it into effect then be built, step by step, adapting to what is learned along the way. This logic draws on what strategic management calls the resource-based view, which holds that sustained advantage comes from an organization's resources and capabilities that others find hard to imitate ( Barney, 1991 ) . Whatever sets a university apart, whether its strong disciplines, its region and that region's problems, its relationships or its students, is what its ecosystem should be built on. Self-assessment tools are available to help universities with this diagnosis. Among the most prominent is a framework for entrepreneurial universities developed by the European Commission and the OECD, which allows a university to assess itself in areas including leadership and governance, organizational capacity and incentives, entrepreneurial teaching and learning, support for student entrepreneurs, knowledge exchange and collaboration, internationalization, and impact measurement ( European Commission & OECD, 2012 ) . The value of this framework lies in its being a tool for self-reflection that helps a university see itself by its own standards; it loses much of its usefulness when used for comparison and ranking. Diagnosis also needs to hear directly from students and faculty. In a study published in 2023 of one hundred and one faculty members at a Saudi university, participants viewed the needs of students with creative characteristics along three dimensions: developing the creative personality, a stimulating university environment, and support for the creative process and product development. This support could take the form of training linked to students' interests and awareness of opportunities aligned with Saudi Vision 2030 (Alsamani, 2023 [Arabic]) . This kind of local knowledge is precisely what cannot be borrowed from another university's report. Table 20.1 presents the core diagnostic questions. Table 20.1 Questions for diagnosing a university innovation ecosystem from within Domain Diagnostic questions Distinctive strengths Which disciplines are strong? Which problems are characteristic of the region? What relationships exist with agencies and companies? Students What are their interests and needs? Where do they spend their time? What do they know about the innovation units, and what keeps them from reaching them? Faculty Who actually practices creative teaching? What do they need? Which of their efforts does the evaluation and promotion system count? Existing units What does each unit offer? Who actually benefits from it? How is it connected to courses and to other units? Successful attempts Where within the university itself, in a course, a department or a student club, are there successful experiences that can be built on? Researchers and staff Do faculty research partnerships with external organizations count? Is there a channel for staff ideas on improving university services? Cost and sustainability What is the total cost of each unit? And what does it deliver in return? The question of successful attempts deserves particular emphasis. Every university has faculty members who turn their courses into spaces for creativity without anyone asking them to, student clubs that run real projects, and departments with living relationships with outside organizations. These are the seeds that the iterative adaptation approach advises looking for and building on, because they have already proven that they work in the university's own context. It is not enough for the strategy to be written from within; it must also be understood and shared . search.s: 20.3 Parallel systems that do not connect
search.t: Several systems operate within a single university, each with its own logic: innovation and entrepreneurship units with their competitions and programs, gifted-student services with their criteria and offerings, formal education with its study plans, courses and exams, and administrative offices with their procedures. Often these systems simply sit side by side: the gifted-student unit does not know what the accelerator offers, the faculty member in the classroom does not know what goes on in the lab, and the academic system does not count what the student accomplishes outside it. The student thus lives in separate worlds and has to connect them alone, if they can. Weick offered an early explanation of this phenomenon, describing educational organizations as loosely coupled systems : their units respond to one another, yet each retains its identity and independence, so that what happens in one carries over to the others only to a small degree ( Weick, 1976 ) . Weick did not see this as a pure flaw; loose coupling allows each unit to experiment and adapt without bringing the whole organization to a halt. Its cost for innovation, however, is clear: an initiative succeeds in one unit, fails to travel to others, and its value remains confined to whoever happened upon it. This explanation converges with what Clark found when he studied five European universities that had successfully transformed into entrepreneurial universities and identified five elements they shared ( Clark, 1998 ) , as shown in Figure 20.1. A strengthened steering core Leadership able to set direction and connect the parts An expanded developmental periphery Units that reach beyond traditional departmental boundaries to work with the outside world A diversified funding base Multiple sources rather than reliance on a single one A stimulated academic heartland Departments and colleges themselves adopt the orientation and take part in it An integrated entrepreneurial culture Shared values that bind the parts together Figure 20.1 Elements of the transformation into an entrepreneurial university, adapted from Clark (1998) . The fourth element is the key to the opening case. Clark stressed that peripheral units, such as centers and incubators, are not sufficient on their own, and that transformation is complete only when the academic heartland, the departments and colleges where teaching and research take place, embraces it. The university in the opening case built its periphery and neglected its heartland: a lab in the middle of campus, and classrooms with no connection to it. What is needed, then, is the design of deliberate connection points among these systems while each retains its own identity, since merging them into a single unit would strip them of their flexibility. Connection points mean that each unit knows what comes before it and what comes after; that formal education counts some of what the student accomplishes outside it; and that units share information about the student with the student's consent. One possible form of such connection is to view the scattered units from the student's own vantage point, as stations along a single journey the student travels, as Figure 20.2 illustrates. search.s: 20.4 The everyday environment: classroom and administration
search.t: A university may have well-integrated innovation units, yet its students spend most of their time in an environment that does not invite them to think: a lecture delivered, an assignment that measures memorization, an exam that rewards the single right answer. A staff member may have an idea for improving a procedure and find no one in the office willing to hear it. It is the everyday environment, in the classroom and the office, that ultimately determines whether people experiment or stop trying. This environment begins with the faculty member. In a study of students at several Saudi universities, faculty support in day-to-day teaching was associated with students' confidence in their creative abilities and with their innovative behavior ( Alsamani & Alqahtani, 2026 ) . The faculty member in the classroom is the point in the ecosystem closest to every student, and the course is the gateway through which everyone passes. A systematic review of creative learning environments, mainly in school education, identifies recurring features: flexible use of space and time, availability of materials, learning outside the classroom, play-based approaches that give learners a degree of autonomy, respectful relationships between teacher and learner, opportunities for peer collaboration, partnerships with outside organizations, awareness of learners' needs, and planning not bound by rigid templates ( Davies et al., 2013 ) . Most of these features require neither buildings nor budgets; what they require is a faculty member who sees students as partners in learning. This environment is most visible in student assignments . Research on high-impact educational practices has shown that practices such as undergraduate research projects, service learning, internships and capstone projects are associated with deeper engagement and better learning ( Kuh, 2008 ) . By contrast, a qualitative study with teachers of the gifted found that a focus on grades and standardized tests narrows the space available for creativity ( Alsamani, 2019 ) , and an assignment that measures memorization alone may reproduce this barrier at the university. Turning some assignments into projects that address real problems makes the course a channel for capturing problems and ideas, and makes the innovation unit an extension of the classroom. This can take many forms, from a project within an existing course to a common course in creativity and entrepreneurship assessed through a project; diagnosis determines which of these suits the university. This support also needs to accommodate differences among students. The high academic achiever differs from the student who is creative in a performance domain such as the arts, design or programming, and both differ from the innovator who produces a tangible project or prototype. The most likely to be overlooked is the gifted student whose abilities are not reflected in their GPA, because systems that see nothing but grades do not see them. An environment that treats everyone by a single standard loses some of them without knowing it. Administration is part of this environment. A decision delayed for no reason, a response given without explanation, a procedure that requires the person with an idea to obtain one approval after another: these are messages that teach students, faculty and staff that initiative is a burden. A university that celebrates innovation at its events and then obstructs it in its procedures teaches more through its procedures than through its rhetoric.

search.s: 20.5 Motivation and recognition in the university system
search.t: People learn what an organization values from what it counts and rewards, more than from what it proclaims. One reason students are slow to take up what innovation units offer is that their effort there appears nowhere: not in their academic transcript, not on a certificate, not in what they present to employers. Recognition holds a special place for the gifted and for innovators. Saudi innovative entrepreneurs described a supportive community as one that begins by acknowledging the innovator's distinctiveness and valuing their talent, then invests in them, enables their initiatives, and offers them a flexible environment in which to build their innovative identity (Alsamani, 2026 [Arabic]) . The aim is for students to feel that innovation is an integral part of their university journey: that they are invited to it, welcomed in it, and valued for it. Forms of recognition are many, and they need not be costly: a record issued by the university documenting the student's participation in projects and challenges alongside the academic transcript; micro-credentials recognizing specific competencies acquired in a short program ( OECD, 2021 ) ; a minor that complements the student's major; and an annual day on which students showcase what they have accomplished with their supervisors. Each university chooses from these, or from others, whatever fits its own regulations. Recognizing faculty effort matters no less than recognizing student effort. A faculty member who turns a course into a space for innovation and supervises real projects puts in more effort than traditional teaching demands. If the evaluation and promotion system does not count this effort, the orientation remains dependent on the enthusiasm of a few individuals, and it ends when they move on or burn out. One possible form of motivation here is for faculty members to enter student projects as partners, in addition to their role as assessors: co-supervising a team, bringing along a problem from their own research area, and sharing in whatever results, whether a publication, a patent or a prototype. The student gains a mentor close to their work, and the faculty member gains live research questions and junior colleagues from whom they learn as much as they teach. This is completed by details that cost little: naming the supervisor alongside the team when projects are showcased, counting the supervision in the faculty member's performance file, and granting protected time for this work.

Many initiatives in universities begin with enthusiasm: a successful competition, a program that draws strong participation, a faculty member who turns a course into a space for innovation. Then, after a year or two, they decline: the person in charge moves on, the initial funding runs out, or priorities shift. Continuity does not follow automatically from initial success. Wiltsey Stirman and colleagues reviewed one hundred and twenty-five studies on the sustainability of programs and innovations after implementation and found that few of the studies that measured it recorded full continuation of the programs, and that sustainability is shaped by the characteristics of the innovation itself, the organizational context, the capacities available to it in funding, staff and champions, and the processes and interactions among the parties involved ( Wiltsey Stirman et al., 2012 ) . This means that continuity must be designed from the start. An initiative that rests on one person ends when that person leaves, and one that rests on exceptional funding ends when the funding stops. An initiative that enters the regular systems, however, by being written into study plans, having the effort of those who work on it counted in evaluations, receiving a line in the recurring budget, and being measured among the university's indicators, survives the departure of its founders. This is what institutionalization means: the initiative becomes part of the normal way of working, and so it continues after its founders' enthusiasm has cooled. Institutionalization does not mean keeping every initiative forever. Some initiatives are better stopped when they do not achieve what they were meant to, and this is part of portfolio management. The question that distinguishes healthy continuity is this: does the initiative continue because it produces value, or because no one has decided to stop it?

In the preceding sections we considered the faculty member as teacher and the staff member within their administrative environment; this section addresses the faculty member as researcher and the staff member as innovator in university services. The university has three missions, teaching, research and community service, and each is a source of innovation. Etzkowitz and Leydesdorff described the university in the knowledge economy as one of three parties, alongside government and industry, whose roles overlap in producing innovation ( Etzkowitz & Leydesdorff, 2000 ) . An ecosystem confined to students overlooks two other parties within the university itself: the faculty member as researcher, and the staff who run its services. Faculty researchers: from research to impact Many universities tend to measure their contribution to innovation by patents and by startups spun out of their research. A broad review of the literature on university–industry relations shows that this picture is narrow. What researchers call academic engagement , such as joint research with external organizations, contract research, consulting and informal relationships, is more widespread among faculty than commercialization, and closer to their regular research work. Faculty engage in it mostly to obtain resources and questions that serve their research agendas ( Perkmann et al., 2013 ) . This means that a university that sees nothing of research innovation but patents overlooks most of what its faculty actually contribute. The shortest route to research impact may be a real problem that an organization in the region brings to a research team ready to take it on. Ways of supporting this include counting joint research and consulting in evaluation and promotion, simplifying contracting procedures with external organizations, and linking the university's research priorities to the problems of its region. Staff: a university that innovates in its own work The university is also an organization that delivers services: admissions and registration, housing, libraries, e-services, and financial and administrative procedures. What this book has said about managing innovation in organizations applies to it as it does to any service organization: capturing problems from beneficiaries, managing ideas, piloting, and measurement. The staff members who live these procedures daily know best where the waste lies, and the students who pass through them know best what they suffer from them. It is a paradox for a university to call on its students to innovate while processing their requests through procedures that have not been reviewed in years. A university that practices innovation in its daily work teaches by example what its courses teach by explanation. What was said about motivating faculty holds for staff as well: what motivates them most is inexpensive, such as crediting an idea to its originator, involving them in implementing it, and showing its effect on student services.

search.s: 20.8 Governance that moves people and ideas between units
search.t: To turn this approach into practice, the university needs a unit responsible for integration. One possible form is a strategic innovation unit reporting directly to the university president, whose task is to build the innovation strategy from within using the approach set out in this chapter, to connect the scattered parts, and to monitor and adjust implementation. This unit leaves initiatives to their owners and to existing units; its value lies solely in direction and integration. The initiatives it may support differ from one university to another according to their strengths and needs. Here we gather, from tools presented in the book's chapters, what makes an orchestrating unit effective, whatever its form: A strategy from within: search fields that arise from the university's strengths and the problems of its region, are aligned with national priorities, and are expressed in language everyone understands and helps to build. A shared portfolio: a single entry point for ideas, shared gates, movement of an initiative between units according to its stage, and a reasoned response by an announced date. Measuring flow: indicators that track the movement of students and ideas between units, the courses that include innovation projects, and students' confidence in their creative abilities; these say more about the state of the ecosystem than the number of events each unit holds on its own. Total cost: calculating what each unit costs and what it delivers, before any new unit is established. A clear policy on ownership of student ideas: one that encourages students to develop their ideas within the ecosystem. Partnerships that bring in real problems: with government agencies and companies in the region. The most important characteristic of this governance is that it be dynamic : that it review itself periodically, adjust what does not work, and expand what succeeds, as the iterative adaptation approach suggests. A strategy written once and implemented unchanged for years reproduces the logic of the borrowed model, even if it was written from within. Principle A university innovation ecosystem is measured by the number of people, students, faculty and staff alike, who found their way from problem to idea to experiment, and by what they felt along the way, more than by the number of units the university has created.

An ecosystem is not transformed all at once. Figure 20.3 proposes a three-phase logic that applies phased scaling and pull-based scaling. What is fixed in this logic is the order of the phases and the question each phase asks. The initiatives that fill them, and the duration of each phase, are determined by each university's diagnosis. The initiatives mentioned in this chapter are examples to aid thinking, and each should be adapted to what the diagnosis reveals. Phase one Understanding and connecting Diagnosis from within using the questions in Table 20.1 A map of existing units, the cost of each, and what each delivers A search for successful attempts within the university Formulating an understandable strategy with stakeholder participation Designating a unit responsible for integration, and its decision rights Phase two Limited experimentation Selecting one or two initiatives from among those the diagnosis revealed Trying them on a small scale with willing faculty and students Linking them to existing units rather than creating a new one Measuring their impact, then adjusting or stopping them Phase three Scaling and institutionalization Scaling what has proven its impact through attraction and persuasion Embedding it in the systems: study plans, records, and evaluation and promotion Regular partnerships with the region Periodic review of the strategy in light of what the university has learned Figure 20.3 A proposed roadmap for building a university innovation ecosystem: the logic of the phases is fixed, while each university determines their content. Prepared by the author. This roadmap means that the first thing a university does is understand what it already has and connect it, before creating any new unit. In the first phase it may discover that it has more entities than it needs, and fewer connections than it needs between those entities and its students. That discovery alone may save it millions that would otherwise have been spent on yet another isolated entity. Here the threads of the book come together in a single institution: it starts from the problem before the model, and from people, students, faculty and staff, before buildings, and it builds the ecosystem as connections before building it as entities. A university that does this becomes an innovative institution in its own right, not only one that graduates innovators.

search.s: Chapter tool: diagnosing the university innovation ecosystem
search.t: Use this tool with a team that includes representatives of leadership, departments, existing units and students. Rate each dimension at one of three levels: absent, partial or established. Then choose just two dimensions to work on in the first year, giving priority to those that lie in the academic heartland, that is, the departments and colleges. Chapter tool Diagnosing the university innovation ecosystem Dimension Diagnostic question Rating Next step Strategy from within Do the innovation arenas arise from the university's strengths and the problems of its region? Clarity of strategy Can students, faculty and staff name the university's innovation priorities? Did they take part in building them? Integration across systems Do the innovation units, gifted-student services and departments know what the others offer? Does formal education count any of what the student accomplishes outside it? The student journey Does the student know where to take an idea? How many steps does it take to reach someone who can help? The everyday environment How many courses include projects that address real problems? Do administrative offices respond to ideas by an announced date and with a reasoned reply? Faculty support Do students feel that their professors encourage their ideas? Is faculty effort counted? Recognition and documentation Does the student's innovative effort appear in a record or certificate? Continuity Do existing initiatives depend on individuals or on exceptional funding? Has the total cost of each unit been calculated? Researchers and staff Is faculty research engagement with external organizations counted? Is there a channel for staff ideas on improving services? Measurement Does the university measure flow and impact, or the activity of each unit in isolation? Partnerships Do real problems from the region reach the university on a regular basis?

Under ambiguity, universities tend to imitate the models of successful universities, transferring the forms without the capabilities that make them work. A university innovation strategy begins with a diagnosis of the university's strengths and needs, and it does its work when it is understood, persuasive and shared among students, faculty and staff. Innovation units, gifted-student services and formal education generally operate as parallel, loosely coupled systems; the remedy is to design deliberate connection points among them that preserve each one's flexibility. The transformation is complete only when the university's academic heartland embraces it. The everyday environment, in the classroom, in student assignments and in administrative procedures, is what determines whether people experiment or give up. People learn what an organization values from what it counts and rewards. Appreciation and recognition hold a special place for the gifted and for innovators, and most forms of recognition cost little. After its initial success, an initiative needs designed continuity, achieved by embedding it in the regular systems, while stopping whatever does not produce value. The university innovation ecosystem extends beyond students: faculty researchers contribute through engagement with external organizations, not only through patents, and staff have a role in improving the university's own services. The ecosystem needs a unit responsible for integration that measures flow between units, reviews itself periodically, and is built in phases: understanding and connecting, then limited experimentation, then scaling and institutionalization. The initiatives mentioned in this chapter are examples whose relevance is judged by each university's own diagnosis. Key Terms Mimetic isomorphism Mimetic isomorphism The tendency of organizations, under ambiguity, to imitate organizations they regard as successful or legitimate. Isomorphic mimicry Isomorphic mimicry Adopting the forms of successful organizations without the capabilities that make them work. Problem-driven iterative adaptation Problem-driven iterative adaptation An approach that builds solutions locally, starting from problems, through continuous experimentation, learning and adaptation. Academic heartland Academic heartland The departments and colleges where teaching and research take place, as distinct from peripheral units. Loose coupling Loose coupling A condition in which units respond to one another while each retains its independence, so that what happens in one carries over to the others only to a small degree. Institutionalization Institutionalization Embedding an initiative in an organization's regular systems so that it continues without depending on the enthusiasm of individuals. Student innovator journey Student innovator journey An extended pathway that connects university units around what the student needs at each stage. Academic engagement Academic engagement Faculty collaboration with external organizations through joint or contract research or consulting, as distinct from the commercialization of research. Micro-credential Micro-credential Formal recognition of specific competencies acquired in a short educational program. Review and Discussion Questions What is the difference between learning from other universities' experiences and isomorphic mimicry of them? Understanding Ask ten students, faculty and staff at your university about its innovation priorities, and compare their answers with what the strategy states. What does the gap reveal? Analysis Apply Clark's five elements to your university or educational institution, and identify the weakest. Analysis Map the student innovator journey at your university as it is today, and identify the station at which most students drop off. search.s: Conclusion: Innovation management as an integrated system
search.t: Conclusion Innovation management as an integrated system We opened this book with a question: how does an organization move from scattered initiatives that celebrate innovation to a sustained capability to produce it? In this conclusion we draw together the answer the twenty chapters have offered, then pause at the limits of that answer and the open questions it leaves for research. What ties the chapters together? To a reader who takes its chapters one at a time, the book may look like a collection of adjacent topics: leadership, strategy, culture, governance, experimentation, measurement. In truth, they are parts of a single picture resting on three pillars that we set out in the preface, and it is now clear how the chapters are distributed among them. First pillar The problem Innovation starts from a priority need, and the idea is a hypothesis for solving it. This pillar defines the “what” and the “why.” Chapters: 1, 4, 11, 12, 13 Second pillar People The innovator, with their motivation and needs; the leader who shapes their environment; and the people who adopt what is created. Chapters: 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 15 Third pillar The system What connects people to the problem and turns effort into repeatable results. Chapters: 5, 6, 10, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19 Value Achieved when a motivated person meets a clear problem within a system that enables them. Chapter 20 applies all three pillars together to the university. Figure C.1 The book's three pillars and the chapters that address them. The pillars were linked by a concept that recurred in different guises: autonomy within boundaries . Leadership and the system define the problem, the goal and the constraints, while people own the way to the solution. The concept appeared in Chapter 3 as a leadership principle, in Chapter 4 as search fields and challenge questions, in Chapter 8 as necessary tensions within culture, in Chapter 10 as decision rights, and in Chapter 12 as solution requirements that leave the form of the solution open. It is the practical formula through which the pillar of people meets the pillar of the problem without either overwhelming the other. Ten takeaways The yield of the chapters can be distilled into ten takeaways: Innovation is an implemented outcome that creates value. An idea that never reaches use remains, at best, a source of learning. Chapter 1 The innovation journey begins with understanding the problem, and the time spent on this understanding is the least costly and most consequential stage of the journey. Chapters 11 and 17 People are the heart of the system. Innovators have needs, foremost among them recognition and opportunity, and a system that does not meet them stays hollow however much is spent on it. Chapters 7 and 8 Culture is shaped by what happens after the first failure and the first objection, more than by stated values. Chapter 8 The absence of a decision is more dangerous than a wrong decision; a reasoned response teaches the person with the idea, while silence teaches them to stop trying. Chapters 5 and 10 The value of an experiment lies in the learning it makes possible; an experiment designed so that it cannot fail, or run under ideal conditions, says little about reality. Chapter 14 To endure, a good solution needs a model to carry it and an owner to champion it, and ownership is built from the start of the journey. Chapters 13 and 15 Administrative mandates produce compliance; conviction produces adoption. Chapter 15 Organizations become what they measure; it is therefore more useful to measure what happens to people's ideas than how many ideas they submit. Chapter 16 The system is built from within, from the organization's own strengths and needs, and it requires a strategy that is understood and shared, along with connections among its components that ensure its initiatives continue.
